items.articleBody:
Flacon Cargo Module turns SHIPPING CONTAINER INTO MICRO-CABIN

 

Designed by architects Evgeny Makarenko and Andris Shneps-Shneppe, this 24-sqm micro-cabin transforms an intermodal steel shipping container into a self-contained, relocatable residential module. Located within the ‘Derevnya’ creative community, an experimental rural settlement established by the Flacon Design Factory team, the project accommodates a double bedroom, kitchen, living area with a fireplace, and a full shower room within a compact footprint.

all images ©Evgeny Makarenko

 

 

BIRCH PLYWOOD SHELL INTEGRATES FLUSH JOINERY AND BUILT-IN FURNITURE

 

The interior is lined in an unbroken shell of hand-selected, second-grade (BB) birch plywood, chosen for its natural grain variations. Built-in furniture, work surfaces, and concealed storage integrate directly into the wall and ceiling planes to leave the central circulation path clear. Wall panels are installed using a hidden mounting system with flush joints, eliminating exposed fasteners and hardware to reduce visual clutter. A semi-matte lacquer finish reflects natural light entering through an expansive glazed end-wall, which connects the indoor living space directly to an outdoor wooden terrace. Fitted with radiant floor heating, the off-site prefabricated cabin, designed by the collaborative team between architects Evgeny Makarenko and Andris Shneps-Shneppe, was completed in two and a half months.

the 24-sqm micro-cabin is converted from an intermodal steel freight container the unit is engineered as a self-contained, relocatable home that can be transported between sites

 
 

 
 
 
 

the exterior retains the industrial corrugated steel profile of the original shipping container

 
 

 

the interior is lined with hand-selected BB-grade birch plywood panels a semi-matte lacquer finish highlights the natural grain of the birch plywood surfaces

 
 

 
 
 
 

the open-plan living area includes a compact fireplace and integrated seating

 
 

 

a double bedroom occupies the rear section of the shipping container layout large glazed openings connect the interior living zone with the surrounding landscape the kitchen module is built flush into the plywood perimeter wall before

 

project info:

 

name: The Flacon Cargo Module: Rational Integration

architects: Andris Shneps-Shneppe | @andrisshnepsshneppe, Evgeny Makarenko

location: ’Derevnya’ Creative Community by Flacon Design Factory, Moscow, Russia

area: 24 sqm

structural engineer: Evgeny Makarenko

consultants: Anton Brazhnikov, Alexander Makarenko, Mikhail Arutsev

support: Mikhail Arutsev

photographer: Evgeny Makarenko

items.articleBody:
Wer einen Film oder eine Serie schauen möchte, muss dafür nicht zwangsläufig ein Streaming-Abo abschließen. Neben den öffentlich-rechtlichen Mediatheken gibt es weitere Anbieter, die Inhalte kostenlos bereitstellen. Die Suche danach kann allerdings mühsam werden, besonders wenn man noch gar nicht genau weiß, was man eigentlich sehen möchte.

Auch La La Land wird von Kinogrid gefunden

Hier setzt die neue iPhone-App KinoGrid an. Das Angebot des Entwicklers Pascal Boehlen ist seit wenigen Tagen im App Store verfügbar und bündelt kostenlose Filme und Serien verschiedener Plattformen. Die zugehörige Webseite kinogrid.com lässt sich unabhängig davon im Browser verwenden.

Aktuell führt der Dienst über 4.000 Titel von 16 Anbietern auf. Darunter befinden sich die Mediatheken von ZDF und 3sat sowie Angebote von YouTube und Rakuten TV. KinoGrid zeigt dabei nicht nur, wo ein Film verfügbar ist, sondern auch, ob Werbung eingeblendet wird oder eine Registrierung beim jeweiligen Anbieter erforderlich ist.

Gratis-Alarm für vorgemerkte Filme

Anders als klassische Mediathek-Suchmaschinen richtet sich KinoGrid auch an Nutzer, die sich erst einmal inspirieren lassen möchten. Ein Feed präsentiert Filme und Serien, die sich anschließend auf einer persönlichen Merkliste sammeln lassen. Ein Benutzerkonto ist dafür nicht erforderlich.

KinoGrid liefert Bewertungen, Cover und Synopsen

Interessant ist der sogenannte Gratis-Alarm. Wer einen bestimmten Film sehen möchte, kann diesen vormerken und sich benachrichtigen lassen, sobald er bei einem der erfassten Anbieter kostenlos verfügbar wird. Damit dreht KinoGrid die übliche Suche gewissermaßen um: Nicht der Nutzer muss regelmäßig nachsehen, sondern die App meldet sich bei einer passenden Gelegenheit.

Für bereits verfügbare Inhalte lassen sich zudem Erinnerungen einrichten, bevor diese wieder aus dem kostenlosen Angebot verschwinden.

Ablaufdaten statt verschwundener Favoriten

Gerade bei den öffentlich-rechtlichen Mediatheken ist die Verfügbarkeit einzelner Titel häufig zeitlich begrenzt. KinoGrid führt deshalb eine eigene Übersicht mit auslaufenden Angeboten und nennt das jeweilige Ablaufdatum.

Auch die Verfügbarkeit behält KinoGrid im Blick

Nach Angaben des Betreibers stammen diese Informationen aus den Schnittstellen der Anbieter und werden täglich überprüft. Am 23. Oktober listet der Dienst 214 Titel, deren Verfügbarkeit innerhalb der kommenden 30 Tage endet. Für die nächsten sieben Tage werden aktuell rund 60 auslaufende Angebote angezeigt.

KinoGrid ergänzt damit bestehende Lösungen wie MediathekViewWeb, das insbesondere die Suche und den Download von Mediatheken-Inhalten erleichtert. Auch die Mediatheken-Suchmaschine Vavideo bietet bereits eigene Anwendungen für Apple-Geräte an.

Ohne Konto Nutzbar? KinoGrid listet anbieter

KinoGrid setzt dagegen stärker auf die Entdeckung kostenloser Inhalte und darauf, gewünschte Filme nicht aus den Augen zu verlieren. Gerade für Nutzer, die mehrere Mediatheken und werbefinanzierte Streamingangebote im Blick behalten möchten, ist das eine praktische Ergänzung.

★ iPhone-Ticker bei Google bevorzugen ★

Der Beitrag KinoGrid: Neue iPhone-App findet kostenlose Filme und Serien Wurde zuerst auf iphone-ticker.de veröffentlicht.

items.title: What It Was Like to See Nina Simone at the Village Gate, c. 1961
items.subtitle: An announcement interrupted the hum and buzz of audience conversation: “At this time, ladies and gentlemen, the Village Gate takes the greatest ple…

items.articleBody:
An announcement interrupted the hum and buzz of audience conversation: “At this time, ladies and gentlemen, the Village Gate takes the greatest pleasure in presenting the amazing Miss Nina Simone.” Fresh on the heels of cutting short a run at the Round Table in New York City because of noisy audiences, Simone stepped out onto the raised stage and her presence set the tone. She was taking control in her personal and professional life. The whistles and applause on the recording of the concert bleed into a song to a love, “Just in Time.” She sang, “Just in time you found me just in time. / Before you came my time was running low.” She was expressing gratitude to a romantic partner who had rescued her from loneliness. She could just as well have been thanking the Village Gate for being a dependable space for her artmaking during the past three years.

Leading up to the 1962 release of Nina at the Village Gate, she had maintained a grueling schedule of touring and recording. She often found herself rushing from city to city, chasing financial freedom, as her artistic goal of being a classical musician remained out of reach. She released seven albums in four years, beginning with her debut, Little Girl Blue, in 1959. Fans adored her, but their praise was no substitute for the closeness of intimates. Her third live recording, Nina at the Village Gate, offers both a portal to the event and a window into how she constructed her musical and political worlds.

Simone…commanded a room, captivating audiences with unexpected combinations of genres and her ability to surrender herself completely to the music.

Entering the club to hear Simone perform between March 30 and April 27, 1961, felt different than in 1959. In the intervening years, she had performed at the Town Hall and recorded a hit record, At Newport, that included the single “Trouble in Mind”/“Cotton Eyed Joe” that rose through the Billboard Hot 100 R & B singles chart to number 11 and 92, respectively. She had also graced the pages of Ebony magazine; and had appeared on Hugh Hefner’s variety show, Playboy’s Penthouse; the Today show; and The Ed Sullivan Show.

She was a star whose energy radiated through the four hundred or so audience members who each night sat huddled around tables waiting, listening, and watching. Simone not only demanded attention; she commanded a room, captivating audiences with unexpected combinations of genres and her ability to surrender herself completely to the music. Her full-body performance expressed her intentions rather than her audience’s expectations. In the recording from those nights, her set moved from the romantic sound of the Midtown Manhattan Broadway stage, to foreboding Appalachian-influenced blue notes, to an unfurling sonic breakdown at a Southern church revival meeting. Within the Gate she built for herself a place that could gently hold her.

Nina at the Village Gate unfolded in layers: The performance’s moments of familiarity and predictability drew the audience close, while unexpected musical references kept it surprised and at a distance. Sitting near enough to feel Simone’s presence, the audience heard a bass line followed by her striking a soft minor chord on the piano; the sound entered the audience and the space. She sat at the piano and her band formed an arc around her. The musicians included long-time collaborator guitarist Al Schackman, bassist Chris White, and drummer Rob Hamilton. Together they formed an elegant quartet. “Just in Time” from Bells Are Ringing was followed by “He Was Too Good to Me,” a jazz standard with music by Richard Rodgers and lyrics by Lorenz Hart, written for the 1930 musical Simple Simon.

The sound moved from familiar romantic standards to a haunting guitar-backed rendition of Josh White’s version of “House of the Rising Sun.” Bob Dylan recorded the song months after Simone, and in 1964 it became a hit record for the Animals. The song is a cautionary tale about a brothel in New Orleans known for ruining many poor girls. Its speaker has hoped that her life will serve as a warning to her younger sister because, although the speaker’s fate is bound to unfold beneath the rising sun, her sister does not have to follow in her footsteps. Said to be inspired by English folk songs, the Appalachian artists Tom Ashley and Gwen Foster first recorded it in 1933. White released his version in 1942 while he was still involved with the Left.

Miriam Makeba recorded “House of the Rising Sun” in 1960. It is one of five songs in English on her eponymous fourteen-song album. Her rendition situated her as a part of the South African diaspora that drew musical inspiration from Africa as well as from the American folk music scene.

The influence of Black internationalism can also be heard on Simone’s Nina at the Village Gate through the inclusion of that song in the same set as the Black freedom song “Brown Baby”; the song “Zungo,” composed by Nigerian teacher, activist, and drummer Babatunde Olatunji; and the African American spiritual “Children Go Where I Send You.” Freedom songs have a musical tradition in the US and throughout the world: It’s a tradition connected to the spirituals that enslaved Africans sang in the US and that free African Americans, among them the Fisk Jubilee Singers, performed abroad in the nineteenth century. In the US and South Africa, freedom songs also drew on the tradition of work songs and incorporated call-and-response to engage listeners in the performance. Simone’s set at the Gate was itself steeped in that tradition, with folk music sitting alongside the gospel and spiritual songs she had heard in church during her youth, the classical music of her training, and the jazz standards she had perfected in nightclubs. The folk tradition, especially, connected her to international Black freedom movements that emphasized labor conditions as a key part of the struggle.

When Simone sang “Brown Baby,” she invited the example of the composer Oscar Brown Jr. into the room along with the calls for Black pride that always accompanied him. He had contributed to We Insist! Max Roach’s Freedom Now Suite. The audience may have also heard echoes of Mahalia Jackson’s gospel-inspired 1960 recording of the song. As with “House of the Rising Sun,” “Brown Baby” is performed for a future generation, in anticipation of brown children drinking “from the plenty cup.” The singer charges, “I want you to stand up tall and proud / And I want you to speak up clear and loud.” The song ends with a call to action. It expresses the desire for a future where the reward matches the contribution.

In the performance at the Gate, she sang not only to her live audience but also to those who would hear the recording in the future.

“Brown Baby” became a part of Simone’s repertoire. She sang it on October 21, 1960, at a concert that Art D’Lugoff produced for Hunter College. A review of the performance recalled, “At the end of the last group of songs, the audience rose to its feet and would not be satisfied until Miss Simone returned and performed once more for them. She chose for an encore ‘Brown Baby,’ a song which has the feeling and pathos of the Negro’s long struggle for a better life.” With the performance Simone had joined her friends Hansberry and Baldwin, who frequently engaged with and encouraged college students who were on the front lines of the civil rights movement. Through the encore at Hunter College, she spoke specifically to a new generation. In the performance at the Gate, she sang not only to her live audience but also to those who would hear the recording in the future.

“Brown Baby” anticipated the complicated emotional state expressed in Simone’s later recording of “I’m Feeling Good.” Her bluesy rendition of “Brown Baby” imagines the collective comfort of being together, but does so with her familiar haunting sound. When we hear the blues, we know there is no beauty without brutality. In “I’m Feeling Good” the upbeat horns counter the melancholy tone of her voice. In “Brown Baby,” the predominance of her singing with only piano accompaniment intensifies the juxtaposition of pain and promise. As much an acknowledgment of survival as a rallying cry, the song draws out sadness as well as satisfaction from the audience.

On Nina at the Village Gate, she transitions from “Brown Baby” to “Zungo,” a song composed and taught to her by Olatunji for the album. Like her friends Baldwin and Belafonte, he had cultivated a relationship with Martin Luther King Jr., which included visiting him in the South and later attending the March on Washington. In the performance at the Gate, Simone sang “Zungo is my home” in Yoruba, affirming the diasporic nature of her work as early as 1961.

To conclude her performance at the Gate, Simone transformed the nightclub into a Black church, and she returned to a familiar, sturdy foundation reminiscent of the crescendo of sound at the end of her live 1960 concert in Newport, Rhode Island. In the penultimate song at the Gate, “If He Changed My Name,” she offered a dirge of suffering and sacrifice in the service of self-transformation. “Jesus,” she sang, “told me I would go hungry if He changed my name / But I told Jesus it would be all right if He changed my name.” The lyrics point to an understanding that change requires sacrifice. In later years, she accelerated the tempo and intensity of the song in order to emphasize the cost of seeking and realizing a different political order. The potential danger of her political turn came into sharp relief when she gave dimensions to a sound that would envelop the audience. Because Simone’s exposure to global Black freedom movements through her collaboration with Olatunji and friendship with Makeba had brought worlds of possibility into view, she would be all right if the world ended up hating her, as it had Abbey Lincoln before her, for turning away from popular music toward freedom music.

Simone draws her audience further into the gospel tradition with “Children Go Where I Send You.” She asks, Have “you ever been to revival meeting?” Her band members reply slyly, “They don’t know nothing about that,” to which she replies, “I bet you don’t even know what I’m talking about,” as the bass line drives forward and the audience laughs. She clarifies, “Well, you in one right now.” In that moment, Simone has transformed the Gate into a stage of her own for making meaning. The audience came to a famous nightclub to hear a jazz star, but what she has conveyed is that when they arrived at 185 Thompson Street, they entered a sacred place of her divining. Her live performances blurred the lines between theater, church, and concert hall, creating a new artistic space where sound, dance, and oration meet in a constructive arrangement.

_______________________________

items.articleBody:
by Sean Murphy

i.

Here’s the thing about clean-up hitters: they strike out a lot.

Then again, consider some of baseball’s most prodigious home run champions: Barry Bonds, Hank Aaron, and Babe Ruth, the top three, had career batting averages of .298, .305, and .342, respectively. In baseball terms, excellent, but that also means they didn’t hit safely about sixty-to-seventy percent of the time they stepped to the plate. And these are the best of the best. Making a career at writing is not dissimilar to becoming a big league ball player: a hit every third attempt might enable you to remain employed, to call yourself a professional.

Thom Jones, in this umpire’s opinion, struck out a lot. He was a fastball hitter, and when he saw a meatball down the middle, he could get hold of it. Epilepsy, punch-drunk boxers, and wounded men battling addiction (to drugs, to drink, to bloodshed) comprised his sweet spot, and he returned to it often, albeit with increasingly diminished returns. When he stepped outside his comfort zone, the results could range from embarrassing to unreadable, and those moments occur with distressing frequency in his second (Cold Snap) and especially third (Sonny Liston Was a Friend of Mine) collections.

With very few exceptions, no honest (or sane) writer would quibble with a publishing history that confirms every third or fourth story is generally regarded as a home run, or a minor classic. Indeed, many of us would giddily settle on completing just one worth remembering. More, a great many writers would be perfectly content with every third or fourth story being an extra base hit. And then there are the thousands (millions?) of undiscovered writers who would trade years of their lives for a solitary single.

No sane or honest writer would ever want to be measured by their batting average of every published piece, over the course of a career.

You write often, as well as you can, and pray that, with a ton of practice and a little bit of luck, you manage to knock one clean out of the park. Mostly you just hope to make contact; to not strike out. Most of these failures, at least, don’t offend any audience; they languish—half-finished drafts, false starts and unattainable visions—in desk drawers or recycling bins.

Most writers, aware of the long odds and erratic whims of both publishers and potential readers, do their best to craft honest work considered more or less within the bounds of conventional taste, trusting the material is at once sufficiently unique and, for lack of a better word, straightforward. That’s to say, most writers (and it could be argued whether this applies more to obscure authors or established, even famous ones) are singles hitters. This is at once a function of the way publishing works (or doesn’t work—another topic altogether), and the internal battle most genuine writers wage that weighs originality vs. acceptance.

Note: I’m not talking about writing publishable work; writing that, for practical purposes, constitutes a single. I’m referring specifically to writers who, through ego, ability, or ambition—or some combination of all three—set out to transcend cliché and write something unadulterated, that breaks some type of mold and becomes a new standard of sorts; something inimitable that itself will be emulated by future writers.

ii.

Thom Jones, like many famous writers, resists easy interpretation. A good chunk of his work is redundant, repurposed rather than convincing variations on a theme, and his penchant for stilted dialogue and ham-fisted histrionics mars some of his output. (Considering the publications he appeared in and the editors he worked with, it’s at once amusing and appalling to count the clichés throughout his three collections.) Another good chunk is serviceable, solid: a string of singles and the occasional double. He even hit a triple or two (These are recorded in Cold Snap; Sonny Liston Was a Friend of Mine is extremely tough going; taken on their own, the stories are underwhelming; compared to the previous collections they are somewhat excruciating…it can be debated that Jones burned out, lost his edge or, for any number of documented health reasons, couldn’t produce like he once did). But what separates him, and makes him worth celebrating, is that he had the audacity—and the skill—to make contact in historic fashion. We’re talking home runs like Carlton Fisk in ’75, Kirk Gibson in ’88, and Joe Carter with the walk-off World Series shot in ’93.

As it happens, all of these occur in his game-changing debut collection The Pugilist at Rest. A remarkable effort that deservingly became a National Book Award Finalist, it established Jones as a writer who, like Roy Hobbs, seemingly came out of nowhere, fully formed as a superstar. The title story’s publication is every writer’s dream; that one-in-a-billion fantasy: rescued from the slush pile and published by The New Yorker. This feat alone would more than satisfy most aspiring authors, but Jones, having alternately labored in obscurity and deferred his dream with years of substance abuse and self-sabotage, was ready for the big call-up. Unlike his next two books, there’s not a solitary stinker in the bunch (and the sheer quality of the winners elevates the handful of more pedestrian efforts). More significantly, of the eleven stories, (at least) six of them are no doubt dingers. Sabermetrically speaking, that’s well over .500, enough to ensure Jones legend status, one of the seminal debuts in the second-half of the 20thCentury.

(To belabor the Hobbs metaphor, had Jones simply produced Pugilist, at 48, and then strode off into the sunset, he really might be considered the Wonderboy of short fiction.)

Opinions will—and should—vary, but in this critic’s estimation, six of these stories could be anthologized and studied by anyone hoping to ascertain what makes fiction memorable; what makes it resonate, what makes it work. The aforementioned title story, “Mosquitoes,” and “Rocket Man” (allegedly Jones’s personal favorite) all clear the fence and will impart delight (and envy) upon repeated readings.

With “A White Horse,” Jones manages to shoehorn Dostoyevsky, Hunter S. Thompson, and the New Testament into a compressed tour de force—as well as any other story, this one best captures the outcast-in-search-of-epiphany. As a metaphor, the wealthy but unsettled protagonist shelling out hundreds to save a dying horse he encounters (à la Nietzsche) in the slums of Bombay seems at once familiar and surreal—Jones deftly combines pathos and desperation in the service of a postmodern parable, cutting it (crucially) with humor.

Another masterpiece, and grand slam, is the story of a dying woman entitled “I Want to Live!” Older (but not that old), semi-estranged mother dying, alone, of cancer. Sound familiar? It’s to Jones’s considerable credit that he takes a potentially hackneyed subject too often played for crocodile tear aesthetics, and deals, indelibly, with the heaviest—and trickiest—of issues: dread of death, longing for love, fear of a life wasted, et cetera.

Her friends came by. It was an effort to make small talk. How could they know? How could they know what it was like? They loved her, they said, with liquor on their breath. They had to get juiced before they could stand to come by! They came with casseroles and cleaned for her, but she had to sweat out her nights alone.

In less than thirty pages, Jones modernizes “The Death of Ivan Ilyich,” without the lugubrious sermonizing and melodrama Tolstoy, even at his best, struggled to suppress. It’s an unflinching, albeit harrowing tour of a helpless but not completely hopeless woman’s death courtesy The Big C. In addition to merely working, as literature, it will console one with intimate experience with the disease or prepare uninitiated readers for something too many families are forced to confront.

 “The Black Lights,” a novel in miniature, could work as a longer piece (the writing is so unsullied, the characters so memorable, the recurring tension so concentrated), but illustrates the curious, often ineffable magic of the short form. There’s enough history related through flashback to provide a sense of who the narrator is, but the action occurs in the present; we have no idea what the future holds, nor should we. In one of many astonishing passages, a Vietnam veteran stuck in a neuropsych ward to recover from anxiety-induced epileptic seizures describes his first experience in a straitjacket (after driving the fellow patients to distraction with his paranoia that a large homicidal rabbit is lying in wait beneath his bed):

I forced myself to lie still, and it seemed that my brain was filled with sawdust and that centipedes, roaches, and other insects were crawling through it. I could taste brown rabbit fur in my teeth. I had a horror that the rabbit would come in the room, lie on my face, and suffocate me.

Finally released, months later, our anti-hero exits the base in one of the more memorable—and satisfying—endings of any modern short story. A bit of dialogue he exchanges with a fellow Marine typifies Jones, at the height of his powers:

“…You want to know something?”

“What’s that?”

“I stole this fucking car. Hot-wired the motherfucker.”

“Far out,” I said. “Which way you going?”

“As far as five bucks in gas will take me.”

“I got a little money. Drive me to Haight-Ashbury?”

“Groovy. What are you doing, man, picking your nose?”

“Just checking for cockroaches,” I said weakly.

This is a story that does everything the best writing aspires to do: it stays read. It’s capable of changing the way you read, and understand, subsequent work. (In terms of Jones’s work, he arguably set the bar too high to approach that level again himself, but in the final analysis what matters is that he ever got there in the first place.)

iii.

To once again invoke Tolstoy, it could be said that all writers are unhappy, but each writer is unhappy in his or her own way.

Thom Jones, by any benchmark, had a difficult life before, during, and after The Pugilist at Rest was published (1993). An absent father who later committed suicide in a mental institution, Marine boot camp, boxing injuries resulting in epilepsy: these themes, which recur like grisly hallucinations in his fiction, all derived from his actual life. Indeed, by the time he was twenty, he’d already experienced the trauma and tragedy that would inform his best work.

Like Raymond Carver, Jones excels at depicting the seedier side of life, black and blue faces with blue collars as opposed to suits and suburban existential howling. Like Charles Bukowski, it’s not difficult to detect a clear line connecting the characters, situations, and the person writing about them. Like Tim O’Brien, it’s not so much that his personal history serves as impetus but rather, the obsessions of memory, pain, and regret are at once a unifying theme and creative cul-de-sac.

(Put another way, he was the anti-Updike; it’s at once refreshing and a little heroic that his work bulldogged its way into The New Yorker, unapologetic—but indubitably worthy—turds in that pristine, if sanitized literary punch bowl. Reading him in this century, he’s also the anti-MFA stereotype, meaning his writing illustrates an individual whose work reflects a life and tutelage extending beyond workshops and undergraduate experiences.)

Jones circled around these washed-up palookas, chemically altered outlaws, and quiet nobodies in search of a rock to crawl under because he knew them; he was (or had been) one of them himself. His most compelling pieces seem unforced and unfettered because, while undeniably autobiographical, Jones used fiction as exploration, not therapy. In “The Pugilist at Rest,” the narrator invokes Theogenes, “the greatest of gladiators,” who fought—and won—fourteen hundred and twenty-five life and death battles. The statue commemorating this fighter (an image of which decorates the front cover) becomes the central metaphor not only for this story, but the entire collection. Indeed, the notion of a scarred and skillful brawler being called into the ring, yet again, to provide a spectacle, a distraction or voyeuristic pleasure, is an appropriate allegory for Jones’s career.

Jones once remarked that “in the act of writing I’m not Thom Jones. And it’s such a relief to not be Thom Jones.” How inspiring, how refreshing, how sad. It doesn’t seem a stretch to imagine that Jones had a strenuous life, even after 1993, and the inability to retain his title simply means he’s more Jake LaMotta and less Sugar Ray Robinson—not a one-shot wunderkind but a career scrapper who banged back at a world intent on beating the shit out of him. Whether or not he had a great deal more to write, the only fact that matters is that he took his one shot and made it count. Hopefully he redeemed a great deal of disillusionment with that triumph, but regardless, he had to know he’d escaped the most ignoble fate: obscurity.

His refusal to quit and unwillingness to sentimentalize his past is a testament to his character (that he wasn’t obliged to sensationalize his past is testament to the extraordinary obstacles he overcame). That he plugged away, before and after he was famous, effectively turning his vocation into one long battle is a testament to his resolve, and artistic integrity. And while he wrote about manly men doing macho shit, Jones was the anti-Hollywood writer in the sense that he understood the sadness and futility of fighting, boozing, womanizing, and hatred directed inward or outward. He learned how to write the way he learned how to survive: the hard way, with no short cuts and few excuses. His ability to craft unforgettable tales of otherwise forgettable people will endure as the ultimate testament to his distinct talent and warrior’s heart.

items.articleBody:
Holmes's charm is still unsettling on screen: Even knowing the full Theranos story, the documentary captures how effectively Holmes plants seeds of doubt—journalists who interviewed her in her prime later admitted she had fooled them completely.

Peer review isn't a perfect safety net: Science's built-in fact-checking system has real cracks—10,000 papers were retracted in 2023 alone, and preprint servers, press releases, and social media now routinely bypass it.

Reporters face the same vulnerability as investors: Even seasoned science journalists rely on trust and expert opinion to vet claims, raising an uncomfortable question: how confident can anyone really be that they wouldn't have fallen for it too
" data-chronoton-post-id="1147610" data-chronoton-expand-collapse="1" data-chronoton-analytics-enabled="1">

Earlier this week, I attended a screening of You Can See Everything, the buzzy new documentary about the disgraced former biotech CEO Elizabeth Holmes. 

I went in not really knowing what to expect. I’d avoided spoilers (and won’t be giving anything away here, either!). I was wondering what new information this film could reveal, given how familiar many of us are with the Theranos story thanks to years of media coverage, the best-selling book Bad Blood, and the Hulu series The Dropout, starring Amanda Seyfried.

Like many others who have seen the film, I came away feeling unsettled. But not just about Holmes’s fraud and the somewhat disturbing interactions between the subjects. The film reignited a concern I’ve had about covering science for most of my career: Despite our best efforts, we never can actually see everything.

In case you’re rusty on the details, Elizabeth Holmes dropped out of Stanford University in 2003 to run Theranos, a diagnostics company she founded, when she was just 19. She went on to claim that her company had invented a way to run over 100 diagnostic tests on just a few drops of blood.

Holmes raised hundreds of millions of dollars for Theranos, which was valued at $9 billion in 2014. Forbes named her the youngest self-made female billionaire—she was worth $4.5 billion when she was just 30 years old.

Things started to unravel in 2015, when an investigation by the Wall Street Journal raised concerns by former Theranos employees that the tests didn’t work. Some also said that the company’s device had not been tested properly, and that blood samples had been analyzed on machines from other companies instead. MIT Technology Review named it one of the biggest technology failures of 2015.

Forbes had revised Holmes’s worth to $0 by 2016. That year, a damning government report said that the company’s lab was struggling with basic procedures and gave patients results even when they knew they could be wrong.

In 2018, Theranos, Holmes, and former company president Ramesh Balwani were charged with “massive fraud.” In 2022, she was sentenced to a little over 11 years in prison for defrauding investors. She began serving her sentence in May 2023.

It was around a month before this that filmmakers Nathan Fielder, Lance Oppenheim, and their colleagues began documenting Holmes and her partner, Billy Evans, at home with their two young children. I’m not giving anything away when I say it’s an extremely intimate portrayal—at least of how the two adults interact with Fielder, who is also a central character in the film.

As you might know if you’ve seen the trailer, there are plenty of super close-ups. I felt as if I spent most of the film staring straight into the faces of those people. And almost the whole way through, they all seemed to be trying to figure each other out. Holmes is known for her dishonesty, but she invited cameras into her home in an apparent bid to reframe the narrative and position herself as an honest person with an unusual mind. Will anyone believe her?

I couldn’t help feeling some empathy for Holmes, a mother we see preparing to leave her two kids for a lengthy prison sentence. And even though I have long known the facts, Holmes is clearly an effective manipulator. You can see her plant the seeds of doubt in Fielder’s mind. At times, I felt she was convincing me, sitting in my cinema seat. Maybe she really didn’t mean to lie?

But then I remembered how other journalists felt after being taken in by her claims. “I blew it,” Fortune’s Roger Parloff reflected in 2015, a year after profiling Holmes and her company. “I’m pretty sure she lied to me,” STAT’s Matthew Herper wrote recently, having interviewed Holmes in 2015. Even the former employee turned whistleblower Tyler Shultz, who knew the product didn’t work, said that he could “have a five-minute conversation with her and walk away feeling like my work was changing the world,” he said in 2022.

I didn’t cover Theranos in the 2010s. If I’d interviewed Holmes, would I have fallen for it all?

One of the early red flags in the Theranos case was the lack of published, peer-reviewed data. Much of the company’s work was classified as a “trade secret.” Scientists tend to publish their work in journals—a slow process that involves having the work evaluated by often anonymous experts in the field, who provide feedback, highlight questionable conclusions, and often ask for clarification. Peer review is meant to add rigor to the publication process. You should be able to trust published scientific papers.

Except that sometimes you can’t.

Scientists aren’t perfect. Some will exaggerate their results or inflate their importance. Some manipulate data to serve a hypothesis. Sometimes these infractions are caught during peer review, but not always. There are plenty of examples of scientific findings that could never be replicated by other labs and ended up collapsing under the weight of real evidence. Many papers ultimately end up with corrections. Some are withdrawn—10,000 research papers were retracted in 2023.

At any rate, there’s been a shift to sharing research in other ways. Today, many scientists opt to publish their work at preprint servers like arXiv, medRxiv, and bioRxiv before they submit them to established journals. Those outlets bypass peer review. So do company press releases, social media posts, and many conference presentations. And I get a lot of my stories from conversations and interviews.

I’ll admit I’ve looked at a scientific finding and thought: A scientist has just said they’ve done that. How can I be sure they really have?

I like to think that I hold myself to high journalistic standards here, as does everyone at MIT Technology Review. I would never publish a story about some new scientific development without doing my own form of peer review, and asking scientists—ideally people I know and trust—what they think of a new claim. 

But the film is a stark reminder of how easy it can be to fall for an appealing narrative. While most scientists are, I hope, pretty honest, and Holmes is certainly an outlier, we should all continue to interrogate the claims being fed to us. If you’ve seen the film, let me know what you think!

This article first appeared in The Checkup, MIT Technology Review’s weekly biotech newsletter. To receive it in your inbox every Thursday, and read articles like this first, sign up here.

items.title: "Getting people into space is one thing. Creating somewhere they actually want to live is quite another"
items.subtitle:
Photo by Laurian Ghinitoiu

For most of the space age, architects could fantasise freely about building off-world.

items.articleBody:
Photo by Laurian Ghinitoiu

For most of the space age, architects could fantasise freely about building off-world. Inflatable lunar villages and glass Martian domes could be sketched out without anyone having to worry too much about who cleaned the toilets.

That luxury is disappearing as we start to seriously consider the possibility of living in space. Next year, the first commercial space station will be launched – Haven-1 – and will be joined by a second, Axiom, a few months later. 

NASA will return to the moon in 2028 with plans to start building a semi-permanent base. A nuclear reactor will follow by the end of the decade, as might the Chinese, and by the time the International Space Station (ISS) is retired in 2030, there will be tens of private stations available to replace it.

The elegant visions of 2001: A Space Odyssey are now giving way to the messy business of everyday existence

And that's before we talk about Elon Musk and his ambition to create a city of a million people on Mars by the 2050s.

But getting people into space is one thing. Creating somewhere they might actually want to live is quite another. 

That is where architecture comes in, and firms such as Foster + Partners, BIG, SOM (pictured top) and others have already turned their attention to what might be possible beyond Earth. The elegant visions of 2001: A Space Odyssey and the like are now giving way to the messy business of everyday existence and the problems of extraterrestrial construction.

The obvious challenges are formidable but well-rehearsed: how do you shield people from radiation? Where does the oxygen come from? How do you recycle water?

 
 
 
 
 
 
 

 

 Read:
 

 
Space architects are preparing for humanity's return to the moon

 

 
 
 

Engineers have mostly answered these questions. But once people are asked to live somewhere for years rather than just visit, other questions arise. Such as: who gets a window? It may sound trivial. It isn't.

A window in space is both expensive and a potential point of failure. The engineers would prefer a solid metal tube.

Yet astronauts value their views of Earth enormously and "Earth-gazing" is a favourite way to unwind aboard the ISS. In fact, being able to see out is considered essential for morale.

So imagine the first lunar settlement. There are six bedrooms but only two windows. Who gets them? The commander? The tourist who pays the most? Does everybody receive 10 minutes of Earth-gazing a day? 

History should certainly make us wary of who gets to dictate what extraterrestrial living looks like

Or, does the window belong to everyone, because something so precious cannot become private property?

The same applies to almost every spatial decision. Who gets a room with a door? How large is it? Can inhabitants personalise it? Where can somebody go to be alone? Where must they encounter other people? Who controls the thermostat, lighting or music? 

In a lunar base containing 30 people these are potentially bones of contention. There has been at least one stabbing in the Antarctic, so the danger is real. 

And that's before we even decide who gets to run the place. Would you prefer a government body or a corporation like SpaceX or Blue Origin, which, after all, are manufacturing the rockets that are likely to haul people and materials to the moon and Mars?

 
 
 
 
 
 
 

 

 Read:
 

 
SAGA completes astronaut training habitat to simulate life on the moon

 

 
 
 

History should certainly make us wary of who gets to dictate what extraterrestrial living looks like. Take Henry Ford's Fordlandia, established in the Amazon in the 1920s to secure rubber. 

That was conceived not simply as an industrial settlement, but as an attempt to export Ford's version of American life: workers received company housing – segregated, of course – but had prescribed diets and had to follow strict behavioural rules. The American managers had running water and got the best views, while the Brazilians had to rely on wells. 

Copenhagen studio SAGA built a four-bedroom habitation unit to train astronauts for life on the moon. Photo courtesy of SAGA

The company town is an old model: housing, employment, shops and infrastructure controlled by the same organisation. On Earth, at least, you can leave. What does "leaving" mean when the exit is miles across the moon and stepping outside without permission might mean dying?

This matters because the economics of space point towards precisely this danger. The first extraterrestrial settlements will require immense investment. Governments will fund some, but corporations will provide most of the transport, communications and habitats. 

Architects should be arguing about (and hopefully agreeing) extraterrestrial design standards before settlements exist

Commercial necessity can gradually become governance. The East India Company provides an extreme historical precedent: a trading firm that accumulated taxation, administrative and military powers as business slid into tyranny.

Space could easily witness a 21st-century version. Imagine a Martian settlement where one corporation supplies your employment, accommodation, oxygen, water, communications and return ticket. You are simultaneously worker, tenant and customer. Architecture could make that unequal relationship physical, as in Fordlandia.

None of this is an argument against commercial spaceflight. Without private capital, much of the extraordinary acceleration now taking place would be impossible.

Nor can architects wish away physics. A window genuinely is more dangerous than a wall.

 
 
 
 
 
 
 

 

 Read:
 

 
NASA says "living and working on the moon will become reality" after 2032

 

 
 
 

But if we are to start producing extraterrestrial architecture, it must do more than ensure survival. A habitat that maintains oxygen while steadily degrading its inhabitants' mental health has failed. 

Circadian lighting, vegetation, privacy, views, places for leisure and for ritual are not decorations to be value-engineered away. They contribute to people's ability to function and remain sane.

This is why architects should be arguing about (and hopefully agreeing) extraterrestrial design standards before settlements exist. I would argue the time for that is now.

The danger is not that our first extraterrestrial settlements will look insufficiently futuristic. It is that they will reproduce the worst terrestrial arrangements: workers' barracks, gated communities, company towns and luxury enclaves – only this time with airlocks.

If we leave those questions until the rockets arrive, someone else will already have answered them for us

Conversely, architects rarely get to establish the principles of an entire built environment before it exists. Here we can.

We should use that opportunity to ask difficult questions now, while the answers are still cheap. Who owns the habitat? Who can modify it? What constitutes an acceptable home in space? 

What must remain communal? What degree of privacy ensures dignity? And, yes, who gets a window?

If we leave those questions until the rockets arrive, someone else will already have answered them for us. You might not like who that person is.

Jonathan Morrison is an architecture journalist based in London. He was previously the architecture correspondent for The Times. His first book, How to Build a Space Station, was published in September 2026.

If you enjoy reading Dezeen's interviews, opinions and features, subscribe to Dezeen In Depth. Sent on the last Friday of each month, this newsletter provides a single place to read about the design and architecture stories behind the headlines.

items.title: How Did ‘American Gothic’ Become So Iconic? This Art Historian Spent Five Decades Investigating.

items.articleBody:
In need of a couple’s costume this Halloween? Try a calico apron over a dark dress, a low bun with one loose strand, a cameo broach at your throat; dress a partner in overalls and wire-rimmed glasses, holding a three-pronged pitchfork. It won’t take much to be immediately recognizable as the duo from American Gothic, Grant Wood’s 1930 painting and subject of Wanda Corn’s new book, The Couple with the Pitchfork: American Gothic from Easel to Icon. Why, Corn wants to know, did this painting become so iconic?

 Corn, an eminent scholar of American art, has been thinking about this question for five decades. The painting intersected with her own trajectory as an art historian and with her personal history as a descendent of the Midwest: the book includes a photograph of her grandparents posed side-by-side at their home in Indiana, her grandfather in denim overalls, and her grandmother with hair pulled back and a homemade dress. The parallels between the family photograph and American Gothic show how thoroughly Wood, himself raised in Iowa, was tapping in to regional Midwestern identity. Yet a portrait of a midwestern couple is hardly a promising candidate for global fame.

 Of course, the pair in American Gothic aren’t a couple, at least not in Wood’s view. He claimed to have intended the twosome to represent a small-town father and daughter, basing the figures on his sister Nan and his dentist. When he made the painting, Wood was searching for a way of working that would be distinctive to the Midwest. He’d tried his hand at French Impressionism, taking several trips to Paris, and worked as a decorator back home in Cedar Rapids. Growing support for the arts in small town America, funded by philanthropists including the Carnegie Foundation, created more opportunities for Wood to make work that felt characteristic of his region.

 

 

 
 

 
 
 
 

 
 

 
 

 American Gothic marked Wood’s embrace of a new style as an Iowa painter, developing a pictorial language suited to the visual culture of the Midwest. Rather than straightforward realism, Corn shows American Gothic to be the product of a thorough engagement with pattern and form. Vertical lines, from the tines of the pitchfork to the church steeple in the background, organize and order the composition. Round and oval forms—the figures’ long faces, the woman’s brooch, the pattern on the calico, the shape of the man’s ears—create harmony within the scene. Wood identified what he called a “decorative” quality in his subject matter, basic geometries and hard lines that he translated into paint with such precision that the work was taken to be self-evident rather than deeply thought.

 The painting was immediately misunderstood. After winning a prize in a juried exhibition at the Art Institute of Chicago, American Gothic—which reproduced well in newsprint thanks to those straightforward, geometric forms—became a sensation. Labeled by the press as a farmer and his wife, the depiction of the couple found detractors in both Iowans and art critics. Locals saw the pitchfork as outdated—four tines would have been more appropriate—and the woman unforgivably dour. Critics couldn’t place the work, finding it out of step with modernist abstraction. Everyone agreed it was an image of marriage.

 For Corn, this misunderstanding is key to the painting’s success, allowing for endless adaptation of the archetypal form of two figures joined in union. She traces the painting’s influence in both art and popular culture, drawing on a personal archive of hundreds of reappropriations of the work: American Gothics in butter at a state fair, gay American Gothics in support of same-sex marriage, feminist American Gothics showing the woman heading off to work. Surprisingly, for a painting often dismissed as conservative and reactionary, some of the first adopters of its form were Black urban artists who saw the painting in Chicago in the 1930s. (The Art Institute acquired the painting soon after it debuted.) Certain African American artists saw in Wood a model for a self-taught artist from farm country. Reproducing the motif of a couple posed before a family home became a way of telling stories about migration for artists like Walter Ellison.

 Corn’s explanation for American Gothic’s popularity is that it shows the archetype of marriage, a motif that can be traced from Egyptian princes to Etruscan terra cottas to Dutch golden age portraits, rendered in an accessible manner for the modern era. Yet unlike those other examples, beneath the smooth surface of Wood’s painting is a felt unease, a tension that animates the painting and motivates its adaptation. Wood, likely gay, experienced his own failed marriage five years after painting American Gothic. If his aesthetic was one of plainspoken values, he was also singularly able to capture all that goes unsaid when, as is so often the case, reality strains against the expectations of form.

items.articleBody:
A rescued mink from a Utah fur farm Julie Leopo for ProPublica

The strain of bird flu that’s ripped through American barns for the last four years has killed two people who caught it from sick animals. But as far as anyone can tell, humans can’t spread it. The virus has remained a true “bird” flu, tailored to attach to avian cells, not invade human throats and noses, where coughing and sneezing reliably spew droplets. 

Under the right conditions, however, that could change. A single mutation could give the bird flu a foothold in people and spark a pandemic that experts fear could be deadlier than COVID-19. 

For that to happen, this bird flu would likely need to find an intermediate host — an animal vulnerable to viruses that infect both birds and humans. These animals would be crowded together, each infection raising the odds that a new strain could arise through mutation. Then, for that strain to jump across species, it would have to have access to humans and time to spread among them undetected. 

That perfect petri dish exists right now, a ProPublica investigation found. For over two months, an outbreak of bird flu has raged uncontrolled on a Utah farm that raises thousands of mink for fur. Mink have lungs and airways that on a cellular level are remarkably similar to those of people; they have caught and spread other flus and infected some humans with COVID-19. 

Instead of trying to stop the outbreak and prevent it from spilling into humans, state and federal officials have done little except try to keep its existence quiet, our investigation shows. The failure to act amounts to a cascade of missteps flu experts called “irresponsible’’ and “puzzling.’’ One called it “playing with fire.’’

C&T Fenn Farms, a mink fur farm west of Provo, Utah, on Sept. 25 Julie Leopo for ProPublica

Utah agriculture officials learned in mid-August that mink were dying of bird flu on C&T Fenn Farms, about an hour’s drive south from Salt Lake City, according to communications released under the state’s public records law. 

Had poultry been infected, the playbook would have been clear: The strain is so virulent that if a single chicken tests positive, the U.S. government requires farmers to kill the whole flock to protect other farms as well as public health. Poultry farmers are reimbursed for the loss.

But there are no federal rules for how to deal with sick mink. 

Handling Utah’s response was state veterinarian Amanda Price, who sought help from the U.S. Department of Agriculture, which takes the lead on bird flu outbreaks involving poultry and cows. 

USDA officials said they didn’t regulate mink or have a vaccine that was approved to give them. And though officials with the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention spoke with Price’s health department counterparts who were less involved with the outbreak, they never talked to her, and she never reached out.

The threat of spillover has been far from the minds of Utah officials, records and interviews show. Instead, front and center have been the interests of a business raising animals to skin for luxury pelts to ship overseas. 

“It has been devastating,” Price told ProPublica of the outbreak and its impact on the farm’s owner. “This is his life’s work that he’s seeing be destroyed. I really hope that you understand the humanity behind this situation.”

Flu experts were unequivocal that the government should have ordered the farm to cull its mink, as other countries have done. 

But Utah never seriously considered it. A fur trade representative warned Price that doing so would kill the business and, ultimately, the industry. Farms spend decades breeding mink to develop unique genetic lineages. 

“There’s just not a lot of options out there other than kind of sitting and waiting and seeing what happens,” Price said, noting that USDA officials did not urge her to kill the mink or make her feel like bird flu in mink was any riskier than infections in other animals that have caught it, like ducks and cows.

Flu experts found that response surprising.

“Every other country that I’m aware of that has had H5N1 in fur farms, depopulation has happened pretty quickly,” said Tom Peacock, an avian influenza researcher at the Pirbright Institute. “The fact that the first instinct wasn’t just to depopulate and figure stuff out later is very concerning to me.”

And all the while, officials didn’t monitor the mink workers for symptoms, as guidance from the CDC urges. 

Their exposure is significant: Mink sneeze. They escape. They attack. “The mink are fierce,” said a Spanish-speaking “minkero” who works on a nearby farm, showing the scars he got from the aggressive, solitary creatures. “You get scared because the fucking thing bites, and it claws at you.”

A mink farmworker, sometimes referred to as a “minkero” among the Spanish-speaking community, shows scars from mink bites and scratches in Payson, Utah. Workers typically wear long gloves to protect themselves but can still be bitten or scratched. Julie Leopo for ProPublica

Right now in Washington state, officials are working to track down the contacts of a symptomatic person exposed to dairy cattle infected with bird flu. The patient is isolating at home. Utah public health officials used to do similar, proactive monitoring. But they stopped after complaints from their colleagues in the agriculture department that farmers were annoyed by it.

“Us doing active monitoring was making it so that farms didn’t want to work with them,” said Pamela Gomez Pinedo, a respiratory disease epidemiologist for Utah’s health department. As a result, public health workers had a “pretty difficult time” getting details from agriculture officials, she said.

As part of a 2025 agreement, the Utah Department of Agriculture and Food agreed to share information about bird flu outbreaks on farms — so long as the health officials didn’t do anything to track workers’ health. 

“We will only do active monitoring in the case of evidence of human-to-human transmission,” Pinedo said in emails with a CDC epidemiologist. As the outbreak stretched to a month, CDC officials expressed concerns, asking how anyone would know if a worker had been infected if they weren’t getting tested.

Price said the state’s policy not to monitor workers is meant to allow farmers to decide whether to contact the health department, rather than “forcing it on them.” “If we started seeing people actively dying from this, obviously that would change how we respond to this,” she said. 

A telltale sign of bird flu infection in humans is eye redness. It is present in over 90% of cases and is often the sole symptom a person displays. 

Last Saturday, a ProPublica reporter tracked down two people who worked at the Utah mink farm. One had a visibly red eye. 

The CDC explicitly urges testing for the symptom. 

After ProPublica reached out to the farm, its owner, Chad Fenn, contacted the Utah County Health Department about the red eye, which had cleared up by Monday, he told ProPublica. He said the worker got dust in his eye; the department didn’t recommend testing.

“They’re not going to do anything,” Fenn said. “They said they don’t see that there’s a need.” He said the department recommended testing only if other symptoms, like a cough or sore throat, developed. 

A half dozen flu experts had no shortage of adjectives to describe their disbelief at the government decisions not to cull the mink or monitor and test the workers. 

“It’s amazing to me,” said Gail Hansen, a former Kansas state public health veterinarian and epidemiologist. “Utah doesn’t want to be the epicenter of the next human flu outbreak, right?”

Most of the new viruses that have shaken humanity in the past century have spilled over from animals. Ebolas likely came from fruit bats; HIV, from chimpanzees. The leading theory for COVID-19 is that it jumped from bats to humans via an intermediate host mammal such as a raccoon dog. And all the modern flu pandemics have been bird flu viruses that mutated to spread in humans. 

ProPublica reported extensively on spillover in a 2023 series called “Roots of an Outbreak.” To prevent more deadly spillovers, experts worldwide urge governments to take a “one health” approach to viral threats, treating dangers to animals as dangers to humans. 

That’s not happening in Utah, experts said after reviewing ProPublica’s findings. Both the state and federal government are to blame.

“There’s no leader of this ‘one health’ team to take charge,” said Erin Sorrell, a senior scholar at the Johns Hopkins Center for Health Security. “That is going to allow the virus to continue to circulate, potentially adapt and potentially spill over into another host, whether it’s avian, mammalian or human.”

This strain of bird flu, which began ripping through American poultry farms in early 2022, has proved adept at jumping to other species. It took hold in cows in 2024 and since then has run rampant through dairies.

Yet federal guidance to prevent the spread into mink farms hasn’t considered cows a threat. Farmers are encouraged to keep wild birds from infiltrating their barns and avoid feeding them raw poultry. It has said nothing about feeding beef parts to mink, which farmers commonly do in summer months to encourage the animals to put on weight and grow. 

Dairy cows, which are not “depopulated” if exposed to bird flu, can still be slaughtered with the meat sold to farms and humans even though researchers have found the virus in the tissues of sick cows. USDA officials have insisted that beef for human consumption is free of bird flu, in part because the virus concentrates itself in sections of the cow people don’t usually eat. Fenn said that the mink are routinely fed raw organs of livestock, including cows. 

The genomic data from the samples of mink lungs and brains sent from Utah to a USDA lab shows that the mink were stricken with the same strain of the virus that has spread in dairy herds. Officials said they didn’t know whether contaminated beef was the way the mink got infected.

Cows graze in a field in Utah Valley, Utah. Julie Leopo for ProPublica

In mink, the dairy strain of bird flu may have found a much better host for mutating into a human flu, because mink airways have an abundance of the type of cell receptors in people’s throats and noses that are a common pathway for infection. 

A 2024 study of the dairy strain of the bird flu found that a single mutation could switch the virus from preferring the bird-type receptors to human-type receptors. And in studies using ferrets, a close relative of mink, the virus acquired mutations that let it attack human-type cell receptors. 

It’s not clear to scientists just how much of an evolutionary leap would be needed for this strain of bird flu to spread among humans, or whether mink are the host that would allow that leap to happen. 

How this ultimately plays out “really depends on what happens with the virus,” said Meghan Davis, an epidemiologist at Johns Hopkins University.

“We might get lucky, and a response that is not robust may not have dire consequences,” she said. “But we may get unlucky.”

There’s also a risk of something called “reassortment,” where another flu virus could infect the same cell as a bird flu virus and swap wide swaths of genetic code already adapted to humans. 

When the outbreak in the mink farm started, there was very little seasonal flu it could mix with, but September saw one of the earliest starts to flu season on record, compared with November, when flu normally takes off.

“The most likely scenario for a pandemic is that we have a virus that reassorts with another virus,” said Jennifer Nuzzo, director of the Pandemic Center at the Brown University School of Public Health. “Obviously, having this circulate amid human flu season is not great.” 

Utah officials were far more responsive to the threat of spillover in 2020, when outbreaks of COVID-19 spread explosively on mink farms – including this very farm. They invited federal officials to the state to research how the virus adapted and moved.

Given mink’s reputation as escape artists, wildlife experts set up traps around infected farms. The traps frequently caught mink carrying COVID-19 that had originated in the nearby barns. The virus infected both escaped mink and wild mink they had come in contact with. Mink and farmworkers were frequently tested, tracking the way that the virus was spreading and mutating. 

As other states and countries took the same measures, they identified humans infected by the mink with COVID-19 and, ultimately, human-to-human transmission.

There are no similar efforts now in Utah with bird flu. 

A USDA spokesperson told ProPublica that it was more involved in 2020 because the virus that causes COVID-19 had “significant” potential to transmit between humans and animals and vice versa.

Scientists with the USDA sequenced and published bird flu genomic data from the first samples of dead mink. Those sequences didn’t show any particularly concerning mutations, experts and the CDC told ProPublica. 

But in the past two months, experts said, the virus is sure to have continued mutating as it spread – it’s only a question of whether those mutations could confer some advantage in infecting humans as well.

“As long as it continues to go mink to mink, then it becomes more and more likely that it could jump to a human,” Hansen said.

Fenn said new samples were taken two weeks ago. Price said she is still waiting for the results. 

John Korslund, a retired USDA official who helped coordinate the response to COVID-19 on mink farms several years prior, was one of several experts who said officials need to look closely at newer genetic samples to see how the virus is evolving. 

“I really want to know what the virus has done, from when it started to today,” he said. “Are we getting accumulated mutations making the virus more dangerous?”

Mink have the type of cell receptors that a seasonal flu will target in human throats and noses. Julie Leopo for ProPublica

ProPublica began reporting on the outbreak late this summer after the USDA updated a bird flu dashboard that showed seven captive mink had tested positive in Utah. But neither the USDA nor state officials had said anything publicly, and, when asked, they wouldn’t discuss what was actually happening on the farm.

Communications obtained under the state’s public records law — first published by the Animal Welfare Institute and reported on by the Salt Lake Tribune — show Utah officials took pains to protect the farm’s privacy amid the outbreak. The state did not declare an emergency, because doing so, officials said, “may alert animal rights groups,” according to the messages.

Willy Lanier, a public health veterinarian with the state health department, told colleagues to keep the outbreak under “closer hold” than outbreaks of bird flu on poultry and dairy farms. Keeping the information confidential was consistent with state protocol, a spokesperson in his department said, adding that it was still shared with local health officials. But when ProPublica reached out to the spokesperson for the Utah County Health Department about a possible bird flu outbreak, she said, “That would be news to me.”

Price is so deferential to the family that owns the farm that she has not set foot on the property. 

“We might get lucky, and a response that is not robust may not have dire consequences. But we may get unlucky.”
Meghan Davis, Johns Hopkins University epidemiologist

“I’m really the only one here at this facility that’s been dealing with the producer. They’re a very private bunch,” Price said. “A lot of what I’m going off of is what I’ve seen from Google Maps, what I’ve talked to the producer about, what I’ve talked to the vet about. I haven’t felt the need to go out there based on those conversations.”

She said she “became very comfortable” in conversations with the owner that the virus wouldn’t spread off the farm. It doesn’t have animals moving on and off over the course of the year like on a dairy or poultry farm; mink leave only when they’re slaughtered and skinned for pelts at the end of the year. She also said that she was confident the owner would recapture any escaped mink.

Short of a formal quarantine, Price gave the farm a “verbal hold” to not move any mink, or manure or carcasses, off the farm. “We haven’t seen spread off of this farm. We have not had additional cases in Utah that are linked to this, so thus far the verbal hold orders and the measures that have been taken look to be successful: There is not spread happening from this farm from this case.”

Price’s assertion didn’t allay the concerns of experts that ProPublica spoke with. When poultry test positive for this strain of bird flu, all nearby farms are quarantined and tested for the virus. But the approach in Utah relies on farms reporting cases or the public calling in reports of dead birds in the area. 

“If you’re not looking for something, you won’t find it,” Sorrell said. “Unless you’re doing active surveillance, you can’t claim that you haven’t had cases.”

Fenn told ProPublica his conversations with state officials made him less worried about any kind of spread. When the outbreak started, Fenn said, he asked whether the bird flu could infect people. 

“Right off the bat, the state people we reported to, they said you don’t need to worry too much,” Fenn said. “My guys wear masks every day. They have glasses they can wear,” Fenn said. “ Me? I don’t wear it at all. Never have, never will, because I’ve been doing it for 40 years.”

Fenn said he wished he could vaccinate the mink for bird flu to keep the rest of his animals from catching it and dying; Price asked the USDA about a vaccine that had been used to save endangered wild species but said she got nowhere with that request. The USDA told ProPublica its division responsible for protecting animal health has no “species-specific regulatory authority or dedicated programs” for vaccinating mink, depopulating them or paying owners back for such a culling.

Fenn told ProPublica he thinks concerns about mink as a particularly risky bird flu host are trumped up by anti-fur activists, the same forces that he believed were behind the reactions in Spain and Finland, which depopulated mink farms hit with bird flu. “Europeans are a little scared of everything,” he said. “They’re going to do what they’re going to do, and here in the United States, we’re going to do what we’re going to do.”

Price said she was aware that Finland and Spain had depopulated their fur farms when the same strain infected them. “I didn’t really look much further into it,” she said, explaining that she was interested in those cases only for lessons about how to handle the outbreak, but not the particular reasons those countries chose to depopulate the farms. 

A USDA spokesperson said Congress would have to specifically fund a program to depopulate mink. (The program to cull poultry to stop the spread of bird flu has cost well over $1 billion since 2022.)

The events in Utah are a “clear warning sign” about the dangers of mink farms, said Neil Vora, executive director for the Preventing Pandemics at the Source Coalition.

“Fur farms are to produce pelts purely for luxury goods, to make fancy coats,” he said. “It’s absurd that we’re willing to gamble with the lives of millions of people just to keep an industry alive.”

The industry has struggled as American consumers increasingly reject fur. Though domestic farms peaked about a decade ago, selling luxury pelts that often ended up in China, foreign farms have sprung up, threatening the business. 

While animal rights advocates have pushed for Congress to adopt legislation that would phase out the fur industry, buying out farmers over the course of a year to end the practice once and for all, winds in Congress are blowing the other direction. The Senate will soon weigh in on the latest Farm Bill, which now seeks to expand market opportunities for mink farmers by undoing a prohibition in federal law on subsidizing the fur trade. 

The virus continues to spread on the Utah farm, said Fenn, though at a slower pace. Experts told ProPublica it still poses a risk.

“I would want a full on hazmat suit if I were on that farm,” Peacock said. “Or, preferably, I’d rather not to be on that farm.”

items.articleBody:
Selbstständig arbeiten, länger leben? Eine Langzeitstudie mit mehr als 27.000 Menschen aus den USA liefert Hinweise auf ein geringeres Sterberisiko von Unternehmern gegenüber Angestellten. Allerdings zeigt sich dieser Zusammenhang vor allem bei Menschen, die aus eigenem Antrieb ein Unternehmen gründen. Ob die Selbstständigkeit selbst das Leben verlängert, bleibt offen.

Hoboken (U.S.A.). Wer ein eigenes Unternehmen führt, trägt Verantwortung, muss oft lange arbeiten und lebt mit finanzieller Unsicherheit. Dafür können Selbstständige häufig selbst entscheiden, welche Ideen sie verwirklichen und wie sie ihren Arbeitsalltag gestalten. Welche dieser gegensätzlichen Seiten sich langfristig auf die Gesundheit auswirken, war bisher unklar.

Viele Untersuchungen zum Unternehmertum konzentrieren sich auf Stress, Beschwerden oder einzelne Krankheiten. Doch solche Momentaufnahmen verraten wenig darüber, ob unterschiedliche Berufswege auch mit der Lebensdauer zusammenhängen. Dafür braucht es Daten, die Menschen über viele Jahre begleiten.

Forscher des Stevens Institute of Technology um Dr. Cristiano Bellavitis haben deshalb den Zusammenhang zwischen Selbstständigkeit und Sterblichkeit genauer untersucht. Als Grundlage dienten Angaben von 27.501 Menschen aus der amerikanischen Health and Retirement Study (HRS), einer langfristigen Befragung zum Altern. Das Team wertete 137.542 wiederholte Beobachtungen aus den Jahren 1998 bis 2020 mit statistischen Überlebensmodellen aus.

Geringeres Sterberisiko bei Unternehmern

Das Ergebnis: Menschen mit unternehmerischer Berufserfahrung hatten laut den Auswertungen ein um rund zehn Prozent geringeres Sterberisiko als Personen in abhängiger Beschäftigung. Der Zusammenhang blieb auch bestehen, nachdem die Wissenschaftler unter anderem Alter, Einkommen, Bildungsstand und gesundheitliche Merkmale statistisch berücksichtigt hatten. Weitere Prüfungen, darunter Vergleiche eineiiger Zwillinge, sollten mögliche Verzerrungen eingrenzen.

Die Zahl bedeutet allerdings nicht, dass Selbstständige durchschnittlich zehn Prozent mehr Lebensjahre gewinnen. Gemessen wurde ein Unterschied beim statistischen Sterberisiko, nicht eine entsprechend verlängerte individuelle Lebenserwartung. Auch konnten die Forscher mit diesen Beobachtungsdaten keine ursächliche Schutzwirkung des Unternehmertums nachweisen.

Warum die Gründung entscheidend ist

Besonders deutlich war der Vorteil bei Menschen, die freiwillig eine Geschäftsidee verwirklichten oder eine wirtschaftliche Chance nutzen wollten. Wer sich dagegen aus einer Notlage heraus selbstständig machte, etwa nach einem Arbeitsplatzverlust, zeigte keinen vergleichbaren Vorteil. Offenbar ist die Motivation für den Schritt in die Selbstständigkeit ein wichtiger Teil des Zusammenhangs.

„Offenbar kommt es nicht allein auf das Unternehmertum an, sondern auf die Umstände, unter denen Menschen diesen Weg einschlagen. Wenn Unternehmertum mehr Wahlfreiheit und Chancen widerspiegelt, könnten die damit verbundene Selbstbestimmung und das Gefühl von Sinn psychologische Vorteile bieten, die über finanzielle Erträge hinausgehen“, erklärt Dr. Cristiano Bellavitis.

Außerdem war eine längere und häufigere unternehmerische Tätigkeit mit einem geringeren Sterberisiko verbunden. Die Autoren betrachten Selbstständigkeit deshalb nicht nur als aktuellen Beruf, sondern als Erfahrung, die sich über verschiedene Lebensphasen erstrecken kann. Allerdings lassen sich günstige Ausgangsbedingungen und persönliche Eigenschaften nicht vollständig von möglichen Wirkungen der Arbeit trennen.

Psychische Gesundheit als möglicher Schlüssel

Eine mögliche Erklärung liefern Unterschiede in der psychischen Gesundheit: Unternehmer berichteten seltener von depressiven Beschwerden und Einsamkeit. In den statistischen Analysen erklärte die psychische Gesundheit einen Teil des beobachteten Zusammenhangs mit der Lebensdauer. Allgemeine körperliche Gesundheitsmerkmale konnten den Unterschied dagegen kaum erklären.

Auch der Zeitpunkt spielte eine Rolle. Eine bessere körperliche Gesundheit war vor allem mit gegenwärtiger unternehmerischer Tätigkeit verbunden, während die psychischen Vorteile stärker mit früheren Erfahrungen als Unternehmer zusammenhingen. Die Studie belegt damit aber nicht, dass Selbstbestimmung automatisch Depressionen verhindert oder vor Erkrankungen schützt.

„Die meisten Menschen halten Unternehmertum für äußerst stressig, und das kann es zweifellos sein. Aber es gibt den Menschen auch ein hohes Maß an Selbstbestimmung und die Möglichkeit, etwas zu verfolgen, das sie wirklich lieben oder das ihnen am Herzen liegt. Unsere Ergebnisse deuten darauf hin, dass diese Vorteile dauerhafte Auswirkungen haben könnten“, sagt Dr. Cristiano Bellavitis.

Was Angestellte daraus lernen könnten

Aus Sicht der Forscher könnten auch Beschäftigte von mehr Entscheidungsspielraum und einem stärkeren Sinngefühl bei der Arbeit profitieren. Unternehmen könnten ihren Mitarbeitern mehr Verantwortung, Gestaltungsmöglichkeiten und Einblick in die Ergebnisse ihrer Arbeit geben, ohne dass diese die Risiken einer eigenen Gründung tragen müssten. Ob solche Veränderungen tatsächlich die Lebenserwartung erhöhen, wurde in der Untersuchung allerdings nicht getestet.

„In vielerlei Hinsicht könnte das das Beste aus beiden Welten sein. Unternehmen können die Unabhängigkeit, den Sinn und die Begeisterung fördern, die oft mit Unternehmertum einhergehen, und gleichzeitig die Sicherheit einer traditionellen Beschäftigung bieten“, sagt Dr. Cristiano Bellavitis.

Die Ergebnisse stammen ausschließlich aus einer amerikanischen Langzeitbefragung von Menschen im höheren Erwachsenenalter. Zudem könnten nicht vollständig erfasste Unterschiede, etwa bei Gesundheit, Vermögen oder persönlichen Eigenschaften, die Befunde mit beeinflussen. Die zentrale Erkenntnis lautet daher nicht, dass jeder sein eigener Chef werden sollte, sondern dass die Art und die Beweggründe der Arbeit für das langfristige Wohlbefinden bedeutsam sein könnten.
