items.articleBody: ObjectiveTo compare the clinical outcomes of short-term peripheral nerve stimulation (st-PNS), supraorbital nerve pulsed radiofrequency (SON-PRF), and combined supraorbital nerve and stellate ganglion pulsed radiofrequency (SON + SG-PRF) for herpes zoster ophthalmicus (HZO)-associated pain.MethodsThis retrospective study included patients with HZO-associated pain who underwent st-PNS, SON-PRF, or SON + SG-PRF between January 2023 and January 2026. The primary outcome was the longitudinal change in Numerical Rating Scale (NRS) scores over 24 weeks. Secondary outcomes included the clinical response rate, anxiety (GAD-7), depression (PHQ-9), sleep quality (PSQI), and treatment-related adverse events. The incidence of postherpetic neuralgia (PHN) was assessed as an exploratory outcome only in patients with a disease duration of ≤90 days at treatment. Longitudinal outcomes were analyzed using baseline-adjusted linear mixed-effects models, with propensity score weighting used for sensitivity analyses.ResultsA total of 269 patients were included: 84 in the st-PNS group, 96 in the SON-PRF group, and 89 in the SON + SG-PRF group. NRS scores decreased over follow-up in all three groups. In the primary and both propensity score-weighted analyses, the overall NRS trajectory was lower with st-PNS than with SON-PRF, whereas no significant difference was observed between st-PNS and SON + SG-PRF. The overall GAD-7 trajectory was lower with SON + SG-PRF than with SON-PRF, and the overall PSQI trajectory was lower with SON + SG-PRF than with either st-PNS or SON-PRF; these differences remained statistically significant in both weighted analyses. The overall trajectories of depressive symptoms did not differ significantly among the groups. Exploratory analysis did not establish a difference in PHN risk among the three groups. No serious treatment-related adverse events occurred during follow-up.ConclusionTo our knowledge, this study is the first to compare multidimensional clinical outcomes of st-PNS, SON-PRF, and SON + SG-PRF for HZO-associated pain within the same cohort. st-PNS showed a relatively consistent analgesic benefit over SON-PRF, whereas SON + SG-PRF also provided analgesia and showed potential benefits for anxiety and sleep outcomes. These findings require confirmation in prospective studies.

items.articleBody:
A security researcher has demonstrated a software-only partial jailbreak of the Switch 2, gaining "userland" access that he says "lets us run homebrew, reverse engineer and mod Switch 2 games, back up save files off the Switch, and access most of the Switch 2’s peripherals through MMIO."

The hack relies on the original Switch version of SmileBasic 4, the latest in a long-running series of programming environments and interpreters that run on Nintendo hardware. The so-called "tethered" hack also requires access to a macOS or Linux PC on the same network to run a node.js package that helps enable privileged system access.

Researcher Sammy Hajhamid writes that he used OpenAI's Codex to poke at SmileBasic's language interpreter, using a custom harness that could send USB commands to the system and view results via HDMI (as well as power cycling via a Bluetooth light switch flipping device). After "substantial effort for ~2 weeks," that harness discovered a 32-bit integer overflow that occurs when removing items from an array in SmileBasic. That error gives access to an array pointer, which in turn allows read and write access to portions of system memory.

items.articleBody:
Canada’s Parliament is debating a massive expansion of surveillance powers that will threaten the privacy and security of millions of people. Bill C-22, also called the Lawful Access Act, has already passed the House of Commons, and is now before the Canadian Senate. 

Canadians still have an opportunity to speak out and stop this dangerous legislation. The Canadian Civil Liberties Association (CCLA) is urging all Canadians to sign its petition opposing the bill. (The petition on CCLA’s website is governed by CCLA’s privacy policy.) 

Take action

Tell the canadian senate to stop C-22

As we wrote earlier this year, Bill C-22 gives the government new powers to force digital services—including telecom companies, messaging apps, and more—to help with government surveillance. Worse, it allows Canada’s Minister of Public Safety to order companies to create a backdoor to their services for law enforcement, as long as it doesn’t lead to a “systemic insecurity.” That’s a clear recipe for weakening the encryption we all rely on. 

It also requires services to retain metadata for up to a year, which reveals who people communicate with, where they go, and what services they use, even when they are not suspected of any crime. 

Researchers at CCLA and Citizen Lab published a detailed analysis of C-22 and its serious constitutional and cybersecurity problems. The analysis points out that the bill needs more than cosmetic changes—it calls for entirely withdrawing Part 2 of Bill C-22, the section that establishes the surveillance and data retention regime. 

Bill C-22 could also expand the sharing of Canadians’ personal data with foreign law enforcement, including the United States. Canada has been negotiating a cross-border data-sharing agreement with the U.S. that would allow American police to get information about Canadian internet users without any Canadian court oversight. 

Some Canadian senators have already expressed concerns about the bill, and rightly suggested, as CCLA and Citizen Lab have, that it may not be compatible with privacy protections in the Canadian constitution. 

If you’re in Canada, read and sign CCLA’s petition opposing Bill C-22 today. Don’t let the Senate allow this dangerous expansion of government surveillance to become Canada’s new reality. 

Take action

Canadians: defend your privacy and security

items.articleBody:
Turiya Adkins (photo Clyde Nichols); Timothy Yanick Hunter (photo Spring Morris), and Clifford Prince King (photo Clifford Prince King; images courtesy Studio Museum)
Art Movements, published every Thursday afternoon, is a roundup of must-know news, appointments, awards, and other happenings in today’s chaotic art world.

Studio Museum in Harlem Names Three Artists-in-Residence

Multidisciplinary artist Turiya Adkins, artist and curator Timothy Yanick Hunter, and photographer and filmmaker Clifford Prince King have been selected as the Studio Museum’s yearlong artists-in-residence for 2026–27. Starting this November and through October 2027, the three will have individual studio spaces in the institution's new building on West 125th Street. The residency also includes professional development training and material support, and culminates with a group exhibition in one of the museum's galleries. (An exhibition of the latest cohort’s work is currently on view through January 3.)

Brognon Rollin Wins Prix Duchamp
 Brognon Rollin (David Brognon and Stéphanie Rollin) (© Guillaume Blot, Paris Musées)
The Prix Duchamp, France's largest contemporary art award, goes this year to Brognon Rollin, the artist duo formed by David Brognon and Stéphanie Rollin. Winners receive a €35,000 (~$39,200) prize and participate in an exhibition of works by all four nominees, now on view through February 7 at the Musée d’Art Moderne de Paris. The museum’s director, Fabrice Hergott, praised Brognon Rollin’s conceptual practice as “a quiet yet tenacious statement on human vulnerability,” adding that their work “gives tangible form to what usually escapes our gaze: the passage of time spent waiting, addiction and inner resilience.”

Joël Andrianomearisoa, Laura Henno, and Josèfa Ntjam were also nominated for the award this year.

What Else Happened?
“ROADMAPPIN’" (2026) performed by Grantee Kar’mel Antonyo Wade Small, Kennedy Hill, and Anthony C. Wyche III (photo Adi Talwar, courtesy Bronx Council on the Arts)
Queer|Art, the Bronx Council on the Arts, A.I.R. Gallery, and Visual AIDS are among the 59 nonprofit art organizations receiving Reserve Fund grants from the New York State Council on the Arts and the New York Foundation for the Arts. The awards range from $15,000 to $50,000 and total $1,760,000 in support; see all grantees here. 

Anthea M. Hartig, director of the Smithsonian’s National Museum of American History, has been elected to the American Academy of Arts and Sciences.

Americans for the Arts named Matt Ryan as chief operating officer and Cillonia McKenley as chief development officer.

Patrick Eugène is now represented by Vielmetter Los Angeles.

Rachel Kanter and Yana Peel were appointed to the Yale Schwarzman Center’s advisory board.

Acquisitions
Kiki Smith, "Pool of Tears II" (2000) (photo ULAE, courtesy Kiki Smith and NYPL)
The New York Public Library (NYPL) is the lucky recipient of 250 prints by Kiki Smith, one more fantastic and exquisite than the next. Rich hand-colored intaglios, woodcuts, and artists’ books are part of the trove gifted by her sister, artist Seton Smith, which comprises the most comprehensive collection of Kiki Smith’s prints in the United States. In a statement, Kiki Smith said that she “could think of no more wonderful place for my prints to be.”

The Cleveland Museum of Art announced today the acquisition of Teresita Fernández’s “Soil Horizon (Cleveland)” (2026), a site-specific commission consisting of two large-scale glazed ceramic wall murals. The piece will be on view in the museum’s Jane and Jon Outcalt Family Concourse beginning in February. 

Wildcard
Austrian Pavilion, Seaworld Venice by artist Florentina Holzinger for the 61st Venice Biennale (photo Giuseppe Cottini/Getty Images)
For the coda to Seaworld Venice, Florentina Holzinger’s installation for the Austrian Pavilion at this year's Venice Biennale, the artist will present a “final dinner” featuring all the bodily waste collected from visitors over the past seven months. “Closing Étude” at the Scuola Grande della Misericordia in Venice will extend the pavilion's central conceit, which involved filtering urine from on-site port-a-potties into a dunk tank. The “distilled remains serve as a monument for the future” that will be presented outside the closed pavilion on November 22, a statement explains. Okay!

items.articleBody:
Europe has dropped the ball on the prototype for its first reusable spacecraft. Or, rather, the prototype itself was dropped — on purpose — but the outcome of its fall was not what engineers had hoped for. 

The incident occurred during an Oct. 6 drop test of the full-scale Space Rider model, from the European Space Agency (ESA). The robotic vehicle's initial drogue parachute deployed successfully, but its main parafoil detached during deployment, leaving the prototype unable to slow its descent before crashing into the ground, according to ESA officials. The cause of the failure remains under investigation.

"Following several successful tests using representative vehicle masses, the latest system-level drop test in October was not completed as planned due to an anomaly during the parafoil deployment sequence," an ESA spokesperson confirmed in an email to Space.com. "An independent investigation is ongoing to determine its root cause and inform the next steps."

Space Rider is being developed as Europe's first reusable orbital spacecraft — an uncrewed vehicle designed to carry scientific experiments to orbit for up to two months, then return them to Earth for analysis. Its method of return, though, differs from that of any other spacecraft in operation today. Space Rider''s wingless, lifting-body design relies on a steerable parachute, or parafoil, to maneuver toward its landing area. This allows it to perform runway-style touchdowns, as opposed to other, less accurate parachute-aided recoveries in current practice.

This month's drop test was intended to demonstrate that ability, which is a critical requirement for Space Rider's planned reuse after missions in orbit, but the impact of its failure may not end up disrupting its ultimate development timeline. According to Géraldine Naja, ESA's director of space transportation, the vehicle's other remaining qualification tests aren't holding back its path to launch. 

"We hope that this test will not damage, or let's say lead us to modify, the remaining schedule and qualification activities," Naja said during an ESA Council media briefing on Oct. 22. "In any case, the remaining qualification activities are not on the critical path of the development of the Space Rider."

Naja described the incident as an unfortunate but important event. "We have had many successful tests before, but testing and validation is part of the development of a space system," she said.

The lost vehicle was a full-scale test model assembled to evaluate Space Rider's descent and landing systems. The minivan-sized mockup reproduced the size and flight characteristics of its reentry module, with avionics to control its autonomous guidance and navigation systems, but the vehicle was far from a space-ready article.

Render of ESA's Space Rider orbiter. (Image credit: European Space Agency)
The Oct. 6 test took place at a military range on the Italian island of Sardinia, where the mockup was released from a helicopter at an altitude of approximately 2 miles (3 kilometers). According to Naja, the vehicle's initial drogue parachute triggered as expected and began slowing the Space Rider mock-up's descent before its larger, steerable parafoil was supposed to unfurl. The parafoil, however, detached during deployment, leaving the vehicle in freefall before impacting the ground. ESA has subsequently recovered all the craft's components.

This month's event was the first drop test since an unsuccessful attempt in May, when a sensor flagged an issue during preparations, prompting engineers to abort the test before the model was released. Following that, Space Rider's testing range, operated by Italy's Ministry of Defense, was unavailable from June through September.

Space Rider's descent and landing qualification campaign began in 2025, with previous successes demonstrating its parafoil deployment and autonomous capabilities. Beyond its landing systems, Space Rider also underwent separate thermal protection testing earlier this year, exposing its heat-shield materials to temperatures around 2,900 degrees Fahrenheit (1,600 degrees Celsius) in plasma wind tunnel trials.

ESA has targeted Space Rider's first orbital mission for later this decade.

items.articleBody:
Safari Technology Preview Release 255 is now available for download for macOS Golden Gate and macOS Tahoe. If you already have Safari Technology Preview installed, you can update it in System Settings under General → Software Update.

This release includes WebKit changes between: 322011@main…323397@main.

Accessibility

Resolved Issues

Fixed VoiceOver presses dispatching a click event with an event.detail of 0. (322978@main) (187732224)

Fixed radio buttons in a group to be exposed as required when the required attribute is set on one of the buttons. (322894@main) (189100525)

Fixed list box accessibility children not updating when options are added or removed. (323117@main) (189412211)

Animations

Resolved Issues

Fixed getComputedStyle() ignoring the pseudo-element when checking whether a property is being animated. (322681@main) (188502400)

Fixed requestAnimationFrame() handles to use the full unsigned long range defined by the IDL. (322922@main) (189270148)

Fixed view transition setup to flush the update callback queue. (323173@main) (189533643)

CSS

Resolved Issues

Fixed font-family: initial acting like font-family: inherit instead of resolving to the initial value. (322304@main) (54306281)

Fixed box-sizing: content-box being ignored for percentage-height tables (display: table), which caused vertical padding to be dropped. (322812@main) (122587242)

Fixed min-width: max-content being ignored for the min-content contribution of a percentage-width replaced element. (322974@main) (179947068)

Fixed the top color extension to use relative colors with filters when applicable. (323153@main) (186098400)

Fixed Range.getBoundingClientRect() returning empty rects for content inside a content-visibility: hidden subtree. (323204@main) (186165755)

Fixed elements using a background image that depends on currentColor not repainting when the current color changes. (323240@main) (188036420)

Fixed subgrid implicit grid-area line names being matched by the first substring instead of the suffix. (322238@main) (188203288)

Fixed tree-scoped var() and custom function references inside an @function failing to resolve when the function is called from a :host rule. (322679@main) (188206030)

Fixed an issue where duplicate anchor-name values among elements in a spatial portal resolved unpredictably. (322709@main) (188209540)

Fixed @scope so that structural DOM changes correctly invalidate scope membership when the scoping root selector depends on them. (322680@main) (188398757)

Fixed revert inside @starting-style dropping @starting-style declarations from lower cascade layers. (322688@main) (188463947)

Fixed the rotate property to preserve the sign of the axis when serializing. (322682@main) (188493811)

Fixed revert and revert-layer using the wrong cascade origin for visited and unvisited link styles, which wrongly disabled native appearance. (323205@main) (188494505)

Fixed getComputedStyle() serializing the overscroll-behavior shorthand as a single value of the larger axis instead of both axis values. (322685@main) (188534035)

Fixed block-axis multicolumn content being painted at the wrong offset when the column set does not start at the top of the multicol container. (322687@main) (189067503)

Fixed shape-margin values above 65535px on an image shape-outside producing a much smaller float area. (322727@main) (189069223)

Fixed a line-clamp container to establish an independent formatting context. (322767@main) (189090409)

Fixed replaced elements ignoring aspect-ratio when both width and height are auto. (322745@main) (189096923)

Fixed the line-clamp block ellipsis being placed after a in a white-space: nowrap line. (322758@main) (189103913)

Fixed an overflowing preserved tab not wrapping to the next line. (322759@main) (189104880)

Fixed the line-clamp block ellipsis not hanging with hanging-punctuation. (322772@main) (189105782)

Fixed text-overflow truncating a unicode-bidi: plaintext line in the wrong direction. (322866@main) (189108555)

Fixed an image shape-outside dropping an above-threshold run that starts in the last column. (322756@main) (189116534)

Fixed line-clamp: auto not being able to clamp between sibling blocks. (322836@main) (189124610)

Fixed line-clamp: auto clamping inside a box with a set height. (322842@main) (189138321)

Fixed the line-clamp block ellipsis being placed on a line that only contains a float. (322791@main) (189151667)

Fixed the baseline of an empty MathML element to account for border-top and padding-top. (322826@main) (189209081)

Fixed CSS grid intrinsic width computation to resolve auto-fill repetitions against the grid container’s minimum and maximum size. (322848@main) (189223527)

Fixed CSS grid column sizing to resolve percentage rows against the block size rather than the inline size when estimating row sizes. (322850@main) (189230010)

Fixed grid container minimum and maximum sizes to respect box-sizing: border-box. (322856@main) (189235347)

Fixed a percentage-width child of a vertical writing mode box to keep following the box’s width after a style change. (322964@main) (189316242)

Fixed cross-fade() to match the CSS Images Level 4 specification and the behavior of other browsers. (322918@main) (189356185)

Fixed grid layout to return the grid’s used block size, so the container’s size is correct once layout is complete. (323053@main) (189357098)

Fixed grid containers to resolve percentage and calc() values for min-width, max-width, min-height and max-height. (323051@main) (189358198)

Fixed :visited style not updating for links inside shadow trees. (323396@main) (189380898)

Fixed baseline alignment of grid items so it is applied after the items have been sized. (323238@main) (189457596)

Fixed attr() to avoid an unnecessary legacy code path in simple cases. (323098@main) (189485680)

Fixed MediaList writes being silently dropped after the owning rule or stylesheet is destroyed. (323203@main) (189496021)

Fixed collapsed SVG shapes and images being painted when visibility: collapse should be treated as hidden. (323110@main) (189496450)

Fixed block boxes after the line-clamp clamp point remaining visible. (323220@main) (189543433)

Fixed content before the line-clamp clamp point losing its lines when it does not change. (323225@main) (189569400)

Fixed block boxes after the line-clamp clamp point still taking up space. (323253@main) (189570948)

Fixed floats after the line-clamp clamp point remaining visible. (323337@main) (189578173)

Fixed adoptedStyleSheets continuing to apply removed sheets after its length is shrunk, and ignoring changes to a sheet after its duplicate is removed. (323233@main) (189579103)

Fixed an implicit @scope rule in a constructed stylesheet adopted by a document matching nothing. (323237@main) (189584948)

Fixed floats making the line-clamp container taller. (323349@main) (189630233)

Fixed floats adding to the scrollable overflow of the line-clamp container. (323353@main) (189641420)

Fixed line-clamp: auto containers having no line clamp until the clamp point is found. (323357@main) (189652879)

Fixed floats painting past the block-end content edge of the line-clamp container. (323390@main) (189653161)

Fixed container size queries truncating fractional container sizes to integers. (323328@main) (189653185)

Fixed absolutely positioned elements whose containing block is an inline after the line-clamp clamp point remaining visible. (323395@main) (189671905)

Editing

Resolved Issues

Fixed DataTransfer treating any format that merely starts with text/plain, such as text/plainfoo, as text/plain. (322954@main) (189265567)

Forms

New Features

Added support for in the native appearance of . (322716@main) (178876621)

Resolved Issues

Fixed :open no longer matching a whose base appearance picker is still showing. (322666@main) (188911581)

Fixed a element computing its selected option’s style from outdated ancestor styles. (322665@main) (189109118)

Fixed a vertical range slider fill overshooting its value when tick marks are present and the thumb is hidden. (322780@main) (189116567)

HTML

Resolved Issues

Fixed a element’s sheet to be built from its child text content instead of descendant text. (322128@main) (188047912)

Fixed tabbing to a popover invoker to move focus to the popover itself when the popover is focusable. (323172@main) (188267440)

Fixed module elements with an empty or invalid src to fire the error event asynchronously instead of synchronously. (323198@main) (189384155)

Fixed setting src to the empty string on a connected element to fire an error event. (323200@main) (189385352)

Fixed elements with an ASCII-whitespace-only src being treated as having an empty src. (323236@main) (189386063)

JavaScript

Resolved Issues

Fixed Object.defineProperty to read descriptor fields after converting the property key, so side effects from key conversion are respected. (322982@main) (179389067)

Fixed an issue where errors thrown by another realm’s built-ins such as Number, String, and Math functions came from the caller’s realm after DFG optimization. (323152@main) (189057417)

Fixed catch parameters named await to be rejected as a syntax error in contexts where await is not an identifier. (322702@main) (189183089)

Fixed await to be treated as an identifier in a non-async function nested in the parameters of an async function. (322703@main) (189183268)

Fixed unary + so it no longer changes the evaluation order of operands in binary expressions. (322817@main) (189267513)

Fixed constant array literal elements to be evaluated only once when emitting bytecode for array literals. (322943@main) (189295197)

Fixed instanceof with a bound function reading the target’s prototype property when the left-hand side is a primitive. (322956@main) (189388195)

Fixed Array.fromAsync to get next from the async iterator before constructing the this value. (322967@main) (189402953)

Fixed using and await using declarations being rejected inside a function nested in a switch case or default clause. (323061@main) (189472811)

Fixed for-in skipping indexed properties of functions. (323086@main) (189504414)

Media

Resolved Issues

Fixed remote audio participants no longer autoplaying on web sites using real-time calls. (323320@main) (182922583)

Fixed WebVTT cue display so the backdrop no longer overflows outside of the cue. (323325@main) (183472002)

Fixed an issue where video using Media Source Extensions never started playing on some sites, such as disneyplus.com. (322877@main) (184182838)

Fixed WebCodecs ignoring the profile, bit depth, and chroma subsampling fields in VP9 codec strings. (322962@main) (188868426)

Fixed the WebCodecs AV1 encoder reporting support for 10-bit, 12-bit, monochrome, and 4:4:4 or 4:2:2 codec strings that it always encodes as 8-bit 4:2:0. (322975@main) (188882755)

Fixed WebCodecs computing incorrect plane layouts for I422 and I444 VideoFrame objects. (322972@main) (188885351)

Networking

Resolved Issues

Fixed failed modulepreload resource loads getting stuck in the cache by retrying them. (323305@main) (124280450)

Fixed a regression where XMLHttpRequest and fetch sent an empty request body for a disk-backed File when the page is controlled by a service worker. (323318@main) (183071407)

Rendering

Resolved Issues

items.articleBody:
This week, the invitations went out1 for an Apple “experience” next Wednesday in Los Angeles, which indicates a major set of product announcements. One of those rumored products is a new iPad mini with an OLED screen, A20 chip, and improved speakers.

The iPad mini is also in the zeitgeist more than ever right now, thanks to the release of the iPhone Duo, which numerous reviewers are comparing to an iPad mini when open. (The Duo is quite a bit smaller.)

In thinking about the iPad mini a bit this week, a thought occurred to me: Is the iPad mini the best iPad? Obviously, if you’re talking pure specs, it’s not—those iPad Pro models are amazing, and I’m writing this post on one right now. The base iPad is a better value and the iPad Air packs a punch, too.

But let’s think about this a little more broadly. Aren’t the best products the ones that know what they are, that have a purpose, that are well defined? One way to identify such a product is customer loyalty, and when I bring up the iPad mini, I frequently see hearts appear in the eyes of the people I’m talking to. People who like the iPad mini love it. That’s a sign.

The larger iPads fall into that neither-fish-nor-fowl twilight zone too often. Should my iPad Pro really just be a Mac that can also run in a tablet mode? It’s got an M5 in it, so probably.

Not the iPad mini. It’s powerful but small. The size means it’s less likely to be dragged into service as a productivity device, but it excels at lean-back tasks like reading and scrolling and even watching video. I love an E Ink reader, but so many people view the iPad mini as the perfect place to do their reading. And I get it. You can hold it in one hand. It’s so small, you can grip it in one hand. And yet, it will basically do everything an iPad does.

There’s something to be said for a product that’s great at filling its niche, and in this case it feels like there’s a really good niche that’s just the size of the iPad mini.

I don’t know what the new update will bring for fans of the iPad mini. They will undoubtedly be thrilled by getting an OLED screen and a faster processor. They will be less thrilled by the price, which might be as much as $799, according to Gurman. But what Apple product prices do thrill us these days, exactly?

Still, when I do get the new iPad mini in my hands, I will need to keep in mind its special place in the iPad line-up. It’s not frequently updated and (unlike this week) rarely the subject of a lot of conversation, but it’s beloved—and that means something.

Yep, I got one. 

 ↩

items.articleBody:
[Cover image by Pexels on Pixabay]

by Cindy Nebel

While we spend a good deal of time talking about learning strategies and how to balance note-taking, content review, and active retrieval practice, all of those strategies are actually fairly useless if you haven’t taken the time to prepare for learning.

I work at a medical school where learning is a hard job. There is a huge volume of information that students must learn quickly while simultaneously managing research, leadership, and volunteerism in order to prepare for residency applications. The balancing act between all of these requirements can cause a good deal of stress on students. For this reason, even the best students, using the best strategies, working tremendously hard can still falter. Because it turns out that learning requires you to take care of your mental wellness first.

The interaction between wellness and learning operates on working memory. Working memory is the finite space we have to hold onto and manipulate information we are currently working with. It is the space where we connect old information with incoming information, where we reason and problem-solve. Arguably, it is literally where learning happens.

When we are tired, anxious, or overloaded, our working memory suffers.

There is an abundance of research showing that sleep deprivation impacts working memory performance (1). What many medical students don’t realize is that these effects start at a relatively small amount of deprivation, with individuals receiving six hours of sleep per night showing significant impacts on their working memory performance (2). While it has often been seen as a right of passage to sacrifice sleep for the sake of learning, the research clearly shows that getting that extra hour of sleep results in much higher benefits for learning, which becomes more effective and more efficient with sufficient sleep (which is 7-9 hours for most adults).

 
 

 
 
 
 

 

 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 

 
 
 
Image by Pexels on Pixabay

 
 
 
 
 

 

 

 

 
A common reason why medical students struggle to get enough sleep is stress or anxiety. As mentioned above, there are many demands placed on medical students, so it is unsurprising that they might experience some amount of stress. However, too much stress can cause working memory difficulties (3). When we are anxious it signals to our brain that the anxiety-inducing factor is important - probably for our survival. So instead of relying on our top-down attentional control where we decide what we want to pay attention to at any given time, our brain uses bottom-up attention and steals some of our working memory capacity to “look out” for the thing causing us anxiety. This process can happen without our conscious awareness. Anxiety can also cause intrusive thoughts in our conscious attention, which again steals capacity that could be used for learning.

It may seem inevitable that learning is going to suffer, but there are many things we can do to manage anxiety and improve wellness to limit these impacts (4). Healthy living in general promotes better mental health. Here sleep is another critical factor. In addition to providing learning benefits, sleep is a mood stabilizer, increasing positive emotions. While exercise has cardiovascular benefits, it also provides considerable benefits for mood. Nutritious food has also been shown to improve psychological well-being and, in turn, academic performance. Finally, social support is a critical factor in creating better mental health. Often, medical students begin to isolate as their anxiety increases, which in turn makes the anxiety and learning worse. This can begin a negative spiral if it isn’t recognized and remediated. 

Another common misconception among medical students is that working longer and harder will result in better learning, but how students structure their learning and taking frequent breaks can often result in better long-term retention. As we take in new information, we can become cognitively depleted, so taking effective breaks that involve a little exercise or meditation can be really effective for resetting the system. What you don’t want to do is jump on social media, where you are both taking in new information and potentially ramping up anxiety.

 
 

 
 
 
 

 

 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 

 
 
 
Image by Alexa on Pixabay

 
 
 
 
 

 

 

 

 
Learning is sometimes a counter-intuitive process. While it may seem like sacrificing sleep, exercise, or time with friends is necessary to increase time spent learning, the research shows that these very things enhance the learning process. This is great news for all the students out there. It’s like being told you can have your cake and eat it too. You will actually learn more if you are a better adjusted human, so have a nap and a walk and go see a friend in between study sessions. It’s worth every minute.

 
 

 

 
 
 

 

 

 
References:

Frenda, S. J., & Fenn, K. M. (2016). Sleep less, think worse: The effect of sleep deprivation on working memory. Journal of applied research in memory and cognition, 5(4), 463-469. 

Van Dongen, H. P., Maislin, G., Mullington, J. M., & Dinges, D. F. (2003). The cumulative cost of additional wakefulness: dose-response effects on neurobehavioral functions and sleep physiology from chronic sleep restriction and total sleep deprivation. Sleep, 26(2), 117-126. 

Moran, T. P. (2016). Anxiety and working memory capacity: A meta-analysis and narrative review. Psychological bulletin, 142(8), 831.

Dai, P., Yi, G., Qian, D., Wu, Z., Fu, M., & Peng, H. (2023). Social support mediates the relationship between coping styles and the mental health of medical students. Psychology research and behavior management, 1299-1313.

Where: Mox, 1680 Mission St, San Francisco, CA 94103. Please RSVP here for the door code, we will work to make sure people without the code still get in but it’ll be quicker and more reliable if as many people as possible have it.

Who: Anyone who wants. You don’t have to pay money or know anything about the blog. Please feel free to come even if you feel awkward about it, even if you’re not “the typical ACX reader”, even if you’re worried people won’t like you, etc. You’re unlikely to be an outlier, regardless of whether you’re very weird, very normie, or somewhere in between.

Anyone who is caught expressing policy opinions will be herded into a side room and made to help create a San Francisco voting guide; if you expect this to be you, consider bringing your laptop or ballot materials.

items.articleBody:
Documentarian HD1080ide captured great footage of Amphib 2026, the annual European gathering of Les Amis de l’Amphibie in Berlin, featuring the world’s largest group of road-legal amphibious vehicles. The lineup included Amphicars, Volkswagen Schwimmwagen, an Amphicruiser, and custom-built vehicles that were driven into and cruised such waterways as Lake Wannsee and Lake Schwielowsee near Potsdam over several days in August 2026.

From August 1st to 8th, 2026, the world’s largest amphibious car meeting took place in Berlin. Among the partly extremely rare vehicles were numerous Amphicars, Schwimmwagen, Ford GPA (Seep), three Amphi-Ranger, an Amphicruiser, four DUKW and several custom-built vehicles.

The meet moves to a different European country each year, and every vehicle must be registered and able to both drive and swim.

The 2027 gathering is slated to take place in London. Amphibious vehicles have a history there, as seen in 1965 footage of an amphibious water scooter riding on the River Thames.

items.articleBody:
Giant Mirrored Sphere Will Turn the Beach Into a Celebration of Culture at Miami Art Week

Digital rendering of Christopher Joshua Benton’s “A Lore Supreme” on Faena Beach.

During Miami Art Week 2026, Faena Art will transform Miami Beach into a stage for large-scale public art. The program includes a new site-specific commission by Christopher Joshua Benton, an American Abu Dhabi-based artist whose practice brings together architecture, science, and community collaborators.

On Faena Beach, Benton will present A Lore Supreme, a giant disco ball or globe-like sculpture that is half buried in the sand. Standing 27 feet tall and spanning 44 feet, the kinetic sculpture features 7,000 mirrored facets that catch the light and shift with the wind. It features an abstract map, celebrating the countries and diasporic communities that have shaped Miami’s cultural identity. The huge sphere will also feature integrated speakers that will broadcast a soundscape of music and local voices, recorded during Benton’s conversations with local musicians, DJs, producers, and educators.

“Miami is one of those places where the city itself feels like a dance floor, a shared space where different cultures and communities come together, each bringing their own rhythm while moving alongside one another,” says Benton. “My research has taken me all over the city: I practiced some salsa at a pirate radio station, embodied the orishas at a Cuban folkloric dance class, went crate digging with local DJs, sang in a community choir, dived into local archives, played with drum machines at a recording studio, and learned the güiro over a Cuban sandwich at an iconic eatery in Little Havana. And of course, there was so much dancing!”

Other artists exhibiting during Miami Art Week include Marinella Senatore, who will transform Faena Cathedral with her an installation, An Expanded Baroque Crown. Described as a “temporary architecture of light,” the piece is rooted in the traditions of public celebration in Southern Italy and creates a social plaza inside the Cathedral.

You can visit these installations for free during Miami Art Week, running December 1-6, 2026.

items.articleBody:
In 1963, following nearly 70 years of British colonial rule, Kenya declared independence. The nation was not alone on the African continent; in the 1960s, Gambia, Guyana, Malawi, Nigeria, and others freed themselves from Britain’s control in a watershed period of democratic redevelopment and socio-cultural shifts. Wangari Mathenge, who was born in Nairobi, looks to the not-so-distant past in an ongoing series of vivid oil paintings.

Many of the works shown here are part of the artist’s current solo exhibition, Re-membering at Lévy Gorvy Dayan. Inspired in part by scholar Ngũgĩ wa Thiong’o’s 2009 book Something Torn and New: An African Renaissance, Mathenge examines her own cultural identity through the lens of Kenya in the first half of the 20th century. Something Torn and New focuses on the long-lasting impacts of colonialism and slavery in Africa.

“Re-membering XII (The Wednesday Women’s Club)” (2026), oil on canvas, 72 x 90 inches. Courtesy of Lévy Gorvy Dayan

The artist’s recent work depicts herself as all of the women, who each interact in domestic spaces. Toys, books, maps, and the occasional uncanny scenario, such as the green ladder in the wall of “Re-membering XI (To Leave This Steady Unendurable Land),” nod to a period of significant change in Africa. The figures often play with or alter the items in front of them, such as documenting a transatlantic vessel or jostling a teddy bear in an activity that blurs gutting and mending.

Sometimes, Mathenge’s protagonists meet the viewer’s gaze directly, almost confrontationally, while in other settings, she or he relaxes amid an array of items. Through the lens of cultural memory, the artist gathers symbols of resistance and healing. The compositions are sometimes paradoxical in their depictions of toys and nostalgic items with an underlying tension, like “Re-membering XIII (May the Wind Be Always at Your Back)” in which one of the figures readies an arrow in a bow.

“Re-membering signifies not merely the act of recall, but the active gathering and reassembly of what has been fragmented: cultural memory, inherited forms, histories, and ways of seeing,” the artist says in a statement. The exhibition continues through October 24 in New York. See more on Mathenge’s Instagram.

“Re-Membering II (Facing Mt. Kenya)” (2025), oil on canvas, 91.4 x 88.9 inches. Photo by Brian Griffin Art Photography, courtesy of Pippy Houldsworth Gallery

“Re-membering X (I Fall Upon the Earth, I Call Upon the Air)” (2026), oil on canvas, 20 3/4 × 20 3/4 inches. Courtesy of Lévy Gorvy Dayan

“The Ascendants XXIV (Tea O’clock with Neel’s Ringgold II)” (2023), oil on canvas, 84 x 62 inches. Photo by Brian Griffin Art Photography, courtesy of Pippy Houldsworth Gallery

“Re-membering XIII (May the Wind Be Always at Your Back)” (2026), oil on canvas, 71 7/8 x 82 inches. Courtesy of Lévy Gorvy Dayan

“The Ascendants XXIII (Oblivion)” (2023), oil on canvas, 63 x 63 inches. Photo by Brian Griffin Art Photography, courtesy of Pippy Houldsworth Gallery

items.articleBody:
Apple Newsroom:

 
New editorial collections for iPhone Duo apps and games will go
live on the App Store this Friday, with additional app updates
rolling out throughout the year. Apps optimized for iPhone Duo are
easy to identify with a Made for iPhone Duo badge on product pages
across the storefront.

This story highlights dozens of apps that have been optimized. This sort of transition happens every time Apple introduces a major screen change. It happened with the iPhone X in 2017, it happened when the iPhone 6 added a Plus size, it happened when the iPhone 5 changed the aspect ratio from 3:2 to 16:9, and, most memorably of all, it happened when the iPhone 4 went retina. Every time this happens it sucks to some varying degree of suckiness to use apps that haven’t been optimized. And soon enough, all apps still under active development get updated.

Developers know that iPhone users care how apps look and work. iPhone users will switch to competing apps for something like this. I stopped checking Mastodon on my phone for the last week and half because Ivory isn’t optimized. I stopped reading my messages on Signal — I just wait until I’m back at my desk. If I bought a Duo, I’d literally stop using Signal if they don’t update their app soon. Life’s too short to use shitty apps. iPhone developers get that.

Out of all those transitions I listed above, my gut feeling is that there are more third-party apps ready to go on day one for the Duo than for any of those previous transitions. No, it’s not all apps. Some of the apps that aren’t yet updated are quite popular, and others are ones that users can’t easily just switch away from (like, say, your bank’s app). But developer support is not a problem for the Duo. If anything the launch of the Duo has exemplified better than any event in iPhone history just how different the iPhone and Android developer communities are. “Flagship” Android foldables have been out for over 7 years and developer support for them today remains nothing close to developer support for the Duo — and the Duo doesn’t even launch until tomorrow.

 ★

items.articleBody:
Still Counting Episode 7 is ready. This episode is a little bit on the longer side. The original plan was to tell the story of the 2026 campaign through the ubiquitous ads that you’re undoubtedly seeing if you’re in a swing state. But then a bunch of polling-related news broke shortly before taping, such as a New York Times/Siena University poll showing strong numbers for Democrats on the generic ballot, and a scandal involving a fake “polling” firm called Wedgewood Polls.

I’ll have some extensive commentary about Wedgewood later in this post. But first, here’s the Still Counting video…

And here’s the audio. Once again, we’re very grateful for your reviews, comments, likes and subscribes.

The context

In 2009, I published a story at FiveThirtyEight suggesting that the prolific polling firm Strategic Vision was probably faking its data. It might have been a dumb risk. I never vetted the story with a lawyer, though I had asked Strategic Vision for comment, and their cagey responses reinforced my view that something weird was going on.

I thought the case was highly convincing, however. (I guess back then, I applied more of a “big forgiveness rather than ask permission” mindset.) Strategic Vision “polls” exhibited statistical patterns — namely, being far more likely to contain some trailing digits (such as 5, 7, 8 and 9) than others, including on obscure questions they probably thought would never be scrutinized — that were canonical signs of forged election results in authoritarian regimes. (Human beings are pretty bad at picking truly random numbers.) It was extremely unlikely these results had emerged by chance alone. My “spidey sense” also told me something was a little off about Strategic Vision’s results — though I forget exactly which details led me to that hypothesis.

But I was right — or at least I think that’s a reasonably safe assumption based on their subsequent behavior. The American Association for Public Opinion Research censured Strategic Vision for failing to disclose methodological information, and Strategic Vision never really attempted to provide any convincing refutation. They packed up their tent and left the industry.

The next year, in 2010, “polls” from another prolific firm, Research 2000, were discovered to contain similar anomalies. Research 2000 fought back a little harder, sending me a cease-and-desist letter, but Daily Kos, whom they were “polling” for at the time, sued them before they, too, disappeared. This was actually a bigger scandal than Strategic Vision. Research 2000 had frequently conducted “polls” for local newspapers and news outlets, presumably for a healthy amount of compensation.

Subscribe now

Earlier this week, Wedgewood Polls admitted it had fabricated data. It claimed its “polls” were an “experimental project to demonstrate the vulnerabilities, lack of oversight, and overall low barrier to entry in the modern political polling industry.”

My opinion is that Wedgewood’s explanation is bullshit, a pathetic attempt to get ahead of the story after FiftyPlusOne was set to publish a story exposing the fraud. Whether some sort of crime was committed was unclear — Wedgewood allegedly collected crowdfunded money for a poll that may or may not have ever been conducted.1 FiftyPlusOne reports that Wedgewood identified Jack Sims and Andrew Prater as the people behind the firm. Whoever was responsible for fabricating the data probably shouldn't be trusted with anything election- or poll-related again.

These “polls” had made their way into FLIPR, although they weren’t having much influence on the model. When we removed them from our database yesterday, FLIPR’s various averages and forecasts were basically unchanged. That’s a bit confounded because a lot of polls are coming out these days, including a strong series of generic ballot polls for Democrats published before yesterday’s update. Still, FLIPR includes precautions against being overly influenced by any one poll, and new/unknown pollsters start with fairly low ratings by default.

For what it’s worth, here were the Wedgewood “polls” that had entered our database, as compared to the Silver Bulletin averages at the time.

There’s a slight D-leaning “house effect” here, though it’s pretty mild and not particularly consistent. In races where Silver Bulletin was publishing polling averages (there are a couple of caveats here: see the footnote2), their “polls” were about 0.6 points more favorable to the Democratic candidate on average.

Wedgewood showed progressive candidates “polling” especially strongly

One thing that’s a bit unusual is that Wedgewood “polled” several races where there was little or no publicly-available polling at the time. At Silver Bulletin, we turn on the average for a race once there are three distinct polls from at least two distinct polling firms. Four races where Wedgewood issued a “poll” did not meet that distinction. As far as I can tell, in fact, Wedgewood was the first firm of any kind to “poll” Troy Jackson’s race against Susan Collins in Maine as Graham Platner was preparing to drop out; they had Jackson ahead by 5 points. 

In Michigan, meanwhile, Wedgewood was relatively early to “poll” Abdul El-Sayed’s race against Mike Rogers, showing him ahead by 5 points, better than the average3 which had AES ahead by 0.4 points instead. A Democratic candidate who dropped out, Mallory McMorrow, has alleged that Wedgewood’s “polls” hurt donor and voter confidence in her campaign.

In the table, I’ve only listed polls that included the eventual general election nominees because I’m not sure how comprehensive our data is on candidates who lost their primaries. Though an early July Wedgewood “poll” did have Francesca Hong leading by 3 points in the general election against Tom Tiffany in the Wisconsin gubernatorial race when other polls at the time showed the race roughly tied.

So there is something of a pattern here of Wedgewood showing better numbers for notably progressive candidates than the consensus, although it’s hard to know how much to make of three races. Not all of their “polls” ran in this direction, however. In Nebraska, they published a September “poll” showing incumbent Republican Gov. Jim Pillen ahead by 17 points against Democrat Lynne Walz, when subsequent polls have shown the race much closer.

Overall, compared with past fake pollsters — which often tried to fit in rather than draw attention to themselves — the Wedgewood “polls” were a bit more narrative-shaping. Though I also wouldn’t overstate this. Before news of the scandal broke on Tuesday, I was vaguely aware of an entity called “Wedgewood Polls” but couldn’t have told you anything about them beyond that. We tend not to dissect individual polls very much at Silver Bulletin4, especially when they come from polling firms we’ve never heard of. And we’d encourage others to take that approach, too. I generally object to focusing too much on any single polling result. Outlier polls tend to receive more attention than polls that align with the consensus. This isn’t necessarily bad because the alternative is too much herding. But there’s no longer any obviously correct, gold-standard way to conduct a poll. “Just plug it into the average” isn’t a perfect heuristic — there are certain polls I find dubious for various reasons. And our averages weight established pollsters with good track records more heavily. But it’s probably the least-worst alternative versus applying some sort of subjective filter to polls, which may reflect an aggregator’s rooting interests or other biases.

Polls are being vetted, actually

How did the Wedgewood data enter our model in the first place?

The literal answer is that we take our polling data from The New York Times, subject occasionally to some manual additions and overrides. This has several advantages. The NYT feed is fast, comprehensive, and staffed by highly skilled professionals. And contrary to what the Wedgewood fraudsters have alleged, the Times does a lot of vetting. (The NYT didn’t include polls from another fake polling firm, Median Strategies, for instance.) In addition, the NYT feed is fairly explicitly modeled on the old FiveThirtyEight database schema and their criteria for poll inclusion, which I helped to design. So it doesn’t make a lot of sense to recreate their efforts when they’re basically already doing the work in basically the same way that we’d do it.

But what are those “manual additions and overrides”? They fall into a couple of categories. We have a list of 11 permanently banned pollsters whom we know or believe the preponderance of evidence suggests fabricated data or engaged in other gross misconduct — our opinion, not necessarily “proof beyond a reasonable doubt”. Most of these polling firms, like Strategic Vision and Research 2000, are no longer active or are rejected by the NYT feed anyway, but FLIPR just ignores them if they enter our database.

On top of that, we have another set of polling firms we consider “nonprofessional.” We aren’t accusing these polls of being fake; we just think they don’t meet the standard of scientific polls. The official Silver Bulletin rule is as follows:

We don’t use DIY polls commissioned by nonprofessional hobbyists on online platforms such as Google Surveys.

As a result, we exclude certain pollsters, like from SoCal Strategies5 and ActiVote, that are sometimes accepted by other polling aggregators. I’m not sure that I’m eager to discuss these choices on a case-by-case basis. If we flag a polling firm as “nonprofessional,” they’ll almost inevitably lobby us and make their case. Sometimes we find this convincing, and sometimes we don’t. On the other hand, we manually add polls from Rasmussen Reports, which aren’t listed by the NYT, owing to a legacy decision by the post-Nate version of FiveThirtyEight that we strongly disagree with.

We will also sometimes add polls if we catch them right before publication of our daily update, and the NYT hasn’t added them yet. But generally, we’re not doing a lot of this. If the NYT hasn’t listed a poll, it may be because it didn’t pass their vetting.6 None of this is that urgent, and we’d rather wait a day or two to see whether the NYT and other aggregators have included the poll lest we add some fake or nonprofessional datapoint.

What Silver Bulletin generally hasn’t been doing, though, is conducting “secondary screening” once a poll passes through the equivalent of the TSA security perimeter — meaning the NYT database. And that’s because the NYT usually does a very good job with its vetting. As the New York Times explained in an editor’s note, when new pollsters enter their database, they’re subject to a fair amount of scrutiny including emails and phone calls.

Of course, someone willing to fake a poll may also be willing to fake answers in response to a vetting process. And this is probably getting easier because of AI (although AI can plausibly also help with fraud detection). Ultimately, thanks to the smart work of FiftyPlusOne, this particular scam was caught, however.

No vetting process is going to bat 1.000, however. What’s wrong with taking an incredibly strict policy? Well, if you were a frequent flier after September 11, you probably know. Vigorous screening can waste time for the vast majority of people doing nothing wrong. And overly strict screening can produce a lot of false positives and contribute to racial or other sorts of profiling.

At the same time, the American aviation system just doesn’t let people board planes without passing through some sort of screening process. It’s not quite “guilty until proven innocent,” but boarding a commercial airline is treated as a privilege and not a right.

Polling is roughly like that too. Overall, within the broader polling/forecasting community, there’s probably more screening and vetting than there was several years ago. New/unknown pollsters do not enter the NYT database without passing through a vetting process, and most of the other aggregators follow a similar if less formal approach7, including Silver Bulletin in cases where we maintain our own original database.8 

Are fake polls becoming more common?

So the industry is doing vetting and screening. But should the magnetometers be tuned to a more sensitive setting?

Probably. FiftyPlusOne’s G. Elliott Morris says his team will uncover other potential frauds soon too. 

Meanwhile, as I wrote above, I’m not a big fan of amateur/DIY polls and we strive not to include them, but that’s a different problem from fraud. 

Because we’re so close to the midterm date, I don’t expect the various polling aggregators to revisit their policies now, but it’s safe to assume there will be a lot of discussions about this before 2028.

But while fake polls are nothing new — indeed, there are probably some other Strategic Vision/Research 2000-type cases in the historical database that have never been detected — there are a couple of new risks.

One of them is publishing fake polls to manipulate prediction markets. Prediction markets have also been around for a long time but have far higher trading volumes now, potentially making for more profitable trades.9 I don’t know what Wedgewood’s motivations were. But publishing out-of-consensus “polls” or fake polls in sparsely-surveyed races have more potential to move markets.

Another motive might be to discredit the polling industry overall. President Trump and the White House, after all, have frequently used the term “fake polls” to refer to entirely valid polls when they show poor numbers for Republicans. 

And as I wrote above, I expect to see various AI-assisted schemes and scams in every industry, including polling.

Still, the proprietors of poll-collection and forecasting websites are less naive than Wedgewood alleges. People in the industry know the data really well, and from Strategic Vision to Wedgewood, everyone has caught their share of scams at some point. Our instincts about when something doesn’t pass muster are usually pretty good. Or at least, so we’d like to think. The smartest cheaters are the ones who never get caught.

Silver Bulletin news & notes

Look for more about this soon, but we’re planning on co-hosting our election night coverage with The Argument and GD Politics, plus a number of special guests including Still Counting’s Clare Malone. We’re not planning on building an Election Night model — it would be hard to do better than the NYT “Needle” anyway — but we should have a deeply knowledgeable set of panelists to cover both granular details and big-picture takeaways. 

Full disclosure: we need to test-drive the tech setup to figure out exactly what will be possible and what won’t. So no promises on the format just yet. Parts of the coverage will be reserved for paying subscribers, in case that’s any extra incentive to subscribe during what’s sure to be an exciting final 12 days of the campaign.

Subscribe now

1

Wedgewood claims the crowdfunded Nebraska poll was real even though the rest of their numbers were fake.

2

In these cases, I’ve used our average from the day before the final date that the Wedgewood “poll” was in the field. That ensures that the average wasn’t affected by the Wedgewood data itself. For example, if Wedgewood conducted a “poll” from Oct. 8-9, I’ve listed the average as of Oct. 8 because sometimes new polls are added quickly and can enter our averages on the same day as the final field date. Note that we began publishing our averages and FLIPR on Aug. 11 this year. For dates before then, I’ve used our retrospectively-calculated polling averages instead, as these generally closely resemble the averages at other polling websites.

3

Or really our retrospectively-calculated average since, as noted above, our polling averages launched on Aug. 11. There were plenty of other aggregators that had Michigan polling averages up at the time, however, and it was polling roughly as a toss-up at that time.

4

I’ll admit that we sometimes make exceptions for NYT/Siena since they’re among our most highly-rated pollsters and reliably provide an independent point of view. 

5

Sims previously worked at SoCal Strategies, which has, perhaps suspiciously, gone offline.

6

Speed was much more of an issue in 2024, when we relied on the feed from the resource-starved version of FiveThirtyEight instead as our first pass.

7

There is probably some degree of profiling here, to be fair. A poll published on a website from a high-prestige academic institution that hasn’t conducted political surveys before is going to get less vetting than a poll listed on X from a group of people nobody has ever heard of.

8

While we rely on the NYT feed for midterms “horse race” polls — meaning, polls for Senate, gubernatorial and House races — we maintain our own database of presidential approval polls, generic ballot polls, and certain other polling series.

9

I’m an advisor to Polymarket.

items.articleBody:
Ask many successful Indian CEOs, entrepreneurs, or scientists how they rose to prominence in America, and they will tell you that, grit and talent aside, the key factor was the country itself: an economy and a culture that rewarded merit and drew ambitious, talented people from around the world.

Indian Americans are among the most affluent and best-educated groups in the country. What distinguishes them from other immigrant groups is that they have risen to the top in one generation. Median household income for Indian Americans is $151,200, compared with $92,530 for white Americans. About three-quarters of Indian adults 25 and older in the U.S. hold a bachelor’s degree, against a national average of 38 percent. Nearly half have graduate degrees, and the poverty rate, 6 percent, is among the lowest of any ethnic group. Indian Americans tend to be employed and law-abiding.

For a community more accustomed to being called the “model minority” or “tech’s new titans,” a recent rise in anti-Indian rhetoric—now commonplace on sites and apps such as X, YouTube, and Reddit—has been a shock. According to Stop AAPI Hate, nearly half of South Asian adults living in America reported having been targeted in a “race-based hate act” in 2025 alone. From 2023 to 2025, the use of anti–South Asian slurs online surged by 109 percent. The Trump administration has also attacked immigrants coming from India with efforts to severely restrict the H-1B visa program, a legal pathway to American jobs; 70 percent of H-1B recipients are Indian. Despite two different judges blocking President Trump’s $100,000 fee for the visa, the administration claims that applications are down 92 percent at the largest IT-staffing and -outsourcing firms—a decline that it views as a massive success.

Indian immigrants have helped make this country great. America has long needed Indian immigrants, and it still does. But people who don’t understand the great contributions of Indian Americans would rather close the door, and are hostile to those who are already here.

By 1960, Europeans made up 75 percent of all immigrants in the U.S. By 2010, the balance had reversed, and Europeans were just 12 percent of all immigrants. According to U.S. Census Bureau data, in 1990 fewer than a million Indians were living in the U.S. A decade later, their numbers doubled because of a hiring spree for engineers to help avert a potential Y2K crisis. Today, some 5.2 million Indians reside in America, more than 60 percent of whom were born in India. Although they represent just 1.5 percent of the population, their sudden success has made them very visible—and that visibility has made them targets.

[Jonathan Chait: The mainstreaming of anti-Indian bigotry]

Indian-born executives are running several of the biggest technology companies, such as Google, Microsoft, IBM, and Adobe. They have been at the center of some people’s anger over AI and layoffs throughout the tech industry. In politics, the rise of Ro Khanna, Vivek Ramaswamy, Kamala Harris, and Zohran Mamdani has also caused online and real-life hate toward those with Indian heritage. For Americans uneasy about how the country is changing, seeing Indians in charge can feel more like a threat than a hopeful sign about the viability of the American dream.

Immigration politics have always been tangled up with discrimination. In the 1850s, the United States brought in cheap Chinese laborers to work its mines, farms, and railroads. When the economy shrank during the 1870s, the cry of “they’re taking our jobs”—familiar today—led to the Chinese Exclusion Act of 1882, which restricted Chinese immigration for the next 60 years. Japanese and, later, Korean workers met the same antagonism, and the Immigration Act of 1917, also known as the Asiatic Barred Zone Act, effectively shut out immigrants from most of Asia. The country went through a long period of xenophobia that targeted not only nonwhite immigrants but also “undesirable” white immigrants, such as Italians and Eastern European Jews. In 1910, the foreign-born population was 14.7 percent; by 1960, it had fallen to 5.4 percent.

In 1965, the Immigration and Nationality Act eased the old restrictions, in large part because the country was short of skilled labor, particularly in the STEM fields. Two developments drove the change.

The first was Sputnik. In 1957, the Soviet Union launched the first satellite into space. The U.S. military, fearful it was losing the Cold War, began investing heavily in science, sending large sums to top research universities. By the ’60s, the race had accelerated, but engineers were in short supply, so the country began recruiting overseas. Starting in 1950, India, in collaboration with foreign partners, had begun building world-class engineering schools called the Indian Institutes of Technology (IITs). Well-trained, English-speaking engineers began graduating just as the U.S. was desperate for them.

India had hoped that these engineers would help drive its own development, but it offered too few jobs, and the U.S. had found an ideal recruiting ground. Even today, the IITs remain fiercely selective, accepting less than 1 percent of roughly 1 million applicants per year. Sundar Pichai, the CEO of Google; Vinod Khosla, a venture capitalist and co-founder of Sun Microsystems; and Arvind Krishna, the CEO of IBM, are all IIT graduates. The first wave of Indian engineers was recruited after 1965. A second big wave came in the late ’90s, during Y2K preparations.

The second development was a need for doctors. In July 1965, President Lyndon B. Johnson signed the Medicare and Medicaid Act, and almost overnight, 20 million Americans became eligible for health care. Hospitals lacked the staff to cope. The Vietnam War was escalating, medical personnel were being sent to the front, and disabled veterans were returning home needing long-term care. Hospitals looked overseas, and India again supplied trained professionals to a strained system. Indian doctors were on the front lines of the AIDS epidemic in the ’80s and the coronavirus pandemic in the early 2020s.

[Meenakshi Ahamed: America has never really understood India]

The U.S. has benefited from the skills that Indians bring without having had to invest much in their education. Many have earned advanced degrees in America, but the bulk of their training happened in India. A more honest way to see it is that India, along with other poorer countries, has been subsidizing the United States.

Presidents like to define their eras with a slogan that conveys the legacy they hope to leave. John F. Kennedy called his the “New Frontier.” He was determined to win the Cold War and stop the spread of communism, and pushed the country toward space exploration while investing in science and technology. Johnson’s was the “Great Society.” His goal was to care for the elderly and the poor. Having known poverty firsthand, he wanted to extend health care to the vulnerable, and he signed both the Medicare and the Civil Rights Acts. Both of these presidents’ visions leaned on importing talent from abroad.

Trump’s slogan is “Make America Great Again.” Yet one of his lasting legacies may be that he turned his back on the very talent that helped make America great in the first place.

items.articleBody:
Wer nach einer Bonitätsprüfung eine Absage bekommt, kann unter Umständen erfahren, wie sein Score berechnet wurde. Ein Handyvertrag wird abgelehnt, und niemand sagt so recht, warum. Viele von euch kennen das. Der Bundesgerichtshof hat jetzt festgelegt, wann die SCHUFA genauer offenlegen muss, wie ein Scorewert zustande kommt. Entscheidend ist, ob ein Unternehmen seine Vertragsentscheidung wesentlich auf den übermittelten Score stützt.

Urteil von 2023 wird entscheidend

Den Anstoß gab der Europäische Gerichtshof im Dezember 2023. Die Luxemburger Richter stellten klar, dass die DSGVO Entscheidungen mit rechtlicher Wirkung grundsätzlich untersagt, wenn sie allein auf automatisierter Verarbeitung beruhen. Außerdem müssen Betroffene Zugang zu ihren Daten bekommen, um die Berechnung nachvollziehen zu können. Hierzulande änderte das zunächst wenig, weil das Bundesdatenschutzgesetz eine Ausnahmeregel enthielt.

Vier Klagen, wechselnde Urteile

In Karlsruhe ging es um vier Verfahren. Ein fünftes hatte sich vorab durch eine Einigung erledigt. Die Kläger hatten 2023 von der SCHUFA eine Datenkopie erhalten. Darin standen die gespeicherten Daten, Scorewerte, Ratingstufen und die genutzten Datenarten. Dazu kamen die Werte, die in den zwölf Monaten davor an anfragende Unternehmen gegangen waren. Den Klägern reichte das nicht. Sie hielten das Verfahren für intransparent und verlangten außerdem ihre außergerichtlichen Anwaltskosten zurück. Die Landgerichte wiesen die Klagen ab. Das Oberlandesgericht Dresden gab den Klägern dagegen teilweise recht und verpflichtete die Auskunftei zu weiteren Angaben.

Der BGH hob diese Urteile nun auf, soweit sie die SCHUFA belasteten, und verwies die Fälle zurück nach Dresden. Das Berufungsgericht habe nicht ausreichend geprüft, ob überhaupt eine automatisierte Entscheidung mit rechtlicher Wirkung oder erheblicher Beeinträchtigung vorlag. Eine Erklärungspflicht entsteht nämlich nicht bei jedem Score. Sie greift erst, wenn der Score für eine folgenreiche Entscheidung maßgeblich ist, etwa für die Ablehnung eines Vertrags.

Der zeitliche Zusammenhang genügt

Beweisen müssen das zwar die Betroffenen, die Hürde dafür liegt aber niedrig. Hat die SCHUFA einen Score übermittelt und folgt kurz darauf eine Absage, gilt die Vermutung, dass der Wert den Ausschlag gab. Bekommt ihr also nach einer Bonitätsabfrage keinen Mobilfunkvertrag mit neuem iPhone, müsst ihr nicht belegen, wie stark der Anbieter den Score gewichtet hat. Offen bleibt, wie ausführlich die SCHUFA ihre Berechnung erläutern muss. Dresden prüft nun, ob die Kläger erheblich beeinträchtigt wurden. Die Kläger dürfen ihre Anträge außerdem präzisieren, und über die Anwaltskosten ist noch nicht entschieden.

Bemerkenswert ist, dass der Streit noch das alte Scoring betrifft. Seit März 2026 nutzt die SCHUFA ein neues Modell, das den Basisscore aus dem Jahr 2008 ablöst, Apfelpage berichtete. Es beruht auf zwölf offen benannten Kriterien, darunter Zahlungsstörungen, das Alter des ältesten Bankvertrags und ein bestehender Immobilienkredit, der bis zu 55 Punkte bringt. Das alte Verfahren soll bis Ende 2028 auslaufen.

Der Beitrag SCHUFA-Score: BGH stärkt das Auskunftsrecht nach abgelehnten Verträgen erschien zuerst auf Apfelpage.

items.articleBody:
This article is crossposted from IEEE Spectrum’s careers newsletter. Sign up now to get insider tips, expert advice, and practical strategies, written in partnership with tech career development company Parsity and delivered to your inbox for free!

If you’re an engineer, you may feel like your skills aren’t commanding the premium they once did. Many engineers have faced layoffs or restructuring. But even for those of us who still have jobs, something corrosive is happening. You may have heard some version of this:

“ChatGPT answered that in five seconds. Why can’t you?”

Or, “I made this app in a weekend. Why is our team taking so long?”

I worked on a team where leadership said things like this directly to engineers. This was in 2024 and 2025, when the AI craze was in full swing and Claude and ChatGPT adoption was rising.

Demo-Driven Development

Generative AI (and the marketing behind it) gives people the illusion that the work is simpler than it is. A working demo hides complexity, and once someone has a website that works, they may decide they no longer need engineers, or start to distrust the ones they do have. 

Some CEOs want to believe they can replace an engineering team with a few sexy prompts. Many companies also want them to believe this.

That website works great in the demo—under specific conditions and without users with thumbs for fingers. Then it has to plug into a system with millions of lines of old code, satisfy legal requirements, meet accessibility standards, and be delivered in a complex deployment process.

Thinking that writing code was the only bottleneck for deploying new software is like the Titanic seeing the tip of the iceberg and assuming there was nothing underneath it.

What you can do about it

Engineers have a unique position in the AI space, because you have the capacity to understand how these models work much better than the average person. Use this to your advantage.

Learn how AI models work. If you can’t already explain that LLMs are probabilistic, what tokens are, or why training data matters, spend a weekend fixing that. You don’t need to become a full-blown AI researcher. A few fundamentals will put you ahead of most people making the AI decisions.

Teach upward. Turn that knowledge into teaching moments for the people who lead you. Explain the limits of these tools, and why a demo and a production system are different animals. It keeps people from truly believing that a notebook full of prompts can replace an engineering team.

Consider the criticism of today’s processes. Some of what we do has been treated as ceremony for too long. Be willing to say, “you know what, maybe you’re right, this process is too slow for the speed we can work at now.” Conceding that earns you the credibility to defend the steps that matter.

I still believe that speed at the cost of everything else is harmful—but that’s a topic for another time.

Find your voice. Engineers at the forefront of AI adoption need to push back and explain why we do things the way we do. Nobody else in the room is going to do it for us.

Don’t chase (too many) shiny objects

Your goal, in my opinion, is to save your organization from buying into the hype so much that they chase the wrong thing. Our job, before and after AI, is building safe and useful products for human beings, and engineers are still best suited for that.

—Brian

We Need to Embed Ethics Into Our Engineering Courses

The need to educate engineering students about ethics and social responsibility is widely recognized, but today’s curricula often miss the mark. Three professors propose a new approach: adding ethics training directly to core technical coursework. 

Read more here. 

The U.S. Just Bet $1 Billion on Quantum Chip Manufacturing

Looking for a career in quantum computing hardware? An IBM spin-off called Anderon could receive up to $1 billion in funding from the U.S. CHIPS and Science Act for its quantum foundry, established earlier this year. Could Anderon do for quantum hardware what TSMC did for conventional chips? 

Read more here. 

Meet the Anthropic Engineer Keeping Its AI Agent Trustworthy

When Gurmeet Saran joined Anthropic’s technical staff in 2025, he entered a role focused on a key question: How do you know whether you can trust a chatbot like Claude? Learn more about Saran’s path and his work at the AI company. 

Read more here.

The October 8 shooting of Oscar Belgal by Immigration and Customs Enforcement agents in front of his 5-year-old son in Manhattan forced into the open a question that had been on many New Yorkers’ minds: What would the New York Police Department do when ICE broke the “rule of law” in the city, and how would Mayor Zohran Mamdani, the person who has the power to hire and fire the NYPD commissioner, respond?
