items.articleBody:
NYPD Commissioner Jessica Tisch and Mayor Zohran Mamdani attend an unveiling ceremony for a new 9/11 Memorial Wall on Sept. 9, 2026, in New York City. Photo: Michael M. Santiago/Getty Images 
 

The October 8 shooting of Oscar Belgal by Immigration and Customs Enforcement agents in front of his 5-year-old son in Manhattan forced into the open a question that had been on many New Yorkers’ minds: What would the New York Police Department do when ICE broke the “rule of law” in the city, and how would Mayor Zohran Mamdani, the person who has the power to hire and fire the NYPD commissioner, respond? 

Shortly after the shooting, Mamdani addressed the incident with an appropriate amount of outrage, declaring ICE “rotten to its core,” and calling for the department to be abolished. His frustration was visible, but he was much less expressive when it came to his appraisal of the city’s response to the situation. He had nothing substantive to discuss with respect to his police department’s involvement, despite NYPD officers arriving on the scene only to find unidentified ICE agents holding guns, wearing plain clothes and disguises and masks, in apparent violation of federal laws requiring identification. (A recently passed New York state law prohibiting federal agents from wearing masks and other face coverings was temporarily blocked by a judge.) NYPD officers applied first aid and transported Belgal to NewYork-Presbyterian Allen hospital.

According to many eyewitness accounts and widely circulated video, members of the NYPD appeared to assist ICE agents by forcefully helping with crowd control — at one point, an NYPD officer shoved congressional candidate Darializa Avila Chevalier, whom Mamdani personally stumped for, to the ground. Later, NYPD cleared a path for federal agents to whisk Belgal away from the hospital to a federal detention facility downtown. 

 

 
 
 

 Related 

 
ICE Shooting in NYC Inflames Mamdani’s Policing Problem

 
 
 

After the shooting, the Democratic Socialists of America, several legislators, and Avila Chevalier all called on Mamdani to fire NYPD Commissioner Jessica Tisch and demanded the mayor uphold his campaign pledge to disband the NYPD’s infamous Strategic Response Group. Mamdani repeatedly refused to fire Tisch but said he was reviewing the 24-hour period around the shooting. When asked directly about Avila Chevalier being thrown to the ground, the mayor called it unacceptable, saying, “That is not something I will look to justify.” He reminded New Yorkers to be patient with efforts to reform the NYPD, ordered a review of the department’s use-of-force policies, and added funding for the inspector general’s office. But once again, he stood by his commissioner, citing “her record of uprooting corruption from the upper echelons of the NYPD while lowering crime across our city.”

Noticeably absent from any of Mamdani’s public remarks about the NYPD or Tisch was any public acknowledgment of the NYPD officers in relation to ICE agents during the Belgal incident. 

Federal and city law enforcement occupy similar spaces but never really interact with each other. Mamdani made no mention of the ways in which the actions of federal agents put pressure on the NYPD as mediators — the primary function of police — to liaise in moments of conflict. 

The NYPD typically relishes this role, which is why the department consumes so much of New York’s budget and shuns any attempts to redirect funds to other services that might reduce the need for police mediation to begin with. ICE forces local police to make choices in policy and in practice about how to deal with violent (often illegal) immigration operations.

If the NYPD believes itself to be the thin blue line, on which side of order and chaos do New York’s force and Mamdani believe these federal outside agitators to be?

When it comes to ICE, Mamdani’s rhetoric and policies haven’t always aligned, which has opened him up to questions about the kind of mayor he really is.

This omission — or evasion, depending on how you look at it — of this predicament is strange considering Mamdani’s willingness to speak with moral clarity about even the most contentious issues and confront them head-on. It’s also bizarre considering his penchant for weaving shared experiences together and for putting the lived experiences of New Yorkers front and center. 

On the campaign trail, one of Mamdani’s most alluring traits was his ability to speak to the actual problems of everyday residents. It wasn’t just because he possessed once-in-a-generation oratory skills; candidate Zohran achieved this because, as a proud democratic socialist, there was an analysis — an explanation of the material conditions of life — baked into his politics. His rhetoric seemed in line with, or at least not alienated from (see: establishment Democrats), how fast reality was moving and how it was impacting the lives of everyday New Yorkers.

When it comes to ICE, however, Mayor Mamdani’s rhetoric and policies haven’t always aligned, which has opened him up to questions about the kind of mayor he really is. On one hand, he has shown that he will speak out against Trump’s fascist and inhumane immigration efforts. On the other hand, Mamdani hasn’t moved with the same level of force as his words. Many have pointed out that Mamdani seems to be engaging in realpolitik in an effort to get his extensive progressive agenda passed. It’s certainly not easy to bring the machine of the New York government up to speed while also being transparent about the ways in which he is moving the needle. But that’s exactly what he was elected to do.

Had Mamdani got into office and done nothing different than previous mayors — or even been exceptionally corrupt, pro-cop, and willing to help the Trump administration like predecessor Eric Adams — he might have been able to avoid his current moment of reckoning. But his administration’s genuine efforts on immigration set into motion a future where the NYPD and ICE would come into conflict. 

One of Mamdani’s first moves as mayor was to take stock of how the city’s many agencies were upholding existing sanctuary city laws. In February 2026, he signed Executive Order 13, his first major order pertaining to immigration, to create the Mayor’s Office of Immigrant Affairs and establish baseline guidance, such as explicitly prohibiting ICE and other non-local law enforcement agencies from using city-owned garages and vacant lots. Crucially, EO 13 also required an audit of several agencies, including NYPD, to review their immigration-related policies.

 

 
 
 

 Related 

 
Local Cops Flout Sanctuary Law to Help ICE Deport Immigrants

 
 
 

NYPD already has a problematic history dealing with immigration enforcement. During the Adams administration, there were documented cases where the NYPD assisted or collaborated with immigration enforcement, sometimes in accordance with NYPD policies. A December 2025 report by Jocelyn Strauber, then-commissioner of the New York City Department of Investigation, found at least one incident in which “an officer violated local law by providing assistance to federal authorities in connection with enforcement of the federal civil immigration law,” as well as evidence that NYPD did “not fully comply with documentation and reporting requirements concerning requests for assistance with federal civil immigration enforcement.” The report also found that there were numerous examples of NYPD policies and practices that elevated the “risk of improper information sharing or assistance to federal authorities for purposes of civil immigration enforcement.”

The resulting audit, which was released on May 22 by Mamdani’s deputy mayor, built on those findings and recommended NYPD (and other city agencies) update its reporting requirements. But the audit also left a lot of open questions, which numerous legal advocates attested to, about areas in which NYPD protocols and policies keep avenues open to potentially collaborate with ICE. The NYPD was “not being held to a high standard of accountability or scrutiny for collusion,” the audit found, and there were significant “gaps” in documenting potential violations of department policies. The question of what the city and its mayor could do to ensure compliance also remained unanswered.

Sanctuary laws prohibit using city resources for immigration enforcement, and a January 2025 NYPD internal memo specifically barring officers from facilitating street closures to enable immigration enforcement seemed to solidify that directive. But several high-profile incidents involving the NYPD have tested the department’s compliance with sanctuary laws. In October 2025, before Mamdani was elected, during an immigration raid in Chinatown, eyewitnesses and viral videos showed NYPD officers establishing perimeters to create a path for federal law enforcement agents. In another instance in May 2026, ICE reportedly “dragged” a Nigerian immigrant out of a Brooklyn hospital after agents used force in his arrest; NYPD officers brutalized and arrested numerous protesters and cleared debris from the road to enable ICE to escape the crowds and abscond with their target.

When the NYPD arrives at an ICE raid or at a protest against an immigration abduction, what are officers supposed to do?

Both of these incidents happened under the watch of Tisch, who has insisted again and again that the department follows all sanctuary laws. When asked about the Brooklyn incident, Mamdani insisted NYPD was responding to 911 calls about the protest, not helping ICE. “Our laws leave nothing, no room for interpretation about the fact that our NYPD will not participate in civil immigration enforcement,” he said. NYPD told the Guardian US: “Upon arrival, officers observed numerous individuals acting in a disorderly manner, obstructing vehicular traffic, and blocking emergency entrances and exits at Wyckoff Heights medical center.” 

 

 
 
 

 Related 

 
LAPD Won’t Do Immigration Enforcement — But Will Shoot You With Rubber Bullets for Protesting ICE

 
 
 

When the NYPD arrives at an ICE raid or at a protest against an immigration abduction, what are officers supposed to do? On this point, NYPD and Mamdani have offered little clarity. But October 8 doesn’t pass the smell test for anyone who lives in overpoliced neighborhoods or closely observes the activity of police and their behavior.

NYPD officers were responding to an unrelated call nearby when they heard the report of shots fired. When they arrived, they encountered several men in various forms of attire, including some in construction-style vests, face masks, and at least one carrying a long gun, which officer body camera footage released by the Department confirms. The official account of the NYPD’s interaction offers no mention of ICE. There are no additional insights or explanations of department protocol that might shed light on how officers are supposed to act given the circumstances. Curiously, what those officers thought when they encountered several masked men with guns, and the conversations that took place between the ICE agents and the police, is a mystery, too. All we know is that officers agreed at some point that the NYPD would place Belgal in a vehicle, apply aid, and take him to the hospital. 

Since that evening, Mayor Mamdani has stood firm in his condemnation of ICE and their operations. “We will not normalize ICE’s viciousness,” he said, calling for the agency to be abolished. That’s the least he could say to reassure New Yorkers he understands the stakes they feel in their bones already. The shooting of Oscar Belgal and his subsequent inhumane treatment — his lawyers say Belgal is still in solitary confinement with a bullet in his neck — is a reminder of how normalizing ICE operations in New York City is already well underway. 

 

 
 
 

 Related 

 
Bill de Blasio Promised to Change the NYPD. His Courage Failed Him, and Us.

 
 
 

There have been more lower-profile ICE sightings and kidnappings, which echoes what has been the case in other parts of the country. What Mamdani will do to bring the city’s response into alignment with the needs of New Yorkers in this moment still remains an open question, including clarifying the NYPD’s role in the city’s ongoing fight against the Trump administration’s gestapo tactics.

If this month’s incident offered a lesson for Mamdani, it is that clearly articulating what is right is a full-time job that requires an unwavering willingness to confront reality. It’s not enough to say the thing on one issue — calling a genocide by its name, publicly dragging FIFA for pandering to wealthy elites, or deriding the inhumane practices of slumlords — but not stand on business when it comes to the reality that New Yorkers are seeing on their own streets. 

Sometimes, an actual seismic event can reveal what needs to be done and that there are alternatives that may not have been fully realized before. Hope isn’t lost. There is still time for Mamdani to update his analysis. But in this moment, the mayor must make a choice: renew his commitment to the truth, or be defined by its absence. 

The post Mamdani’s High-Wire Balancing Act Between ICE and NYPD Can’t Last appeared first on The Intercept.

items.articleBody:
Warm welcome to Basil Chatha, our newest cohost from the Forward Deployed side of the AI Engineering world! We’ll be ramping up a new show with him and couldn’t pass up an interview with Modal’s CEO Eric on the occasion of their monster Series D!

Two years ago, we spoke with Erik Bernhardsson about his vision for truly serverless AI infrastructure: developers should be able to run code without provisioning clusters, predicting load, or paying for idle resources. CTO Akshat then joined us to talk about Modal’s infra primitives and stack to offer those primitives and agent experience.

A lot has changed in the past 5 months. Since their $5B series C, Modal now reports it crossed $1 billion in annualized run rate, raised a $750 million Series D at a $16B valuation, and has spun up nearly three billion sandboxes. In this conversation, Erik joins Vibhu to explain the infrastructure and economics behind that growth—and why demand for compute rarely looks like the contracts used to buy it.

Watch the full conversation on YouTube →

GPU demand isn’t rectangular

A typical capacity contract gives a customer a fixed number of GPUs for a fixed period. Plot capacity against time and you get a rectangle. Real workloads behave differently: they grow, spike, and fall throughout the day. Buy enough for the peak and you pay for idle hardware; buy less and you risk missing demand.

Erik describes Modal’s bet as a kind of duration transformation: pool demand across thousands of customers, secure capacity underneath, and let each customer use what they need when they need it. The smoother the aggregate demand, the more useful that pool can be. It’s a useful companion to our conversation with SF Compute’s Evan Conrad: Evan focuses on making capacity tradeable; Erik focuses on making it usable in smaller, elastic slices.

There is a financial risk on the other side. If a provider locks in capacity at today’s prices and GPU prices later fall, it can be left holding expensive supply. Erik says he doesn’t expect an imminent collapse, but thinks the possibility matters when building the business. Jump to the GPU price discussion →

The sandbox that almost didn’t make it

Modal launched sandboxes after Erik and cofounder Akshat Bubna noticed that language models could generate code—and that someone would need a place to run it. Early adoption was modest enough that the team discussed shutting the product down. Then coding agents, background agents, and reinforcement learning created new demand. Erik says sandboxes have grown to roughly a third of Modal’s revenue, a result he didn’t predict at launch.

That growth also changes what infrastructure has to do. An agent may create an environment, run code, inspect the result, and try again many times. The latency of starting and restoring those environments becomes part of the experience. In our recent interview with Akshat, we explored this shift from developer experience to agent experience; here Erik adds the product and business story. Jump to the sandbox discussion →

Fast startup is an infrastructure feature

Elasticity only works if capacity can arrive quickly enough to matter. Modal’s serverless GPU write-up describes the machinery: a buffer of available GPUs, a custom filesystem, process checkpointing, and GPU memory snapshots. Those pieces reduce the work needed to bring another model replica online. It is a concrete example of how infrastructure decisions show up in an application’s responsiveness and cost.

We also discuss Erik’s path from Spotify’s recommendation system to Modal, how the company buys compute, alternatives to NVIDIA, forward-deployed engineers, and why code review is optional at Modal. Jump to engineering culture →

0:00 Thanks for coming on, Eric Fern-Hartson from Modal. Could you explain the business a little bit and maybe how you got here? Yeah. So we build, the easiest way to put it is we build AI infrastructure. So we offer a compute platform and a storage platform that enables a lot of customers like Dacagon, and Suno, and Runway, and Cognition, and many others to essentially build AI applications. So what that means in practice is a lot of inference, a lot of sandboxes, sometimes training and fine-tuning, sometimes batch jobs and other things. So we have basically built a software SDK that enables customers to move really fast and build this. We manage all the capacity underneath, make it easier to deploy and scale and run these things in production. So you were on Light and Space like two years ago, a lot has happened since then. How big were you back then, like whatever numbers you can share and comparatively, how big are you now? I actually don’t remember where we were, but it’s probably like at least 50X, there’s revenue and users and users. Yeah. I use it actually for a side project that I have. Nice. Yeah. It’s like, yeah, turn 2D images into 3D models. Yeah. So yeah, just hosting a couple of models here. What do you think? Any feedback? I mean, I love it. Nice. Good. I mean, yeah, that’s why I use it over any competitors or anything. Good. So before you started Modal, you were at Spotify and also like better.com, I think.

1:30 That’s right. Yeah. Yeah. What were you doing at Spotify? I actually did a lot of different things at Spotify, but my main contribution was I built a music recommendation system. The first version I joined after school in 2008, 2009 maybe, and spent seven years at Spotify. And most of that time was building basically from scratch and music recommendation system and built up a small team and we launched a bunch of features like related artists and Discover Weekly and a bunch of other stuff. So a lot of, a lot of matrix factorization, a lot of compute intensive stuff. And arguably like a lot of what sort of later became the genesis of Modal was just building AI applications and realizing like the infrastructure fucking sucks. Like, there’s got to be a better way to do that. So a lot of sort of, you know, the rationale for Modal was like kind of building a tool I always wanted to have throughout my years at Spotify. Yeah. So Modal was more of an offshoot of the stuff you learn at Spotify, not much from Better.com. Better.com was a little bit of a side tour. It was kind of a roller coaster, a long story about the company. We talked about it separately. But I was a CTO for five years of better and grew to a tech team from, I think, you know, two to three, four hundred. So I learned a lot about management and building teams and hiring and also learned a lot about developer productivity. I thought a lot about tools and things like that. Did a lot more like full stack stuff. But yeah, I kind of came back to my, was close to my heart, which is infrastructure and AI and machine learning after that. What was Better.com doing again? Mortgages. Okay. Yeah. How did you get into that?

3:00 I mean, we don’t have to spend too much time on that. Yeah, no, it’s fine. Like this guy, Zach Frankel, who I didn’t know at that time, ended up recruiting me to Better as a CTO and the company was 10 people. And, you know, for whatever reason, you know, the founder of Vishal, very interesting guy, very, very smart, a little crazy in mostly positive ways. We got very well along. So we, yeah, we started building it in 2015 and I spent five years growing that company and then, you know, eventually turned out that doing mortgages is pretty hard and, you know, interest rates went up very quickly after the pandemic and that cost a lot of issues at the company. But by then I had already left. That was like 2020, 2021 when you left? Yeah, something like that. Yeah. So, OK, you left before you had the idea for a model or you left and then you started? It’s hard to say. I had a lot of random ideas when I left Better and I, I actually wasn’t sure if I wanted to start a company. I was kind of just, you know, during the pandemic, I sort of almost took like a sabbatical at two kids. I mean, I still have kids, but I mean, at that time there were there were I think two and four and so I decided to hang out and took some time off and was kind of working like part-time, like hacking on certain things and wasn’t sure maybe I should do some consulting and I started building stuff. And I just got like super pumped about this idea that eventually became model. But actually both, you know, model was like, I think the 30 I built that I got, you know, that so there were like a few attempts before then that went nowhere.

4:30 But my model was like the first idea was like, this is kind of cool. Like I should do this. This is like, this could be a really cool platform. Were the other ideas like also in a similar vein like developer tools? The first thing was like some sort of web scraping thing, which went nowhere. But actually, you know, in hindsight, maybe could have gone somewhere. And was this before the chat GBT launch? Yeah. Yeah. 2021. Oh, OK. So chat GBT was late 2022, right? Then I started building, so maybe actually to rewind a little bit context, like when I worked at Spotify, I released an open source framework, Kaluigi, which is like workflow orchestration. So sort of the same categories, airflow and pre-effect index or sort of dated categories to some extent, like people don’t talk about as much. But for a while, it was like, you know, got a lot of attention. Anyway, I never turned it into business. But a couple of years later, when in 2021, when I was thinking about business ideas or things to work on, I kind of came back to workflow orchestration. And I started hacking on a bunch of ideas of, you know, running code in the, you know, like basic orchestrating code running in the cloud. And what I realized was like, you know, at the end of the day, like core puzzle pieces, not just like orchestrating the computer, it’s like executing the computer. And I was like, that’s kind of a bigger problem actually to solve. So in a way, I actually like, you know, left it on the shelf and then said, like, actually, I’m going to like go to this other thing over here and I’ll go back. I’ll get back to the workflow scheduling a little bit. But, but like, you know, I never got back to long story short and ended up building modal, which is like the focus is more like, let’s just figure out a way to make it easy to run code in the computer, in the cloud. And the focus was initially like fairly general purpose.

6:00 And it actually in a way like it’s always, we’ve kind of gone full circle more recently, but, but we focused on so many different applications. It’s kind of the idea was like, let’s just make it super easy to run code in the, in the cloud. Could be GPU code, AI, machine learning. It could also be like data stuff. And focused a lot on, you know, how do we scale it up? How do we make the developer experience awesome? Realized super early that like in order to do that, we’d have to go very deep in a stack and built on file system, built on container runtime and did a lot of, you know, solved a lot of hard engineering challenges. And then you mentioned chat, CPT, that was actually not quite the killer app. But like, if you remember, like that fall, another thing came out around the same time, which was stable diffusion and stable diffusion turned out to be a killer app for our, for what we’re building at that time. We were only four or five people at that time. So we started seeing a lot of people coming to us and wanting to run a stable diffusion model. And then we were real, that, that, that made us realize like maybe gen AI inference is actually a really good use case for us. And how are you finding it? I’m just like compulsive tweeter. I was even more like now, like I’m too distracted by building a company, but I always like tweeted a lot. I was blogged a lot. So I think I had a little bit of a following. And so, you know, in the early days, I like a lot of what drove the growth was just like me just compulsively just like tweeting about model and like what I was building and getting people excited and writing long blog posts about where the cloud is going and all these things. And I call it a bit like founder led marketing. I always like feel like you kind of have to lean into like what you’re good at

7:30 and like what I’m good at is like, I guess like just shit posting and being terminally online. And so, you know, like work, it’s still like, you know, I think a lot of our growth is we’re just kind of good at social media and just like being, you know, online a lot. Nice. How long until you had your first customer? It took a while. Also, did you raise like early on? We didn’t raise for a while. I actually self funded it for a while, even with up until the first few employees, which in a way was like kind of nice because it may be really like frugal about money and like wanting to see like ROI. I wasn’t taking out a salary for a while for a long time. Actually, at some point it became a problem because I needed the money, but we didn’t raise for a while. And until early 2022, we raised the seed rounds. So at that point I’d already been working on it for about a year. Akshah joins the CTO and co-founder in about five years ago, about now August, maybe 2021. But then it took until like basically like late 2022 for us to see any meaningful revenue. I guess that’s why I’m proud of you. Yeah. And stable diffusion then in our case was the main thing that’s sort of, so we went from like, you know, $100 a month in like, I think like November, 2022. And the next month we did like $2,000 a month. And then like January, 2023, we did like 30,000 all of a sudden. And, you know, so finally I felt this like massive, just like anxiety thing off my chest. I’m like, maybe this is actually like we’re onto something. It feels like we’re onto something. And then 2023 we grew very fast.

9:00 And I guess we’ve been growing very fast since then basically. That 30 K a month moment, was that just like a couple of big customers or was it like very diverse? It’s just one. And I don’t know if I ever talked about like who that was and if they even know it, but I think they suspect it. It was a company in New York called Mage. They’re doing like a stable diffusion company. So at some point, you know, in the first, I think first quarter of 2023, I think there were like 80, 90% of our revenue. But then after that, you know, it started diversifying a little bit. And late 2023, we got soon as a big customer. They were a big chunk of our revenue for a while too. But then, you know, it’s over time, like we actually have really good revenue diversification now. Yeah. For the stable diffusion stuff, I remember using it for like comfy UI. I’m assuming a lot of people were using comfy UI, like running comfy UI workflows on it. Some people were, but I think the people that were using model, they tended to be more like low level stuff. Like they did like complicated stuff. What they like with models, like it’s always been pretty hackable. So they deployed their own custom workflows with adapters and custom inference and a lot of optimizations and all the stuff we had done in order to get the developer experience to be really good, turn out to be really good for also running production workloads. Cause auto scaling turns out to be actually a very similar problem. Like you want to scale up containers up and down very fast. So we just happened to be like very well positioned to capture a lot of those workloads in the early days. Did tools for auto scaling like not exist? Like why did you have to build those yourself?

10:30 In general, like my thesis is like, you know, every new sort of era of like, you know, technology kind of runs up against limitations of tools. You know, whether that’s you look back, you know, like the web or the cloud or, you know, mobile or PCs or, you know, AI or whatever. So I think, you know, it’s often the case that tools exist, but, but they’re often not like particularly good. And often you kind of need to rethink a lot of those tools in order to reap the benefits of, you know, and really turbo charge and start building for this new world. And you saw this with cloud, you know, we have to invent things like Kubernetes and Docker and things like that. And in a similar way, you know, like with, with gen AI, you could build these things on the sort of prior generation of tools. Like you can, you can build these things on top of Kubernetes and Docker and in these things, but, but, but those technologies are built for a very different type of workload. They’re built for a very sort of steady work, steady back end workloads. They have an even, you know, steady number of requests, like running a pretty low utilization because CPUs are normally pretty cheap. And so people don’t really worry so much about cost. And, but now we’re entering this new world and you have, you know, very expensive GPUs you want to manage capacity and utilization. You have very large models that you need to load over network into CPU into GPU. And, and it turns out like a lot of these tools, like, you know, like they were just not built for that. So we felt that, you know, we had to rebuild a lot of that, you know, building our own, I mentioned the file system, but we also spent a lot of time over the last few years, like building, you know, some really cool stuff around like CPU

12:00 snapshotting, GPU snapshotting and audit, we built on autoscaler and scheduler and, and, and in all kinds of capacity management tools. And we kind of feel like you have to do that because like you can’t build, you know, for this new generation of software on top of, you can’t build like a wrapper on top of the old stuff in order to do the new stuff. You kind of need to start over a little bit from scratch. So I guess like the auto scaling, like did you, did you see any like weird behaviors on the platform? Like was there anything that like broke while you guys were scaling? I mean, capacity is always from time to time been, been a challenge. Like how do you get like, you know, hundreds and thousands and tens of thousands of GPUs? So that’s, that’s always challenging. We had to go multi region very early. So I think that was like kind of a fateful decision in hindsight, like doing that and kind of just biting the bullet and building it. Like we always thought of like our capacity management as like one big pull. Like it’s like one big pull over the entire world. Like we don’t think of it as like separate clusters running in each region. And so that was like one of the like very consequential decisions we made early to kind of think about it that way. So I don’t know if there’s like been like, you know, specific issues. I mean, we’ve obviously had bugs and, you know, outages and I hate, you know, as much as I, you know, would love for a model to be a hundred percent uptime, you know, and I think recently we’ve basically hit four or five nines, but throughout the history of model, of course, we’ve had, you know, some run up against scaling issues. Yeah. The GPU market and well, actually before that. So you guys use AWS like GCP, like all these cloud providers underneath.

13:30 Like do you also buy any infrastructure? No, let’s talk a bit about like cloud capacity. Because I think it’s actually changed a lot. Like in the first few years we did, we got almost all the capacity pretty much from, from the hyperscalers spot and on demand capacity, mostly spot capacity, running in all the different regions, you know, using initially AWS, but also GCP and overtime measure. We started renting some capacity from Oracle pretty early because we wanted the eight tens and eight 100s and we got really good rates on those. And over time we added a couple more clouds, like doing reservations, but, but like still up until like actually end of last year, like most of our capacity was either spot or one year reservations. Spot means you’re just like renting it right there and then. Exactly. Yeah. And it’s also preemptible, which we had to deal with. But, but it sort of works in Agria because you can sort of just, you know, aggregate capacity from many, you know, hundreds of regions basically. So that, that, that model worked really well until we started running up again. I mean, first of all, like modal started growing like very fast as we needed more capacity, but fundamental also like the cloud market started changing a lot. So in the last year, basically now in order to get the capacity we need, we had to work with a much larger set of clouds. We actually work with almost 25 clouds at this point. And in many cases, in order to get the capacity we want, like we, we have to go into, you know, three plus year deals and you have to pay a meaningful amount of money upfront. And you’re locking in pricing on a three year term, right?

15:00 So, you know, like, and, and, and so we have to spend the entire, you know, last six to nine months, like, you know, kind of rethinking how we get capacity. We have to build a whole procurement like desk, like we have like four guys working full time basically, all they’re doing is like procuring capacity, calling Neoclouds, you know, doing deals, vetting the capacity. We’ve had to build a whole engineering team, basically 10 people just like managing like bare metal capacity from all over the world and dealing with network issues and bad drives and GPUs falling off the bus and, and all these things. We don’t own capacity. We rent all the capacity so far, um, you know, on, on, on typically this three year deals. And that’s like a big decision. Like, should we buy, should, should we, you know, or should we keep renting? I’m actually like not like mega dogmatic about it. I think renting is nice because there’s a certain amount of capital efficiency to it. If you’re buying, you know, like, I mean, first of all, there’s not this like operational complexity of it. Like you have to, you know, deal with vendors and suppliers and, and, you know, power and, and, and cables and all kinds of stuff. But there’s also, you know, financial complexity to it. Like, how do you fund it? Like, should you raise equity, you know, and, and you can raise a billion dollars and go buy hardware for it. That’s a very dilutive way to do it. Um, you can raise debt, but you know, if you raise that, you know, you typically want to have like locked in long-term revenue to, to, to pay the interest rates. That’s also not trivial. But you know, like we look at the economics, we look at, uh, the operational

16:30 complexity, we look at the risks. Uh, it’s a complex trade-off and, and we’re open to, to, to buying. We’ll, we’ll sort of, there’s other constructs too. Like we’re, it’s to get the capacity we need for, for 2027. It’s going to take a lot of work on, on, you know, going a lot of different avenues to, to lock it up. So do you have to hire a lot of like finance people to do all this stuff or not? Really? You know, I’ve had to spend a lot of time on this and we’ve had to, to, to spend a lot of time on this. And I do think over time, I mean, there, there is a lot of, you know, these are very expensive assets, uh, the hardware. And, you know, I think, I mean, it’s kind of staggering. You starting to see like AI investments starting to become like several percentage points of, of, of GDP of the U S and, you know, starting to see like interest rates in, in America, shooting up in the last few weeks. And I mean, I like, at this stage, like, you know, and you go and look at the Neoclouds, like these are very, very sophisticated financial engineering companies. And so yeah, we, we look at that and, you know, we look at all the options and, and it’s possible we might have to do similar things ourselves. I wouldn’t want to like, I would rather focus on being, you know, like a very lean software company, like doing the things we’re good at. I don’t think it’s good in general for software companies to own hard assets. You know, in the same way as like, should you own your office? Like I don’t think that’s necessarily the right solution for most companies. But of course, like in order to get the capacity you want, like, you know, everything is on the table. Yeah. And I guess the supply is going to be constrained for a while.

18:00 So you kind of have to do that. Like, do you, do you agree with that? Or do you think this is just like a moment in time? I don’t necessarily agree with that. I mean, like Nvidia is delivering, you know, several hundred thousand black walls, you know, a month, right? And, and I don’t want to say like the market is like 100% efficient, but like, you know, in general, like if you’re willing to pay a high price, you can get GPU capacity, right? Like if you’re willing to pay more than everyone else, and, and of course, Anthropic and OpenAI is buying up as much as they can. And, but fundamentally, like there’s constantly supply coming on the market. And so I don’t necessarily think it’s like a fully cornered resource. Prices are going up. And I do think it’s worth kind of reflecting on that. It’s like the normal state of hardware is like, it’s like out of like gravity. Like eventually, hardware prices always go down. So we’re a little bit in like a weird sort of period of time where like hardware prices are going up. And, you know, it’s hard to say, you know, how long this is going to last, you know, could be another six months, could be another 36 months. Like it’s really hard to know how long. But I fundamentally don’t know if like it’s true to say, like, you know, you need to buy capacity in order to me, that’s a little bit to sort of almost like the great toilet paper shortage of the pandemic or whatever. Right. Like, you know, at least this like, you know, run on the bank type situations. And, but that being said, like, you know, capacity is going to be tight for a while. And, you know, prices are going up. And, you know, luckily, I think, you know, it’s not even necessarily bad for us. If prices go up, because, because, you know, scarcity also means like we can

19:30 charge more from our customers. And, you know, and the fact that we have a lot of reservations locked in at a rate means like, to some extent, we’re effectively like long GPU prices already. So I don’t necessarily worry too much about prices going up. I do worry more about actually prices collapsing. I don’t think that’s going to happen anytime soon. But I think that would be a quite bad thing for a lot of the players in the market. Why would that be bad? I think it would be bad for if, for anyone who’s locked in a lot of supply. Yeah. Because they paid way too much and they paid too much, you know, so there’s a risk of buying at the top, right? And again, like, I don’t worry about that much. I think it’s like a little bit like with the FDEs. Like I think we initially will do a lot of stuff with our customers to optimize their models. But over time, figure out how do we turn those into products? I think we’ll sort of arguably fail in a certain way. If every time a customer needs to optimize a model, we have to go and work with them. And, you know, long term, it has to be turned into products. And so with the FDEs and with the research team, initially, you’re going to have to do a lot of work with the customers and we are that. But over time, we’re also building a lot of internal tooling and a lot of over time internal products that are fully self-serve. So we’re working a lot of stuff right now in post training space, but also in the GPU performance space. So a lot of cool stuff. A lot of cool stuff. Back to the product strategy stuff that you were talking about. Yeah. Yeah. Like what are your thoughts? Like what do we need over the next year, two years? I think it’s incredibly hard to say. And if I said like, I know exactly what we need to build, I think I would be like delusional. I think what we’ve seen so far, and what I kind of believe in on a more general level is like, we need better building blocks. Like this is a new era of software and we’re unlocking a whole new type of applications that could not be built a few years ago.

1:16:30 Doing all the GNI stuff, code that, LMS that output code that needs to run like in an isolated way. Like there’s so many like new primitives that are needed to work with GPUs and work with LMS. And we built some building blocks so far and that’s unlocked a bunch of applications that the world has seen over the last few years. Not just stuff with us, of course. But I think over the next few years, there’s going to be so many more cool things. And so I mentioned some stuff. Like I’m very bullish on training. I’m very bullish on fast jobs. I’m very bullish on certain things around like agents and low latency and things like that. But like in the end, we consider ourselves like an infrastructure shop, right? Like we’re not trying to build, you know, very narrow things. Like we try to build like very general purpose building blocks and put them in front of customers. And then those customers will combine those building blocks and build some incredible applications that we could have never anticipated. I want to go through some of your tweets. This will be the last part of it. Okay. And we can just like, maybe you want to double click on anything. A lot of long running persistent sandbox stuff right now. Today feels lift and shift. I suspect sandboxes will evolve from dev box into cloud to something more ephemeral, one environment for every command. And now I’m shouting in between so you can pause, resume, clone. Yeah. I mean, we talked about this a lot. Yeah, we talked a bit about it, right? Like I’m fully, I think, I think the median sound box in modal today is like eight seconds long or something like that. Like, which is kind of incredible

1:18:00 when you think about it. And over time, I think it might get even shorter. We want to support long running sandboxes too. Like I think they’re awesome, like very valid use cases around long running sandboxes. But like my vision is like, you know, the world needs also, we need to figure out this like how can we just massively parallelize things and reducing the overhead of starting and stopping sandboxes? I don’t know if I ran an IP already start up engaged in catfax arms race for the competitor, it would be nice to coordinate and paste arms race a bit. No comment. The biggest downside of GPU scarcity is not that it’s hard to get GPUs, but that almost all capacity is sold as three years as a three year rectangle is starting three to six months in the future. That’s not what demand looks like for most users. I think we talked about that a little bit as well. Yeah. And you know, maybe just go a little bit deeper now. Like one thing I think modal has always been very, very good at is fully on demand capacity, right? Like if a customer comes to us and need 100 GPUs, like we can typically give them that like immediately, you don’t even have to talk to salesperson. And a lot of workloads in real life, like they don’t look like these like flat, you know, rectangular workloads, like they scale up and down throughout the 24 cycle, they maybe grow over time, they maybe have certain burst periods. And to me, that is a challenge with a lot of customers today. Like the, and I do think it’s a legit problem for, for the space is like the only, the prime way to get capacities to, to buy these rectangular blocks. It’s not great. I think the world needs to, and that’s fundamentally, I mean, I’m very biased, but like that’s why I think modal can play a very large role in that sort of, you know, whatever you want

1:19:30 to call it, sort of duration transformation of offering more flexible capacity. And we can do that because we can aggregate many, many thousands of customers and the demand gets very smooth and aggregate. So that’s a lot of the value prop of modal is exactly that. Would you say that’s a differentiator? Like the, oh really? Okay. Yeah, massive differentiator. Actually, in fact, like, I think, modals, like if you want to be like very sort of reductive, like you can break down modal’s value prop into two things. What is a developer experience, the ability to like iterate and like build things and not have to think about infrastructure. The other thing is the capacity stuff. The more and more I think about modal and like where we’re going in the long run is like we’re building, like we’re aggregating the world’s compute capacity. And we’re very good at slicing it out like very granularly, because we’ve built all this work around, you know, scaling up and down extremely fast, you know, all this stuff around GPU, snapshotting, working some, some ways to make it much, much faster. And that model works at very large scale, like really, really well, because you can aggregate lots of customers. Every month I keep saying or saying box revenue might apply to it, but it keeps going up 30% every month. It’s kind of nuts. Like I don’t understand, you know, like every month I’m like, well, you know, sandboxes grew a lot, but like clearly the kind of plateau and then they keep growing even more. So I, I, I don’t know. And a lot of VCs, like they’re like, how did you know sandboxes was going to be big? Like, and the truth is like, I didn’t like, like, I thought it was going to be bigger than it was in 2023 for sure. But like the fact that sandboxes is a third of our revenue today, it’s, it’s insane. And, you know, we’re obviously very happy about it. And we have like a very large team investing

1:21:00 in sandboxes. You know, I don’t want to like trivialize it. Like we obviously, I do want to give ourselves like a lot of credit for, for seeing sandboxes for what it is today a little bit back in even 2023. But I think, you know, if like, I probably would have never, you know, taken a bet that revenue would be this large from sandboxes and the market demand would be so much. There’s an interesting structural reason why inference providers should exist separately from model builders. The best model keep changing a lot inference providers keep can easily reallocate resources between models since overall demand is quite smooth. So I mean, if you think about all the Chinese labs and, you know, in the future, hopefully more US labs too, every time a new lab releases, you know, the latest and greatest open source models, like you see big shifts in demand, you know, for these models. And so I think a challenge with, you know, if all these labs independently like held capacity, they would see when they launched a new model demand would go up a lot. And then another lab launches a better model and then the demand goes down. You know, but, but of course, like in the background, they’re working on the next version. So like, I think, you know, there’s like a structural reason, like I said, like why you’re going to start, you’re seeing demand kind of shifting to like the latest and greatest Chinese lab. I mean, not like, it’s not like, you know, this is like, everything just moves overnight because, because a lot of models and prompts and stuff like, like a lot of things that get sort of there’s like a certain stickiness to it. But I do think, you know, there’s an argument that it’s very easy for model to like, you know, right, today we’re running, you know, X number of 1000 GPUs for one model. Tomorrow we need to shift like, you know, 50% of that to another model.

1:22:30 Sure, that’s just like, that’s what the system is built to handle. No one even needs to tell us to do that. It just magically does that. So you agree that basically the LLMs are commodities? And if you agree, then where do you think the business for the big labs is going to be? I’m not sure if that’s necessarily true, right? Like, is Taylor Swift the commodities? Like, she releases a big album and goes on a tour and makes a lot of money. And then, you know, then there’s like a down the air when she goes and like records, I don’t know, this is best analogy. And then she releases a new album, you know, so I don’t know, like she still has like a lot of brand and there’s a lot of, you know, power and like makes a lot of margin. So like, as long as the labs like repeatedly can launch new models, and as long as the margin that they have on those models are such that they can sort of pay off amortized like that the cost of training those models, it could still be like a decent business, I think. So you don’t think that the intelligence is like plateauing? No, I don’t think so. I mean, I think it remains to be seen, right? Like, models are today are like very good at like doing things that can be trained very efficiently, you know, using reinforcement learning. So we’ve seen that initially with, you know, coding and writing simple snippets over time, it’s gotten really good at also writing production like level code. It’s gotten really good at math. It’s gotten really good at cybersecurity. Like these are all like very quite verifiable things. I still think it remains to be seen, you know, our model is going to be really good at whatever, cooking food or I don’t know, like things that I have like more

1:24:00 like diffuse targets, maybe longer feedback loops or whatever, I think humans probably like my feeling is like will be quite good and quite competitive with models for a long time in those domains. But you know, certainly, you know, AI models, they’re getting very good as I’m sure everyone can agree with. Yeah, so obviously, like the models are getting really good at coding, they’re already really good at coding. What other applications do you think maybe that aren’t as big right now are going to become huge over the next few years? For the LLMs? I don’t know, but I think anything that has like kind of a verifiable computational bio, I think you mentioned. Yeah, computational bio, I think those are like, not exactly verifiable, but there’s like certain ways you can sort of run simulate, like you can use an LLM to output predictions, then you can do like computational like, like methods to like simulate molecular dynamics and get like kind of feedback loops. I mean, like I think like material science is like maybe another area where like you have a little bit of that loop where you can sort of, you know, synthetically manufacture certain materials and measure the properties and use kind of put an agent in the loop and like, you know, do things. So, you know, I have a physics background, I’m pretty excited about that. So drugs, materials, what else? I’m drawing a blank, but I’m sure there’s many other things. Cool. I mean, those are all the questions that I had. Is there anything you wanted to talk about that I haven’t? I’m good. This is great. This is a lot of fun. Awesome. Thank you.

items.articleBody:
I spent yesterday in New York City interviewing developers about their iPhone Duo apps and the experience of building for such a new and different device. The depth and breadth of developers Apple assembled was excellent. I spoke to indie developers like Vidit Bhargava about Deck-Man and the team behind Notewise. I also interviewed developers from big companies about their impressive Duo updates, including The New York Times for its NYT Cooking app, Netflix, and Meta’s Edits video editing app. Plus, I met Mark Otero from Azra Games, whose team poured their hearts into UnGodly, one of the best-looking games I’ve seen on iOS in a while.

A few things struck me about my conversations with developers. First, every one of them was excited about the design challenges posed by the iPhone Duo and the many orientations and ways it can be used. Second, every one of them came away impressed by how smooth Apple has made the development process. That’s not to say the design challenges weren’t real, but getting from a design idea to an app that worked on the Duo went better than anyone expected. Third, after months of building and testing, everyone was looking forward to seeing which design choices land with users.

But that’s enough of my impressions. I’ll let the developers speak for themselves in this special bonus AppStories video. I came away from New York with some great interviews, which I’ve shared on the MacStories YouTube channel. Apologies for the sometimes rough audio. There’s only so much I can do with recordings made in a room packed with press and developers, but if you’re into apps, design, and how things are built, these interviews are for you.

Also, I left New York with a Night Sky 512GB iPhone Duo that I’ve only just set up and begun testing. I’ll be writing about the Duo soon, and we’ll start covering the best of the more than 300 Duo-optimized apps that developers have sent Federico and me. Stay tuned, because the busy fall season at MacStories is just going to keep rolling.

 🤖 Anthropic unveils Claude Duet LINK
Anthropic has launched Claude Duet, a proactive AI agent that connects to your apps and reaches out with suggestions before you ask, competing with Meta's Muse and OpenAI's Dots agents.

Built on Opus 5.5, Duet sends a morning brief of important items, rechecks apps every few hours, and completes tasks from admin work to web apps using its own cloud browser, asking approval before sending messages or payments.

The product is in a research preview through a waitlist, open only to Pro and Max subscribers in the United States via the web or an iOS app, with background checks counting toward existing plan limits.
 🛒 Walmart lets AI agents shop for you LINK
Walmart will soon let you set up personal AI agents to shop for you across its main website and Sam's Club, a move that sets it apart from Amazon, which blocks third-party shopping agents entirely.

Arriving in November, a tool called Agent Profiles lets shoppers approve purchases their agent makes, set a spending cap, and keep AI-made orders separate from their own, with purchase approval turned on by default.

A new Agent Gateway gives agents a faster, AI-friendly version of the site, and Walmart can suggest usual items like a favorite milk to an agent without handing over a customer's wider shopping history.
 ⚖️ Meta to pay $25B for deceiving users about privacy LINK
A New Mexico jury found Meta liable for misleading users about its privacy and content rules, and a Santa Fe judge ordered the company to pay $25 billion, one of the largest single-state verdicts against it.

The order follows jurors finding Meta responsible for over 43 million violations of state consumer protection law tied to Cambridge Analytica harvesting Facebook user data for political ads during the 2016 election.

New Mexico was one of two states that skipped the 48-state settlement, in which Meta paid $459 million; Attorney General Raúl Torrez expects an appeal and wants the money directed toward public education.
 🦾 Unitree's new humanoid robot can lift cars LINK
Unitree Robotics has shown off the H2-X, a humanoid robot pitched as an emergency "guardian" that can lift a car in a promotional video to free a trapped victim, disarm a knife-wielding attacker, and pull a pedestrian from traffic.

The H2-X builds on Unitree's earlier H2, which stands about 1.8 meters tall and weighs 70 kilograms, though the company shared no details on whether the new model keeps those specs or uses different actuators, joints, or sensors.

Unitree never said whether the dramatic actions were autonomous or choreographed, gave no release date or price, and ended the clip by warning viewers to stay at least two to three meters away from the robot.
 💰 Mark Zuckerberg threatened to leave California LINK
A Meta regulatory filing released yesterday shows Mark Zuckerberg considered leaving California over Proposition 40, a proposed one-time tax on billionaires, but agreed to stay in Silicon Valley for eight years.

Under the deal, Zuckerberg can immediately sell 20 percent of a new class of nonvoting shares to cover any tax he owes, with the other 80 percent unlocking over eight years only if he keeps living in California.

Prop 40 calls for a 5 percent tax on billionaires' stock and assets held in the state as of January 2026, though recent polling, after about $129 million spent opposing it, suggests the measure will fail.
 👶 Musk compares Tesla robots to toddlers LINK
Elon Musk said on Tesla's third-quarter earnings call on 21 October that teaching the Optimus humanoid robot works much like raising a child, with the machines learning tasks through practice rather than pre-set instructions.

Tesla wants 10,000 to 20,000 robots practicing at an "Optimus Academy," where they generate their own training data through self-play, after first learning by watching humans perform tasks at the new Fremont, California line.

Reaching 20,000 robots a week will take at least another year, with the hand being a key engineering problem; the AI5 chip, roughly 10 times stronger than AI4, should enter Optimus around April 2027.

items.articleBody:
Walking through Budapest, it is impossible to ignore the stunning bridges. One in particular garners the attention of tourists, the Szabadság híd, or Liberty Bridge. It is ornate, green, and connects two very important parts of the city — Gellert Hill and the Central Market. It is also the only central bridge with old-timey trams regularly running across it, making it an iconic photo spot. But if you are lucky enough to find the Danube River level low enough, you can peer over the edge and see the ruins of its former self beneath the river.

The Ferenc József Bridge was destroyed during the bombings of the Battle of Budapest in January 1945. On most days, that is a history that is easily forgotten by pedestrians crossing the bridge and enamoured with the fantastic views of the city that it offers. But when the weather and the temperature along the Danube collude to make the levels low as they so often are in summer, the lost remnants of the old bridge appear close to the surface and sometimes even jut out of the water.

What you're looking at is the skeleton of the bridge that was destroyed by a Soviet shell detonating German explosives left on the bridge on 16th January 1945 in what is now known as the Siege of Budapest.

Unfortunately, this is likely to become a common sight if Hungary (and the rest of Europe) continue to swelter through hot, dry summers brought on by climate change.

items.articleBody:
Akai Professional has launched the MPK Mini Plus II, the next generation of its acclaimed 37-key MIDI keyboard.

The next-gen MPK Mini Plus brings a number of new creative tools “designed to help producers develop ideas and explore variations directly from the controller”. But what are they?

First and foremost, the new MPK Mini Plus II features a redesigned look, departing from that of its predecessor to bring it more in line with Akai’s MPK Mini IV keyboards introduced a year ago.

The front panel features a number of changes, with redesigned pitch and modulation wheels, octave and transpose buttons, and a newly upgraded 37-key mini keybed with eight velocity- and pressure-sensitive RGB MPC pads.

READ MORE: Daft Punk x LEGO: New creative partnership sees viral pyramid stage LEGO Ideas submission brought to life

Elsewhere, there’s a new full-colour display, plus additional creative tools including Glitch, Mutate, Strum, Freeze, Chords and Follow, plus an expanded Arpeggiator, Chord Creator, and Note Repeat modes.

Credit: Akai Professional

“Together, these tools give beatmakers, songwriters and performers more ways to move from a starting idea toward something unexpected while keeping creative decisions in their hands,” Akai says.

The MPK Mini Plus II functions both standalone and with MPC Desktop, allowing producers to expand the MPC workflow to a compact keyboard controller. It also offers dedicated integration with MPC 3, Ableton Live, Logic Pro, Cubase, FL Studio and other DAWs, plus full NKS compatibility with Native Instruments Komplete Kontrol ecosystem.

In terms of ins and outs, you’ve got a USB-C power input, MIDI connectivity – with a full-size five-pin MIDI output for connecting external MIDI instruments – plus three CV/Gate outputs for connecting external synths and modular systems. There’s also a quarter-inch sustain pedal input, too.

“MPK Mini has introduced a lot of creators to hands-on making music, and MPK Mini Plus II is built for the creator who’s ready for the next step,” says Andy Mac, Executive Manager of Content, Artist Relations and Business Development at Akai Professional.

“Tools like Glitch, Mutate, and Strum help turn simple ideas in new directions, while deeper MPC, DAW, MIDI and CV integration gives creators room to build a much bigger setup around one compact keyboard.”

Each MPK Mini Plus II comes with Akai’s Studio Instrument Collection, which features over 1,000 sounds from AIR Music Technology, Moog Music, and Akai Professional.

The MPK Mini Plus II is available now, priced at $169.99 / £134.99 / €159.99. Learn more at Akai Professional.

Credit: Akai Professional

items.articleBody:
by Susanne Dahle, Gaute T. Einevoll, Torbjørn V. Ness

There is an urgent need for better treatment options for many neurological conditions, including Alzheimer’s disease, Parkinson’s disease, depression, and epilepsy. Transcranial electrical stimulation (tES) is a non-invasive, safe, inexpensive, and promising method that could address some of this unmet need. The therapeutic value of tES has been well demonstrated, but the effect is highly variable. To enable tES to reach its full potential requires a better understanding of how tES modulates neural activity so that tES treatments can be tailored to specific neurological conditions and individual patients. The neural response to tES is, however, highly complex, and the parameter space involved in optimizing tES treatments is daunting. This has made it difficult to obtain general insights into how tES modulates neural activity, and a central challenge lies in the cell-type-specific and frequency-dependent nature of these responses. In this study, we investigated cell-type-specific neuronal responses to tES over a broad frequency range, using a large database of biophysically detailed neuron models. We found that pyramidal cells respond strongly to low-frequency tES, but their responses drop sharply with frequency. In contrast, inhibitory neurons show a smaller reduction and, on average, become more responsive than pyramidal cells above ~60 Hz. By leveraging a reciprocity theorem we demonstrated that the effect of tES on a given cell-type is proportional to the frequency-dependent current-dipole moment that determines the EEG-signal contribution of this cell-type. We further identified the dendritic asymmetry as key in determining tES responses across the frequency spectrum. Counterintuitively, we also found that while total cell length increases tES sensitivity at low frequencies, it can have the opposite effect at high frequencies. Furthermore, we derived an analytical formula for idealized neuron models which can approximately predict the tES sensitivity of different cell types at any given frequency. By characterizing the role of morphology and stimulation frequency in determining tES responses of single cells, this is an important step towards a better understanding of tES at the fundamental level. These results also provide an efficient and accurate method for characterizing and comparing the tES responses of different neural populations across the frequency spectrum, which facilitates optimizing tES for cell-type specific targeting.

items.title: The US is letting a convicted Bolsonaro spy chief stay in Florida. Brazil wants answers.

items.articleBody:
It was an unusual request. On Nov. 21, 2025, the owner of an apartment in a luxury complex north of Miami drafted a message asking the building’s management to remove his houseguest immediately, the same man his family had vouched for in writing two months earlier.

The guest was Alexandre Ramagem, a Brazilian congressman and spy chief under former President Jair Bolsonaro. In September, Ramagem had fled Brazil days before being sentenced to 16 years in prison for his role in Bolsonaro’s plot to overturn the 2022 election. The message was drafted the same day the country’s Supreme Court ordered Ramagem’s arrest and two days after a Brazilian news site published photos of him and his wife strolling through the Miami complex in workout clothes, causing outrage back home.

The message was written in the name of Rodrigo Martins de Mello, who was convicted of running an illegal mining operation on protected indigenous land in the Amazon. De Mello claimed he had only just learned from the press that his guest was barred from leaving Brazil. “In order to avoid any issues for the condominium or for myself, I hereby request that the condominium IMMEDIATELY notify him of my directive for him to leave my property,” De Mello wrote.

But Brazilian investigators say De Mello and his family knew all along that Ramagem was on the run. Messages, notes and photos from confidential records reviewed by ICIJ and Agência Pública show that they housed Ramagem for months, vouched for him to building management and sought paperwork needed to obtain a Florida driver’s license for him, including a lease drafted to make it look as if he was renting a room.

The records, obtained by Agência Pública and shared with ICIJ, are part of a sealed investigation by Brazil’s Federal Police into Ramagem’s escape, conducted within the Supreme Court’s sprawling investigation into the plot to overturn the 2022 election.

The Federal Police had an officer in Miami working alongside the U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement. With the officer’s help, the confidential records say, ICE found Ramagem, who Brazil wants to extradite, and arrested him in Orlando in April for overstaying his visa.

Then the case took an unexpected turn. After two days, ICE released Ramagem while he pursues asylum. Days after that, the State Department told the Brazilian officer who had helped locate Ramagem to leave the country, accusing him of trying to extend “political witch hunts” to U.S. soil.

There’s a lot of favoritism and discrimination and double standards in the immigration system now. — Tessa Petit, Florida Immigrant Coalition

Six months later, Ramagem remains free in Florida. Officials in Brazil declined to say whether the U.S. has responded to its extradition request.

Ramagem’s treatment stands in sharp contrast with that of thousands of asylum seekers who have been deported since Trump returned to office.

“There’s a lot of favoritism and discrimination and double standards in the immigration system now,” said Tessa Petit, executive director of the advocacy group Florida Immigrant Coalition.

Most immigrants don’t get the break Ramagem got, said Petit, who fled Haiti in 2001 and was initially denied asylum before winning her case in immigration court. “The reality for the majority of people is: Be vigilant, be careful, and hopefully be lucky enough to not get picked up.”

Neither Ramagem nor the De Mellos responded to requests for comment for this story.

In Brazil and in the U.S., supporters of Jair Bolsonaro, a close ally of President Donald Trump, praised the White House for Ramagem’s release.

On Oct. 25, Brazilians will vote in a presidential runoff in which the narrow front-runner, Flavio Bolsonaro, a son of the former leader, has promised pardons for everyone convicted in the coup plot.

Brazilian presidential candidates Flavio Bolsonaro, left, and Luiz Inacio Lula da Silva attend a presidential debate ahead of the national election in Sao Paulo, Brazil, on October 18, 2026.

‘An illegal alien from Brazil’

Ramagem’s only known run-in with U.S. authorities came after months of living in plain sight in Florida and publicly accusing the Brazilian government of persecution.

Ramagem entered the country legally on Sept. 11, 2025, with permission to stay six months, the Department of Homeland Security, which oversees ICE, told ICIJ. But he “chose to illegally overstay his welcome in violation of our nation’s laws,” the agency said, calling him, “an illegal alien from Brazil.”

Brazil filed a formal extradition request with the State Department on Dec. 30, 2025, according to Brazil’s Justice Ministry.

On April 13, police detained Ramagem in Orlando during a traffic stop and handed him over to ICE. Two days later, ICE let him go, pending the outcome of his removal proceedings, the agency said. He paid no bail, according to Paulo Figueiredo, a U.S.-based Brazilian commentator and Bolsonaro ally who said his immigration consulting firm has assisted Ramagem. Detained immigrants usually must go before a judge to seek release, but ICIJ found no record of Ramagem petitioning the court for his freedom. ICE told Brazilian police at the time that the release was an administrative decision and that Ramagem could remain free while his asylum claim was reviewed, according to Brazilian media reports citing police sources.

Ramagem’s allies credited Washington for his release. “Thank you, President Trump and everyone in the administration,” Figueiredo wrote on X. Eduardo Bolsonaro, another son of the former president, thanked Trump and Secretary of State Marco Rubio. Sóstenes Cavalcante, a leader of Bolsonaro’s party in Brazil’s Congress, said Rubio had helped speed up the release, which he said would otherwise have taken at least two weeks.

RAMAGEM IS FREE AND BACK HOME!

My deepest thanks go to Donald Trump @realDonaldTrump and @SecRubio for their sensitivity and attention in addressing the case of this true national hero, who, even under persecution, has never wavered.

Alexandre Ramagem deserves asylum in the land of freedom, alongside his courageous wife – tireless in fighting for his liberty – and their beautiful daughters.

— Eduardo Bolsonaro (@BolsonaroSP) April 15, 2026

Ramagem himself suggested he had U.S. government support. In November, after the publication of photos showing him in Miami, Brazil’s Supreme Court had ordered his arrest. The next day, in a livestreamed interview, Ramagem said he was safe in the United States “with the consent and knowledge of the American government.”

On April 20, five days after Ramagem’s release from immigration custody, the State Department asked Marcelo Ivo de Carvalho, the Brazilian Federal Police liaison officer posted in Miami to work with ICE, to leave the country. “No foreigner gets to game our immigration system to both circumvent formal extradition requests and extend political witch hunts into U.S. territory,” the department’s Bureau of Western Hemisphere Affairs wrote on X.

The government in Brasília retaliated and suspended the duties of a U.S. immigration agent posted there, who then left the country on April 22. In a statement, the Foreign Ministry said the U.S. had failed to consult Brazil first, as the two countries’ agreement on police liaisons requires, and ignored “good diplomatic practice of dialogue between friendly nations, such as Brazil and the United States, over more than 200 years of relations.”

Neither the State Department nor the White House responded to multiple requests for comment. In its statement, DHS did not explain why Ramagem was released, saying only that he was freed “pending the outcome of his removal proceedings” and “will receive due process.” It added that a pending application “does NOT confer any type of legal status in the United States” and that “illegal aliens are not welcome in our country.”

The handling of Ramagem’s case stands out among those of hundreds of thousands of asylum seekers in the United States.

Since Trump returned to office, immigration judges have ordered more than 440,000 asylum seekers removed, more than in the previous eight years combined, according to a recent Washington Post analysis. Release from ICE detention has also become the exception. By late 2025, ICE was deporting more than 14 people directly from detention for every one it released to await a hearing, according to the American Immigration Council, an advocacy group that analyzed ICE data. In December, the administration paused decisions on all  asylum applications pending with U.S. Citizenship and Immigration Services.

Ramagem’s release was not just an immigration matter. A career federal police officer, he headed Bolsonaro’s security when Bolsonaro was president-elect. He was then appointed head of Brazil’s intelligence agency, becoming part of the inner circle of a president whose prosecution the Trump administration has criticized. In July 2025, Trump imposed 50% tariffs on Brazilian goods, calling Bolsonaro’s trial a “witch hunt,” and his administration sanctioned Alexandre de Moraes, the Supreme Court justice who oversees the coup case against Bolsonaro and Ramagem. A White House executive order that month accused Brazilian officials of politically persecuting the former president.

Brazilian President Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva, a leftist who defeated Bolsonaro in the 2022 election, has accused Washington of meddling in Brazil’s affairs. Last month, Lula used his speech at the United Nations General Assembly to warn against foreign interference in the upcoming election there.

e Court, the Federal Police arrested Rodrigo’s son Celso, on suspicion of helping Ramagem flee. In a statement, the family said Celso is innocent. Moraes also ordered Rodrigo’s arrest, and Rodrigo remains a fugitive. (This week, another Supreme Court justice rejected Rodrigo’s request to overturn the order, the Brazilian news site Amado Mundo reported.)

Ramagem has denied that Celso helped him. In an Instagram post after the ICE arrest, he said he didn’t know “a certain” Priscila or Celso. “They arrested a young man, a kid, who only met me when I was already in the U.S.,” he said. “In fact, this young man is American.”

Celso now wears an ankle monitor while the investigation, which is under seal, continues.

The confidential records show the De Mello family’s alleged involvement began early. Since June 2025, Ramagem, then a member of Brazil’s Congress, had been barred by court order from leaving Brazil and was required to surrender all his passports while on trial. He was charged with using the country’s intelligence agency to help Bolsonaro discredit its voting system. (Ramagem’s defense told the Supreme Court that the evidence against him was “extremely timid.”)

On Sept. 9, while on medical leave from Congress, he crossed from the northern town of Bonfim into Lethem, Guyana. A photo found on the phone of Priscila Freitas de Mello, then Rodrigo’s wife, shows him there the next day, smiling, at what appears to be an immigration post in Guyana. Brazilian Federal Police investigators say Rodrigo took the picture, according to the records.

On Sept. 11, as Brazil’s Supreme Court convicted him, Ramagem flew to the United States on a diplomatic passport that he had kept.

On Sept. 15, Celso messaged Priscila asking for a utility bill in his father’s name so Ramagem could apply for a Florida driver’s license, the confidential records show.

“Hi Pri, good evening,” Celso wrote to his stepmother. “Can you send me a bill for your apartment in my dad’s name? Water, electricity, phone, internet… We’re going to try to get Alexandre’s driver’s license tomorrow at the DMV.” He had drafted a lease, Celso wrote, to make it look as if Ramagem “had rented the room.”

“Let me see,” Priscila replied.

Two days later, Priscila wrote to the condominium’s management asking for a new gate access card. “Since we are traveling, we won’t be able to pick it up,” she said. “Therefore, we authorize a friend of ours, Alexandre Rodrigues Ramagem, to collect the new card on our behalf.” Celso also contested parking fines Ramagem had run up at the complex, the records show.

On Nov. 17, Ramagem’s spouse and daughters joined him in the apartment, according to the wife’s social media posts.

Investigators in Brazil allege in the confidential records that the De Mello family played a key role in keeping Ramagem hidden, both by housing him and by helping him deceive U.S. authorities with false documents. It is unclear whether a driver’s license was ultimately issued.

Rodrigo, the De Mello patriarch, has denied helping Ramagem escape. In November, he called the escape story a “fallacious narrative” meant to persecute the right, and said that when Ramagem was with him, he faced no conviction or legal impediment to leaving Brazil. The two men appeared together publicly in March 2025, when Rodrigo posted a photo of Ramagem’s visit to Boa Vista, De Mello’s longtime base in the state of Roraima, near the Guyana border, calling him “a great ally” of Bolsonaro.
