items.articleBody:
“There are, I find, things I want philosophy to do that it cannot. Or that I cannot do with it.”

That’s Amy Olberding, professor of philosophy at the University of Oklahoma, on the limits of philosophy that life sometimes makes vivid. 

The guest post by her, below, is an excerpt from her truly remarkable book, Kill All The Chickens, which was published last month, and which you should all buy today (Amazon, Bookshop). 

The book is a beautiful example of an academic philosopher breaking free of the standard publishing conventions of the profession (at which she was perfectly adept) to produce writing that is full of wisdom and personality, and that, even as it confronts us with an exploration of life’s difficulties, is nonetheless a pleasure to read.

“Nocturnal Sequence” by J. Jay McVicker

Death Just Got Out of This Truck
by Amy Olberding

Maybe we should just skip the middle step and throw it all straight in the toilet? This is what I ask my mother as we together stand and consider the overburdened farm table. We are bereaved and so a steady stream of neighbors has come by to deliver casseroles and pies, lunch meats and cookies, chicken and potato salad. If death were an appetite, we’d have the means to satisfy and send him off by now. But he is not an appetite, nor have we any of our own. 

Mine are a people of uneasy stomachs. I remember one night spent in the ER alongside some uncles and cousins, waiting to hear what the doctors would make of my grandfather’s alarming stroke-like swoon. That night we shared the TUMS bottle the way others might pass a flask. Bringing food to us bereaved is like giving a dog a pencil. There’s just not much that we can do with it, at least not much that anyone could count useful. 

Grief is an affliction physical and material. It roils the gut and stops the sleep. It can put a tremble in the limbs, a quiver in the voice, a restless agitation run all through. It makes the knees want to let go, the body just to sink. It is tired but cannot ever really rest, a breath you cannot really catch. It can make the gaze go vacant, blank. Grief is eyes that see too much, make sense of little. How long have I now stared out the window into nothing, seeing nothing? Grief sets the body all awry. The body wants, but what? Something it can now no longer have, a voice in the ear gone mute, a touch tactile, now but memory. We stare at food; we do not eat it.

My book on death, the one I will not write, was originally going to have a chapter on the body.  It seemed to me that one of the troubles with philosophy on grief is that it misses out on bodies.  The philosopher’s talk is all of what loss means, what grief can make you think.  It speaks to what the mind and heart may feel, but not the stalling, empty mind or trembling heart.  It speaks to one who speaks and thinks, not the instinctive, aching animal, not the raw creature all sensation without sense.  This is not a novelty where philosophy is concerned—philosophers have long neglected the cruder materiality from which thought transpires.  But still, I wanted some way to make philosophy answer not to thought or feeling or meaning, but to the brute stuff upon which all the rest is set.  I wanted some way to make loss less like an experience of the mind and thought, to make loss on the page more like itself in life, an experience altogether nauseating.  Before the reasoning or meaning, first the gut. 

There are, I find, things I want philosophy to do that it cannot. Or that I cannot do with it. There is nothing wrong with thought, with seeking out some sense. But what can be made sense is rarely all there is; it leaves in remainder much, too much. Worse still, even good sense can be misleading. You can get your thoughts in careful order, root out all mistake, prepare to read the vexations of experience with well-honed training pitched to make vexations yield. But all that practiced thought and careful habits of the mind can leave you unready for what comes. Don’t trust them more than they can bear. The body is not a prison, but neither can thought escape its meaty and substantial bonds. I cannot make philosophy bend to this, I think, not in a way that is not all false and false confidence.

Many years ago now, when the farm was still a working dairy and the place was hectic with cows and work, my grandfather hired a milker to come in and help. The milker had a love of the drink and would sometimes cry off work for a hangover, but he was, I suppose, reliable enough that they kept him on. One day, he’d taken the farm’s yellow truck into town to retrieve some feed. At a four-way stop sign, he was briefly bested by a fancy man in a fancy car, the kind of man who didn’t want to wait on a beater truck that got there first and instead just blew the stop sign so he’d get ahead. The milker would have none of this, so he drove that yellow truck right up to and behind the man’s bumper for blocks that soon turned into miles. Finally, the fancy man pulled over in a parking lot, the milker close behind. Both men got out of their vehicles. The fancy man planted his feet wide and bellowed out a caution meant to be severe: I have to warn you that I just got out of karate! The milker didn’t even pause before he answered quietly, Well, I just got out of this yellow truck. Before aught else could happen, the milker’s fist had found that fancy man and laid him flat. 

Karate class is fine and so, too, is philosophy. But make no mistake, you can’t really get ahead of it. Loss comes at you like a fist.

“Death Just Got Out of This Truck,” from Kill All The Chickens by Amy Olberding.

items.articleBody:
With System Collapse out now on Dax J’s Monnom Black, Berlin’s Lars Huismann shows us around the attic studio where it was made.

The eight-track release follows his 2024 Monnom Black debut, Mechanized, and the Sounds From The Past trilogy on Mutual Rytm. A trained drummer who has run his own LHR imprint since 2015, Huismann builds his tracks from hypnotic percussion, dub chords and long filter movements. Here he talks us through the room, the hardware and the FL Studio techniques behind the record. 

"One thing first, because I hear it all the time. I make this music in FL Studio, and I'd choose it again"

The Studio

The studio is on the top floor of my flat, around 20 square metres in total. Having it at home matters more to me than any piece of gear. I run a consultancy alongside the music, so production happens whenever there's a gap in the day. I change rooms, and I'm in the studio. Everything is patched and ready, so an hour between two calls is a real hour of work.

Twenty King Kong bass traps from Kiss Your Ears in Berlin handle the mid and low end. In a small room under a sloped roof, bass frequencies are the whole problem. In 2022 I also had extra layers added to the floor and walls: Fermacell boards and polystyrene on top of the parquet for the neighbours below, and Diamant boards, plasterboard, and rock wool on the walls. 

It's all only screwed together, so when I move, it comes off again. That's my tip for anyone renting: you can treat a room properly without touching the building.

Yamaha HS8 And SPL Phonitor One

My monitors are Yamaha HS8s. Nothing special, but I like the neutral sound, and in a room this size, neutral is what counts. I've had them for about fifteen years, so I've mixed every record I've made on them. 

On top of the HS8s I run Sonarworks SoundID Reference. There's no subwoofer in here yet, and the HS8s are a bit shy in the sub range, so the correction fills in what I can't hear otherwise.

For details, I go to headphones a lot, and they run through an SPL Phonitor One. The Phonitor's crossfeed makes a headphone mix feel more like speakers, so what I hear there translates better when I switch back to the HS8s.

RME MADIface USB And Ferrofish Pulse 16 MX

My sound card is an RME MADIface USB, and the analogue side is handled by a Ferrofish Pulse 16 MX AD/DA converter. The two communicate over MADI, with one optical cable carrying all the channels, and the Pulse converts them into sixteen analogue inputs and outputs. 

Every synth, the tape deck, the compressor and the desk have their own channels, so I can route all my hardware in and out of FL Studio without re-patching anything. I open the project, and the hardware is already there.

Mackie SR24-4-VLZ Pro

The newest piece in the room: I've only had the Mackie since early October, from Tarkno, a producer and DJ, and I'm already a big fan. I use it mainly to record drums. 

What I love is the dirty character, especially when you drive it slightly into the red. The preamps and the EQ add grit that a plugin saturator doesn't give me the same way, and because every channel has its own gain and EQ, I can treat each drum element separately on the way in. It's the opposite of a clean summing box, and that's exactly why it's here.

What I don't love: the faders, knobs and switches are old and sensitive, and you can hear them crackle when you move them. Part of the character, but also a reminder that it's a desk from another decade. Several tracks have already been recorded through it; they're going on my next Monnom Black EP and my next Mutual Rytm EP. 

[quote align=right text="People on a floor don’t dance to the kick drum; they dance to what happens between the kicks"]

Tascam 122MKII And Alesis 3630

The Tascam 122MKII is a three-head cassette deck, and the Alesis 3630 is a compressor that most people would call cheap. Together they were the sound of the Sounds From The Past trilogy on Mutual Rytm: I used the combination partly on the master and partly on the drums. 

Tape is the glue over everything. I like the imperfections of early-2000s sampling, the audible limits of the machines people used then, and tape is my way of getting that back: dirt instead of polish, so the record doesn't sound like it was made in 2026.

The three heads are the reason it's this deck and not any old cassette player: you can monitor off the tape while recording, so you hear the saturation as you set the level. The downside is just as real: sometimes a pass comes back a bit too lo-fi for a techno production, and then I have to fix it in the DAW. That's the price of the glue.

The track where you can hear the tape most clearly is 'Orbital' from the Mechanized EP. There it's only the drums that went through the tape: listen from the first bar.

Roland JV-2080 And Super JV-1080

I have two of the classic Roland ROM synths in the rack: a JV-2080 and a Super JV-1080. The one you can hear clearly on record is the Super JV-1080, on 'Fusion' from my Mutual Rytm days: the pad and the bass stab, with the filter resonance turned up high, were recorded from it and then processed further in FL Studio. 

The bass stab is there right from the start; the filtered pad first comes in at 0:30. The JVs take a lot of time to learn and adjust, and the JV-2080 is next in line.

DJ Setup

The room has a DJ wall: an Allen & Heath Xone:96, a CDJ-3000, a CDJ-2000NXS2, a CDJ-2000NXS, a Technics SL-1210MK2, and a Reloop RP-7000MK2. 

I play the Xone:96 and the 3000 at most clubs, so my home setup matches what I use in the booth. Not every booth has 3000s, and I don't want to think about the hardware on the night. Two turntables because I still buy and play records, and because my own releases come on vinyl; test pressings get checked here before they're approved.

FL Studio

One thing first, because I hear it all the time. I make this music in FL Studio, and I'd choose it again. In techno, it still carries its old name, Fruity Loops, and the image of a huge user base in commercial EDM and hip-hop. A lot of people in techno never looked past that image. Their loss. 

It's a superb DAW: hardware integration is easy, and it does everything Ableton does, and more. I've been working in FL Studio for fifteen years, and I know the program from the other side as well: from May 2020 to May 2023 I was Performance Marketing Manager at Image-Line, the company behind FL Studio.

Filters Instead Of Melodies

This is the heart of my production. The short version: instead of writing a melody, I use filters to create variation and patterns.

I start with a chord, usually a minor or major chord detuned slightly so it sits a bit off and creates tension, often as a hybrid of a polyphonic synth and a sample. Then I program a MIDI pattern that's about groove, not melody. And instead of a melody I create a filter-modulation pattern for cutoff and resonance, via an LFO or a second MIDI pattern. Because the resonance highlights certain frequencies, the ear reads that movement as a melody even though there isn't one. Most of the movement in my tracks is one parameter travelling for a very long time. The question stopped being 'what's the melody?' and became 'how does space move?'

The source itself matters less than people think. What the signal goes through afterwards is what decides the character.

Output Movement is the one I've been using for a few years now, and it sits on a lot of my elements, synths and percussion alike. I like its filter because it has a very interesting dirty, slightly distorted character, which is exactly what I want on a dub chord. Movement's rhythm section is the other reason I keep it: it lets the filter move in a pattern rather than just sweep.

The latest step with Movement is a modular stereo effect I built in VCV Rack, which I call 'Dual Motion'. Output Movement sits at the centre, loaded as the host effect. Behind it, I've wired separate filters and delays for the left and the right channel. An eight-step sequencer moves the filters in time with FL Studio, and a slow LFO changes the tone of the echoes. The idea is to get rhythmic and spatial changes from a simple dub chord or percussion track without constantly adding new notes.

DuoPulse

One more filter tool I built myself: DuoPulse. I made it because I wanted to sequence this kind of movement more precisely than the tools I had allowed.

It has two rhythm units that run independently; each can be a step sequence of up to 32 steps, an LFO, or an envelope follower, and each can move the volume, stereo position, and a master low-pass filter with four gently saturating stages. Two rhythm units instead of one is the whole point: one can carry the groove, the other can open and close the filter against it, and the two patterns don't have to share a length.

'Grid' is the clearest example. The dub chord is the driving element next to the drums, and the filter does the work on it. Every eight bars, a second dub chord comes in with a lot of reverb and its own cutoff automation. Almost the whole of System Collapse runs at 145 BPM, and 'Grid' and 'Anomaly' are my answer to the idea that dub techno has to be slow. It doesn't.

FL Studio Patcher

Patcher is a part of FL Studio that many people overlook, and it's one of my main workflow tools. It lets you build complex chains of instruments and effects inside one container and save the whole thing as a single preset. With filters, modulation, and routing already in place, I start from a sound that moves, not an empty channel. If the chain is already there, I'm making music within a minute instead of rebuilding a signal path.

The example in the screenshot is one I use a lot: 'Dub Motion', with Output Movement at the centre, a high-pass and a low-pass around it, separate level controls for the dry and the effect signal and a limiter at the end so nothing gets out of hand. One preset, and a dub chord already moves.

[quote align="right" text="FL Studio is a superb DAW: hardware integration is easy, and it does everything Ableton does, and more"]

Arturia Acid V And Pigments

Two tracks on System Collapse, 'Corrosive' and 'Cult Breaker', use a classic 303 as an emulation: Arturia's Acid V. Ever since the 303 came out, there have been thousands of acid tracks, and they all follow the same pattern. The 303 already has its own filter and its own very particular character. I wanted to put another one on top, so I built my own filter sequence over the acid line, with rhythmic emphasis and LFOs, and kept going until the line stopped behaving like a standard acid element.

The result is a sound that gets very full, and you can play it very deep without losing anything. The extra filtering comes from Pigments, this time loaded as a plugin on the effect side rather than as an instrument. Yes, that works, to my own surprise. My goal wasn't to get too trancy, but to find a middle ground and keep the rhythmic density high.

One thing that helps a lot: don't program too many notes, so the processing step afterwards, Pigments and its filters, still has room to build something new on top.

Pigments as an effect in FL Studio only works under two conditions. First, it needs the Utility engine with Audio In as the source, with the other two engines switched off; in this case, the audio coming in is Acid V. Second, it still needs a MIDI signal, so you build the rhythm anyway. The sequencer inside Pigments then runs while you hold that note and opens and closes the filter step by step. That's where the acid line stops being an acid line.

Rob Papen BLUE-III: 'Neon Shadows'

'Neon Shadows' opens System Collapse. It's also the oldest track on the record. I built the FM synth in BLUE-III from Rob Papen. I reach for FM whenever a track needs a melody: it always has a metallic core and a hint of detune, which keeps a melodic track dark rather than sweet. I recorded it as a sample, then kept working on it in Pigments' sample editor.

The track has two FM sequences that answer each other. The first one has no melody, only a rhythmic sequence, tuned to a drone that runs constantly in the background; think of it as percussion. After the intro, a second FM comes in, the same sound, and this one has a melody that I built in the Pigments sequencer.

The bass drone underneath gives the two FM synths a completely different colour when you hear everything together. The mood is deliberately hopeful. The record is mostly darker, and I wanted a point of contrast. The line between euphoric and cheesy is thin there, and the whole job was staying on the right side of it. I made a lot of versions over the years and only finished it when Dax J showed interest.

Drums

D16 Drumazon 2 is my drum machine for almost everything except the kicks: percussion, hats, the rest. It's on every one of my tracks.

Over the last fifteen years, I've built my own sample library, and the kicks are its core. I keep changing those samples, layering them with others, and every time something new comes out of that, I save it as a new sample and put it back in the library. Everything on System Collapse comes from that library and my own recordings.

'Reversed Alignment' is a good example of how far that goes. The main element is a monks’ mantra. Monk chants have been used to death, especially in Goa trance, and they bore me by now, so I wanted to do something else with one: I reversed the sample, cut it into pieces, and fitted them to the rhythm until the voice stopped being a voice and became percussion.

FL Studio's Edison is the audio editor that every recording and sample is edited in. In the Sampler channel, a volume envelope with a fast decay shapes the tail of a kick or shortens a percussion hit without touching the sample itself.

One plugin I use a lot on the drums: the Black Box HG-2MS from Brainworx, a model of a tube saturation unit. It's there for signature and saturation, the same job the tape and the Mackie do on the hardware side, but inside the box and on every drum channel that needs a bit more weight.

It's worth mentioning that a lot of how I program drums comes from playing them. I spent about fifteen years behind a kit, in jazz and progressive metal bands. Jazz taught me groove; metal taught me to hold a pattern together while everything around it tries to fall apart. A drummer's reflex is to fill, and techno asked me to erase. People on a floor don't dance to the kick drum; they dance to what happens between the kicks.

System Collapse is out now on Monnom Black, digitally and on vinyl. Find Lars Huismann on SoundCloud and Instagram.

items.articleBody:
Frontispiece from The School of Venus, or the Ladies Delight (1680), by Michel Millot, via Google Books. Public Domain.

The first dildo named in English literature appears in a brothel on Valentine’s Day. Thomas Nashe’s The Choise of Valentines, an erotic farce written in the early 1590s, follows Tomalin, an impatient lover visiting a sweetheart in the bordello where she works. He pays the hostess (a “foggy three-chinned dame”) and hurries upstairs through the building’s “crankled wayes.” But his reunion with Mistress Francis is urgent and disastrously brief. “I faint! I yeald!” he cries. Left unsatisfied, Francis briskly reaches for her “little dildoe.”

Francis makes the device’s advantages ruthlessly clear. She prefers it to Tomalin’s “sillie worme”: it is always stiff, cannot make her pregnant, and does not fail through haste or fatigue. The dildo is not a sad substitute, but a youthful “knave”—a mischievous lover and jaunty sexual performer who “playes at peacock,” soon becoming Francis’s true valentine. “Behold! how he usurps in bed,” she cries. For Tomalin, that is precisely the problem; he angrily dismisses the dildo as a filthy, “dasht” toy and “senceless counterfet.” But the violence of the complaint betrays his true feelings. The dildo becomes an antagonist: an obscene rival, a bedroom interloper, one that should be “whipt with nettles,” as one might another man.

The poem treats the dildo with the inflated seriousness of a mock epic, describing its hero with astonishing material precision. This is not the passing joke of older comic traditions—such as the leather penises of Aristophanes’ Lysistrata, used by women during a sex strike—but a Renaissance luxury device. It is made of “thick congealed glasse,” enveloped in white silk, and designed to improve upon flesh by “tickling” Francis in the right places, producing “manie a sighe.” 

At first, Francis’s device seems like an elaborate erotic fancy. But surviving dildos made from Venetian glass, held in museums in Trier and Paris, suggest a startling literalness. The most prized of these “forraine artes,” as Nashe terms them, came from Murano, an island of furnaces on the Venetian lagoon, whose masters had made their name synonymous with spotless cristallo and richly veined glass mimicking precious stones. A few decades earlier, the Italian poet Pietro Aretino described similar devices in an erotic dialogue set in a Venetian convent. In one scene, a boy arrives with a basket of translucent fruit for a banquet—glass carrots and quinces, crystal turnips and other gleaming delicacies. The nuns have a name for them: pastinaca muranese, Murano parsnips. 

*

“Dildoe,” after first entering English in Nashe’s poem, would become associated with delight through the Italian diletto, and later defined more gravely as a penis succedaneus, a penis substitute. But the word’s origins are uncertain; it may have first circulated in the nonsense refrains of merry ballads and tavern songs, alongside euphemisms like nonny-nonny, ding-a-ding, and fa la la. 

The dildo flourished in this unstable register across bawdy verse, pornography, satire, and political lampoon—which is partly why it is difficult to trace. Private, taboo, and vulnerable to censorship and confiscation, the dildo rarely appeared plainly as itself. In Nashe’s poem it was unusually explicit, serving at once as a pleasure-object, comic rival, and threatening joke. But later poems took the imaginative excess further, dressing the dildo ever more elaborately as something else.

Restoration London offers a particularly vivid instance of its public disguise. Between 1660 and 1685, Charles II returned from a long French exile to a nation emerging from Puritan rule. The “Merry Monarch” restored the theaters, patronized the arts, and made courtly pleasure conspicuous. His mistresses became public figures; sexual language, too, became a medium of courtly wit, scandal, and political attack. Outside the royal palace, London was expanding into a city of coffeehouses, playhouses, pleasure gardens, and ill-gotten wealth. New goods moved through its streets and shops, as the literary dildo moved out of Nashe’s brothel and into court satire, where it proved extraordinarily generative. 

In one notorious Restoration lampoon, the dildo enters public life as “a noble Italian called Signior Dildo,” a foreign gentleman whose “virtuous abilities” quickly make him a sensation at court. Ladies “fall down and worship Signior Dildo,” the poet jeers; one conceals him up her sleeve, another steals him from her mother. Unlike the importunate men to whom penises are attached, the obedient dildo is “ready and dumb.” In a later poem, the dildo becomes a Frenchman, “Monsieur Thing,” traveling through London in women’s beds and climbing the social ladder like an ambitious gigolo. In both poems, he is explicitly named a “Rival”—not only a substitute for husbands, lovers, and courtiers but a preferred competitor. One admirer judges Monsieur Thing’s caresses “without denyal the best, most pleasing thing as e’er she felt.” 

The joke makes him a convenient vessel for Restoration alarms: aristocratic excess, women’s appetite, foreign contamination, and the court’s political impotence. But wonderful details emerge, as the poems also make the dildo a commodity—sold in the “Toy-Shop” in Covent Garden, and along the fashionable St. James’s Street, where it can be found among “powder, gloves, essence.” At the Royal Exchange, the dildo appears in a glittering display alongside other imported luxury goods: frangipani-scented gloves, tortoiseshell snuffboxes, and velvet mouches (beauty patches affixed to the face with pine gum). These dildos are made of horn, ivory, or bone; dressed in satin, velvet, and taffeta for enhanced stimulation. One poem claims there are models for “tender Virgins” and others for the “wide salacious Slit.”

Another scandalous work of erotica, The School of Venus, arrived in London from France as a dialogue of sexual instruction, advising young women on pleasure commodities like a life-size bronze lover, complete with an erect, red-tipped penis. But the novel’s readership was often male. Samuel Pepys bought the “rogueish” book on the Strand in 1668, took it home and masturbated, recording the climax in his diary using multilingual code—“una vez to decharger”—then setting the volume on fire. 

*

Across this erotic culture, the dildo was imagined with an increasing attention to likeness. Some were painted skin-tone, veined, and capillaried to “come up so near to Nature.” Others were hollow, equipped with chambers, springs, and pumps able to expel “warm water” or “milk” through an opening at the tip. This was not mere literary invention. An eighteenth-century ivory dildo found in a convent near Paris, hidden in the seat of an armchair, was fitted with a pump to simulate ejaculation. This mechanism answered a period belief that female pleasure depended, at least in part, on male emission. These ingenious instruments were made not only to resemble a penis but to outdo it.

Yet little remains of this ingenuity. Some examples survive in glass and ivory, but exhibits are scarce; leather rots, wax deforms, glass breaks. Even when a dildo survives, it may be given another name—Murano dildos, for example, have entered museum collections as “hoax drinking glasses,” their hollow interiors reassigned from bed to table. In 1992, when excavators at a Roman fort near Hadrian’s Wall found a life-size wooden phallus complete with carved glans, the scholarly speculations took on a certain comedy. Was it a pestle used for grinding herbs? A protective sculpture mounted on the fort’s gate? Or, as it was catalogued for decades, a “darning tool”?

Other records show active destruction. In 1672, customs officers uncovered a “hogshead” (a large barrel) filled with contraband French dildos. The cargo was broken open and burned publicly at a marketplace “without mercy.” The episode inspired poetry, such as Dildoides, a mock epic whose title mimics Homeric register and turns the burned barrel into a fallen Troy: “O barbarous Times, where Deities are made themselves a Sacrifice.”

But the dildo’s comic life has a darker underside. The fifteenth-century German inquisitor Heinrich Kramer imagined artificial penises as instruments of supernatural disorder, long before Restoration poets turned them into figures of satire. His witch-hunting manual, Malleus Maleficarum—or  The Hammer of Witches—documents the clerical terror over penis theft, explaining that witches could take away the male organ by a glamour, leaving a man to find “nothing but his smooth body.” The accused women were said to hoard these living members; Kramer warns they could domesticate stolen penises, keeping them as prisoners or pets. Witches would fatten them up with “oats” and hide them away “in a bird’s nest” or a “box.”

Beneath the fantasy of male loss lies another, more disturbing anxiety that women might possess penises themselves—not inert substitutes, but as things to wear and use. It imagines women’s sexual independence, going beyond solitary pleasure to the potential for sex between women, making male bodies unnecessary.

Occasionally, this possibility becomes visible in the court records. In a trial from fifteenth-century Germany, a woman named Katherina Hetzeldorfer was tried for sexual relations with women. At trial, Katherina scandalized the court by describing a homemade penis that she fashioned with “a red piece of leather” and “a wooden stick.” She confessed to tying it around her waist with “a string” and having sex with a married woman. The crime didn’t have a name in 1477. The angry, baffled judges issued a death sentence and Katherina was thrown into the Rhine.

Such records are rare—not because women escaped regulation, but because the law rarely named their conduct directly. The evidence survives in scattered forms—town trial records, legal treatises, chronicles, and journals. In the sixteenth century, two Spanish nuns were burned for using “material instruments”; in France, a woman was executed for the “wickedness which she used to counterfeit the office of a husband.” Not long after, a weaver who lived as a man and married a woman was hanged in France for using “illicit devices.” By the eighteenth century, such figures were increasingly named “female husbands.”

The unnameable fact was sex between women. The dildo mattered because it seemed to reproduce the penile act, making it recognizable as (female) sodomy. Over the ensuing centuries, courts increasingly displaced the offense into other legal categories; in England, “female husbands” were prosecuted for vagrancy, perjury, or breach of the peace. In the process, Signior Dildo’s dangerous counterpart disappears from view: the woman who possesses, wears, and uses the dildo herself.

 

Izabella Scott is the author of  The Bed Trick: Sex and Deception on Trial (2026), published by FSG. Her writing has appeared in the Financial Times, Granta, the London Review of Books, and The World of Interiors.

items.articleBody:
Sign up here to receive Bellingcat’s biggest investigations by email as soon as they are published.

In September, the AI company Anthropic published a blog post that claimed its models were approaching “superhuman capabilities for geolocating outdoor photos”. Anthropic made this claim by comparing its models’ performance to that of players of the popular online game GeoGuessr, which challenges users to geolocate Google Street View images. 

Bellingcat has been running its own benchmark tests on AI models since June 2025, right around the time when Large Language Models (LLMs) began to challenge reverse image searches for assisting with geolocation tasks. In our first round, GPT 4o-mini from OpenAI appeared to be the best tool for geolocating, a title which was taken by Google AI mode when we performed our second round of tests a few months later in August 2025. 

This time, we significantly upped the ante for the models, providing increasingly challenging photos and asking for only one set of coordinates. We tasked not only closed-weight models from Claude, Grok, Gemini, ChatGPT, and Mistral, but also open-weight models from Moonshot AI’s Kimi, commercial provider GeoSeer and the non-generative geolocation model GeoClip. In total, we fed each model 52 photos that had not been published anywhere on the internet before.

The results showed that the current generation of models have markedly improved geolocation capabilities. Anthropic’s Opus and Fable, as well as Google’s recent Gemini 4 Argon model, performed the best on geolocation tasks, narrowing down locations from images faster than a human could under specific conditions. Preliminary tests of a set of agentic skills and tools being developed internally by Bellingcat also showed promising results in further improving the geolocation performance of generic-use AI agents.

But crucially, the tests also showed why humans remain necessary for accurate and trustworthy geolocation work, as no models were foolproof. This is particularly important given the increased use of AI in military contexts. The Anthropic blog post focused specifically on geolocating photos for military and intelligence purposes such as targeting, a historically labour-intensive process requiring significant human expertise. 

While our tests showed some models performed extremely well at narrowing down results to the correct general area, none were close to being perfect at finding the exact spot a picture was taken. That accuracy is extremely important in geolocation, especially in military contexts where the cost of incorrect information can be life or death. It is also important for organisations like Bellingcat whose reputation relies on pinpoint factual accuracy.

Our Methods

To compare model results, we used two metrics built on the distance in kilometres between a prediction and the real location. GeoGuessr Score was used to assess whether models could systematically identify the general area, while the Mean Log Score (explained below) measured which models most accurately pinpointed the correct location in the final few kilometres. 

The GeoGuessr Score metric is based on the online game of the same name, whose scoring system Stanford University academics reverse-engineered in a 2024 study. This system rewards answers close to the general area an image was taken, but does not strongly distinguish between guesses close to the precise location. For example, an answer 200km from the correct location with more points than one 2,000km away. However, an answer 500m from where a picture was taken and another 5km away achieve a similar score. For real-world geolocations, that distance matters a great deal.

For more precision, we introduced a custom metric that grades models higher if they narrow down the search in the last few kilometres. This metric, the Mean Log Score, assigns a value from 0 (completely inaccurate) to 100 (perfect model) and works on a logarithmic scale instead of a linear one like GeoGuessr score.

Therefore, a 10-fold improvement in distance means the same whether it is from 5km to 500m or from 500km to 50km. You can compare both metrics here.

Below are the model results sorted by either metric, showing how many photos each model geolocated within distance bands from the true location.

Several models placed at least 10 out of the 52 photos correctly within one kilometre, and the top-performing models placed over 50 percent of the photos within 25 kilometres.

NOTE: Geoseer-fast refused to answer on four of the 52 photos, claiming “This image is not suitable for geolocation”, while Mistral-large-4 refused once with “insufficient information in image to identify location”. Kimi-k2.6 also failed to provide a set of coordinates on one photo, and Gemini 4 Argon timed out repeatedly on one photo.

Our Test

To independently assess the models, we sought to give them very specific instructions and some images that were harder to geolocate than those provided in our past tests. The prompt asked for a single set of coordinates reflecting the photographer’s location. The purpose of restricting the response in this way was to prevent hedging, such as multiple guesses or confidence scores, and make the grading more uniform across different models. Models were allowed to use their providers’ built-in tools: search, code execution and page fetch. We capped their token output at 64,000 and ran each model under its default effort setting with a maximum time of 15 minutes per photo. If a model did not return coordinates on the first prompt, we also allowed a single rescue prompt asking it to do so using its previous reasoning and without using any tools.

The images provided were unique, from around the world, not published on the internet before, scrubbed of metadata and provided without any context. They did not contain significant landmarks. We also included images in snowy, foggy and nighttime conditions.

The results show that the LLMs tested could, in many circumstances, successfully narrow down a location much faster than a human can geolocate even without any context. This is not limited to Google Street View-style images. Take, for example, this image of vegetation and a very small part of a rooftop.

An example of a photo used for testing, with annotation added after the test to highlight the only man-made object visible. Credit: Bellingcat.

For an average person, identifying the country this photo was taken in without any context could take a significant amount of time. However, multiple models quickly narrowed it down to Kenya. You can navigate their answers in the map below. Notice how several correctly inferred enough vegetation details to narrow down the exact part of the world and the park itself, but also that for many, the final response was a best guess only. It is important to note that even though some models were correct, others were significantly off.

The full model results for all 52 photos can be seen in the table below.

Of the models tested, Gemini 4 Argon scored highest on the Mean Log Score, and Claude’s models (Opus and Fable) were at the top of the table regardless of the score metric. Even Claude Sonnet, the weakest of its lineup, consistently came close to the real location while being the fastest to answer across all models.

This was followed by GPT-6 Astra and GPT-6.1 Sol, as well as other Claude and Gemini models, and then the geolocation-specific model, GeoSeer Fast, which provided good results but also timed out frequently. We tested GeoSeer’s more competent Agent model, but it refused to answer on eight photos and regularly timed out.

For secondary factors like time and cost, Claude also performed well on both metrics, and Gemini Argon, while much slower, came at a similar cost to Opus. Based on API rates, Argon and Opus models offered the best balance of accuracy and cost, especially compared to Fable and Grok. Grok was the most expensive option and had an underwhelming bottom-half performance. Meanwhile, GeoClip was freely available but only outperformed Claude Haiku.

Model Limitations

While we sought to analyse the most prominent models, there was one that we could not include as it has yet to be fully released.

Support Bellingcat

Your donations directly contribute to our ability to publish groundbreaking investigations and uncover wrongdoing around the world.

Donate

In its blog post, Anthropic claimed its Mythos model beats “even the strongest human baseline on median distance error, scoring 37.0km and 47.2km across 6,000 photos (placing 23.7 percent and 23.1 percent within 1km).“ But Nuno Moniz, Associate Research Professor at the Lucy Family Institute for Data & Society at the University of Notre Dame, told Bellingcat that “the median represents a strong simplification of what would be acceptable to compare AI-based system performance with regards to humans”. 

Anthropic compared its models to competitive GeoGuessr players and their success in identifying the location of Google Street View images. The entire set of test images was online and there was no guarantee the models were processing the imagery for the first time. 

While Anthropic has been relatively open about these methods, not all developers have been as forthcoming. It is therefore difficult to assess whether the same limitations will impact all other models, or whether there will be further caveats that we are simply not aware of. 

Moniz said that “the increasing availability of benchmarking tools and datasets has made it somewhat difficult to measure reliability in test results such as these”. Specifically, due to the ”uncertainty as to whether that data was included in its training”. This is why we ran our Bellingcat tests with non-published photos sourced from Bellingcat staff and the Bellingcat Volunteer Community.

A further limitation of any models comparing performance to GeoGuessr scores is that the game uses images from Google Street View, which is limited to a select number of countries, and within these, a limited number of roads. Street View is also intentionally skewed to feature clear, high-quality photos taken during daytime that are useful for navigation, and users can pan around their view. There are also some well-known tricks that allow GeoGuessr players to bypass actual geolocation to correctly guess the location of photos: for example, Google is known to use a black car in Jordan and a white car in the UAE to capture imagery. While this wouldn’t necessarily impact model performance, it is a drawback of measuring against GeoGuessr score as the game has a set of workarounds that can bypass geolocation skill.

Anthropic’s data consisted of thousands of social media photos of various scenes. Once again, though, these photos were online and may have featured in the model’s training data. Anthropic’s blog post contained four images as an example of this dataset.

Images used as part of Anthropic’s dataset. Credit: Anthropic.

The examples Anthropic shared are relatively easy to geolocate as they feature recognisable buildings and signs. But footage that requires geolocation often comes from regions where access is limited and which do not feature on social media or Street View.

Specifically, in a military and intelligence context, footage often involves low-resolution material and intentionally obscured details recorded in remote or inaccessible areas. Context that could be found online can be uncertain or plain wrong, especially during a developing situation, such as the image below that Bellingcat investigators geolocated when verifying a US strike on a school in the city of Minab in Iran that killed at least 120 children earlier this year.

An example of footage geolocated by Bellingcat. Screen shot from Mehr News.

Anthropic researchers acknowledge this caveat, writing that it “does not as clearly emulate the task of precisely pinning down a location in near-real-time in a less populated battlefield setting; that is a task for future research.”

As noted, it is also possible that similar caveats need to be applied to other models when seeking to understand and interpret any geolocation-related benchmarking.

Supercharged Models

In parallel to the above models, we also tested a set of agentic skills and tools being developed internally by Bellingcat. These are researcher-informed instructions and code that can equip generic-use AI agents to augment their geolocation ability. For instance, we designed skills such as allowing it to download Environmental Systems Research Institute (ESRI) satellite imagery tiles. We also designed another skill that enabled direct access to data from Bellingcat’s OpenStreetMaps search tool, which aims to assist geolocation efforts by comparing items identified in imagery (like the position of a pylon compared to a nearby railway line) to OpenStreetMaps data. GeoSleuth is a similar project that has already been published, which we used for comparison. We picked Claude’s Opus 5.5 model to run both skills customisations because of its strong performance and reasonable pricing, and ran all the photos through the supercharged models under the same conditions – except that they had no timeout enforced as the supercharged models required more time to utilise their extra skills. 

The different timeout conditions and expanded toolset do not allow for a direct comparison of the customised models to the previous off-the-shelf models’ results, even if they both outperformed the barebones Opus model they were based on, and all other models on GeoGuessr Score, with only Argon ranking above Bellingcat’s agent in Mean Log Score.

Still, this test allows us to showcase why skill customisations can bring value. Take the following photo.

An image captured at the Global Campus of Human Rights in Venice. Credit: Bellingcat.

This is not an exceptionally hard geolocation, and 11 of 17 models answered within 5km of the actual capture location in Venice, Italy. GPT-Sol answered with the correct monastery, but only Bellingcat’s agent and GeoSleuth answered with the exact camera position coordinates. This was possible because both model customisations can download and compare satellite imagery tiles, which allows them to validate not just which monastery the photo was taken at but also the correct courtyard position and orientation from visual cues. You can click the buttons in the list below to audit each model’s final answer.

While in this instance the supercharged models got the exact spot, there were other instances where they did not, as the scores in the results table above show. This again emphasises that even with extra skill sets added, these models were still far from infallible.

Tests Conclusions

Despite increased model improvement, our analysis shows that important caveats remain and it is important to keep a human in the loop when seeking to guarantee a geolocation is precise and correct.

Our tests show that the coordinates models provide as answers are rarely an exact match, even with supercharged models. Invariably, even the best models, with the best tools, can confidently claim a wrong position. Anthropic says its Mythos model was able to pinpoint less than a quarter of its social media photos dataset within a 1km radius. But narrowing down a location is rarely the trickiest part of geolocation work. A large part of important geolocation work is in the final stretch: finding specific coordinates from a general area. This level of specificity is needed because a general area is not a match. Matching features and perspective are necessary for an accurate geolocation, and in many cases that is done on very low-quality images or even by cross-referencing multiple sources. 

This level of precision is essential for investigations where it matters what building a person could be found at, what lines of sight individuals might have had, or what impact an air strike might have led to. 

Since LLMs can still confidently get things wrong, as our analysis shows, all results still have to be verified independently. Strong human geolocation skills therefore remain crucial, as the more one understands about geolocations, the better one can verify or take to completion an automated result. 

Though it can speed up geolocation work significantly, especially in narrowing down an area of interest, AI models remain a useful assistant rather than a tool we can blindly delegate geolocations to.

Bellingcat is a non-profit and the ability to carry out our work is dependent on the kind support of individual donors. If you would like to support our work, you can do so here. You can also subscribe to our Newsletter and follow us on Bluesky here, Instagram here, Reddit here and YouTube here.

items.articleBody:
There is a recurring problem with every population that must migrate from one land to another: The next generation will want to assimilate. Then the mother tongue becomes a childhood memory. And the folktales aren’t retold. My parents came to America at the earliest onset of the Vietnamese refugee crisis. There was no time to pass on folktales. My parents worked while my siblings and I were left to ourselves, our grandmother tasked with guardianship duties she only seldom tended to. It’s doubtful we would’ve been interested anyway. Back then, being Vietnamese wasn’t something to be proud of—it was a source of shame. Survival meant assimilation. We didn’t watch or read Vietnamese media—the closest we came was Vietnamese-dubbed bootlegs of Chinese movies coming from Hong Kong. It was not until I was in my adulthood that I felt this cultural gap in my heart. I was in graduate school, learning how to hone my craft as a writer, and finding my most profound inspirations came from drawing on Vietnamese folklore, though I could approach them only through scattered, clunky translations. Even still, the tales stirred something deep inside my heart and began to heal traumas I didn’t know I had endured. I wrote more stories, crafting characters that could find resonance with and draw insight from imagery plucked from Vietnamese folklore and myth, slowly repairing my own broken connections to my heritage in the process.

Treasury of Vietnamese Folk Tales: Volume 1
By Nguyễn Đổng Chi,
Major Books, 2026, 
$34.95, 144 pp., hardback

What I wouldn’t have given in this time for a resource like Major Books’ new translation of Nguyễn Đổng Chi’s Treasury of Vietnamese Folk Tales: Volume 1, which collects a range of traditional folktales in the most popular forms familiar to Vietnamese people today. The tales selected for the volume, deftly translated by Nguyễn Bình and Lan Võ, exemplify how thoroughly Buddhism has saturated Vietnamese folk culture, to the point of inseparability, with both its teachings and cosmology absorbed and integrated into the Vietnamese way of seeing the world. These are some of the most foundational stories to the Vietnamese people, each accompanied by beautiful illustrations, hand-painted by Jeet ZDũng and inspired by traditional Vietnamese art forms, depicting each scene in vibrant and fabulous detail: Heroines adorned in traditional áo dài leap defiantly into the air; celestial immortals abide in heavenly realms, lotuses blossoming all around them; enraged elemental gods crusade into battle against one another in seasonal clashes. 

For the Buddhist reader—of Vietnamese heritage or otherwise—the folktales collected in this volume provide enormous insight into how Buddhism has become an indivisible aspect of Vietnamese culture itself. In the collection’s second story, “Mother Liễu Hạnh,” a fairy princess (tiên nữ, often understood as a “Daoist immortal”) is exiled from heaven, only to be relentlessly pursued and harassed by the Crown Prince of King Lê Thái Tổ. When the king makes prayers to the eight Vajrapani generals to intercede, believing Liễu Hạnh to be a demon bewitching his son, the narrative interjects to explain how Quán Âm, the bodhisattva of compassion, manifested the eight generals—powerful magic-wielding dharma protectors—from lotus flowers to vanquish evil from the East Sea a thousand years prior. Even very well-read and studious Buddhists may be unfamiliar with the concept of the dharma-protector spirit Vajrapani being split into eight separate individuals—while the eight Vajrapani (bát bộ Kim Cương) are mentioned in the liturgies used in Chinese Buddhism, their depiction in Vietnamese monasteries and temples in statuary form positioned in the eight compass directions (replacing the more common motif in Chinese temple architecture depicting the four heavenly kings) began in the Lê dynasty. The motif has since developed into a unique feature of Vietnamese Buddhist iconography: The ferocity of the warrior-spirits is tempered by the initial seed of compassion that birthed them, each Vajrapani general representing one aspect of the eightfold path. Together, they represent the adamantine strength necessary to engage with the world compassionately while protecting the mind from succumbing to defilements.

Jeet ZDũng, Bà chúa Liễu Hạnh – Liễu Hạnh trừng trị hoàng tử (Mother Liễu Hạnh – Liễu Hạnh punishes the Crown Prince). Artwork courtesy Major Books.

In the Liễu Hạnh folktale, the eight Vajrapani find their magic at a stalemate with Liễu Hạnh’s—owing to her being a daughter of the Jade Emperor—and call upon Quán Âm to aid in the fairy’s capture. When the king realizes Liễu Hạnh is not a demon seducing innocent men but a fairy descended from heaven unleashing retribution against lechers, he grants her amnesty. Liễu Hạnh is lionized in Vietnamese tradition as the Sacred Mother, protector of women and children, disciplinarian to the wicked; she has the honor of being the only female member of the Four Immortals (Tứ bất tử), the most recognizable and widely worshipped deities in Vietnamese folk belief.

The fifth folktale in the collection, “Tấm Cám,” is one of the most widely known Vietnamese traditional stories—a telling of what the European tradition knows as Cinderella that follows Tấm, a young orphan in the care of her father’s second wife, and her stepsister, Cám. The story starts off very much like more familiar versions of the tale, with the stepmother and stepsister forcing Tấm to labor tirelessly and tend to the housekeeping chores, until a local prince throws a festival to identify the woman who owns the lost slipper he’s found. But after Tấm weds the prince, there are two whole additional acts, as the wicked stepmother and stepsister scheme to have Cám take Tấm’s place as queen. In a departure from the Chinese telling, in the Vietnamese version the Buddha takes the role of Tấm’s fairy godmother, and the second act begins with the stepmother orchestrating Tấm’s death, with Tấm subsequently cycling through a series of rebirths to orchestrate her eventual vengeance. The telling included in Treasury masterfully renders Nguyễn Đổng Chi’s original adaptation into English, putting the full whimsy and adventure of the fairy tale on display for fans of either the European or Sinitic versions.

Jeet ZDũng, Tấm Cám – Tấm trảy hội (Tấm Cám – Tấm joins the festival). Artwork courtesy Major Books.

The majority of the tales collected here feature Vietnamese women, fairies, and goddesses punishing the wicked, defying lords, or putting terrible husbands in their place. Sociologists describe Vietnamese society as originally matrifocal—women were the heads of households, owned and inherited property, served as political and military leaders—with patriarchy imposed through Chinese colonialism and Confucianism. Though the thousand-year Chinese domination reordered the public sphere to give an appearance of patriarchy, the matrifocal structure persists in the domestic sphere to this day: Property rights typically pass down through maternal lines, as women are “keepers of the treasure chest” (tay hòm chìa khoá) and managers of a household’s finances. Traditionally, men are not even permitted to keep their own money, receiving only a small allowance at the matriarch’s discretion. Several of the folktales in Treasury are morality fables justifying why men are not to be trusted to manage a household’s finances, most humorously in the seventh and eighth stories, “A Wise Wife’s Teaching of Her Idiot Husband” and “Madame Dupe.” In both, the husbands are debaucherous or dim-witted and quickly lose their family fortunes—the former to gambling addiction, the latter to a beautiful woman’s witty scam—forcing their brilliant and capable wives to win it back. Along the way, moral values rooted in Vietnam’s Buddhist and Daoist backdrop are exalted in the female characters, such as filial piety and generosity to the sangha. In Confucianism, a dignified woman is expected to observe the “three submissions”: submission to her father before marriage, to her husband after marriage, and to her son after she is widowed. Folktales like “A Wise Wife’s Teaching of Her Idiot Husband,” “Madame Dupe,” and several others in Treasury subvert this imported moral virtue to emphasize one esteemed in Vietnamese social order, distinguishing Vietnam from the rest of the Sinosphere: An orderly home, in traditional Vietnamese thought, is one where husbands defer to their wives and entrust the well-being of their families to their wives’ wisdom. 

One word of necessary caution is that the book assumes cultural knowledge that readers without personal connections to Vietnamese culture are unlikely to possess—the translation does not provide any context for who the Hung kings are, for instance, and much of Vietnamese culture is taken for granted. However, the folktales can provide novelty and contrast to Western fairy tale traditions, and offer teachings in Buddhist moral values for parents who might want to provide their children with some degree of immersion in Buddhist cultural frameworks, particularly in convert households. 

For those of us who grew up Vietnamese American, the book fulfills a different, deeper kind of need. When I speak to other Vietnamese Americans around my age—those of us who experienced the United States of the ’80s, ’90s, and early ’00s—I find that many of us have gone through the same emotional arcs in relation to our Vietnamese identity: in our adolescence, shame that led to rejection; in our young adulthoods, grief over realizing how much of ourselves we felt we had to suppress in order to assimilate; and now, as many of us enter our middle age, a deep longing to rebuild and nurture our connections to our heritage and our ancestors, a galvanized sense of urgency to ensure the next generation never has to feel that in order to truly be American, they must become alienated from their cultural heritage. This translation of Nguyễn Đổng Chi’s Treasury of Vietnamese Folk Tales is a precious gem toward this end. I hope every Vietnamese family raising their children in the English-speaking world will share these stories with their young ones, the stories our people have been passing down for hundreds—sometimes thousands—of years. In the simple and joyous act of reading a fairy tale with our young ones, we honor and respect our ancestors, and dedicate our merit to them.

items.articleBody:
Steven Kotler is a bestselling author and the executive director of the Flow Research Collective, where he studies the science of peak performance.

Public Release: Oct 27. 
Members have access now.
Join us.

Most of us have felt it. Hours disappear, everything else fades away, and the work seems to do itself. But what’s actually happening in those moments, and can you make them happen on purpose?

Kotler has spent decades studying flow, and he makes the case that it’s far more trainable than most people think. We talk about what brings it on, how hard a task should be before it pulls you in, and why the hobby you gave up as an adult might matter more than you realize.

We also get into what frustration is really telling you when you’re learning, how play compares with practice, how to focus on work you’d rather not be doing, and how to think clearly when there’s more information than ever and fewer people checking it.

Coming Soon: YouTube | Spotify | Apple Podcasts | Transcript

+ Members get the longer, extended version of this conversation, with additional content not included in the public release. Learn more: https://fs.blog/membership/

items.articleBody:
Die Ergebnisse einer globalen Umfrage zum Vertrauen in Wissenschaft, Angriff von KI-Agenten auf Wikipedia und welche Pressemitteilungen von Hochschulen durch Medien aufgegriffen werden. Das Wisskomm-Update gibt alle 14 Tage einen Überblick über aktuelle Themen, Debatten und Trends.

Was gibt’s Neues?

Vertrauen in Wissenschaft sinkt weltweit

Seit einem Peak in der Corona-Pandemie sinkt das Vertrauen in Wissenschaft. Das ergab eine globale Umfrage der gemeinnützigen Organisation Wellcome Trust Global Monitor in 140 Ländern mit fast 140.000 Teilnehmenden. Bisher gab es drei dieser Umfragen, in den Jahren 2018, 2020 und 2025. 

In diesem Zeitraum ist der Anteil der Befragten, die zumindest ein wenig Vertrauen in Wissenschaft haben von 80 auf 72 Prozent gesunken. Gleichzeitig stieg der Anteil derer, die nur wenig Vertrauen haben, von 13 auf 19 Prozent. Dabei sind die Unterschiede zwischen den Ländern groß. In Deutschland geben 93 Prozent an „ein wenig“ oder „großes Vertrauen“ in Wissenschaft zu haben. In den USA stieg das Vertrauen sogar. In Lateinamerika und in Asien hingegen ist das Vertrauen teils deutlich zurückgegangen.

Das Vertrauen in Wissenschaft sei hoch, aber fragil, schreibt Mark Henderson, Executive Director bei Wellcome Trust bei Linkedin. Menschen vertrauten Wissenschaft eher, wenn sie das Gefühl hätten, von ihr zu profitieren. 

Und Vertrauen hängt stark von Wohlstand, Bildung und sozialer Ungleichheit ab, zeigt der Bericht. Auch in Ländern wie den USA, Deutschland und Großbritannien, wo das Vertrauen sehr hoch ist, gäbe es große Unterschiede zwischen den Befragtengruppen. 

„Soziale Ungleichheit geht mit geringerem Vertrauen in Wissenschaft einher“, sagt Rainer Bromme bei Table Media. Menschen, die finanziell besser aufgestellt und höher gebildet sind, vertrauen eher Wissenschaft und Institutionen. 

Die Ergebnisse spiegeln noch keine Krise wider, sagt John-Arne Røttingen, Direktor des Wellcome Trust. Das Vertrauen in die Wissenschaft stehe aber unter Druck. Die hohen Werte aus den Pandemie Jahren zu halten, sei nicht gelungen. 

Angriff von KI-Agenten auf Wikipedia

 „Als gemeinwohlorientierter Anbieter einiger der größten und am meisten genutzten offenen Wissensplattformen der Welt sind wir tief besorgt über die Auswirkungen ‚abtrünniger‘ KI-Agenten auf Plattformen wie unserer“, mit diesen Worten reagiert Selena Deckelmann, Chief Product and Technology Officer bei der Wikimedia Foundation in einem Blogbeitrag auf die jüngsten Angriffe durch KI-Agenten von OpenAI. 

Die Agenten hätten Änderungen an Wikipedia-Einträgen vorgenommen, erfolglos ein von Wikipedia entwickeltes Notiz-Tool angegriffen und die IT-Infrastruktur mit einer hohen Zahl an Abrufen belastet. Dies sei aus einer von Wikimedia selbst durchgeführten Untersuchung hervorgegangen. Wikipedia dient als wichtiger Datensatz für die Entwicklung großer Sprachmodelle. Wikipedia sei aber von und für Menschen gemacht, betont die Wikimedia Foundation.

„Das offene Web ist ein öffentliches Gut. Wir sollten nicht zulassen, dass dieses Verhalten zur „neuen Normalität“ für die Personen oder Organisationen wird, die es aufrechterhalten, schreibt Deckelmann. KI-Unternehmen täten nicht genug, um ihre Systeme zu sichern und die Öffentlichkeit zu schützen. Die verursachten Schäden müssten bisher die Betroffenen tragen. Der gesetzliche Schutz vor der Ausbeutung durch KI-Agenten müsse gesetzlich gestärkt werden. Nötig wären „Melde- und Informationspflichten, die die Betreiber von KI-Systemen zur Verantwortung ziehen“. 

Unterschiedliche Vorstellungen über Wissenschaftsfreiheit in Deutschland

In der Lunchtalk-Reihe “Wissenschaftsbarometer im Gespräch” diskutierten Benedikt Fecher, Geschäftsführer von Wissenschaft im Dialog* und Justus Henke vom Institut für Hochschulforschung an der Martin-Luther-Universtität Halle-Wittenberg Fragen rund um Wissenschaftsfreiheit und Widerstandsfähigkeit des Wissenschaftssystems sowie die Rolle von Wissenschaftskommunikation.

Ausgangspunkt für das Gespräch bildeten Befragungsdaten zur Wissenschaftsfreiheit; laut Wissenschaftsbarometer* bewerten 48 Prozent der Bevölkerung diese als positiv, wohingegen Hochschulleitungen sie mit 76 Prozent und Forschende mit rund 80 Prozent (Angaben laut Hochschulbarometer) deutlich positiver bewerten.

Es brauche institutionelle Antworten auf Angriffe gegen Forschende, hieß es im Gespräch. Schutzkonzepte und Unterstützung durch Hochschulen seien wichtig, damit Einschüchterung nicht zum Rückzug aus öffentlichen Debatten führe. Zudem wurde eine stärkere Spezialisierung auf Politikberatung und eine strategische Zusammenarbeit zwischen Hochschulen und ihren Verbünden, insbesondere auf Landesebene, diskutiert. 

Mit Blick auf die strategische Weiterentwicklung des Wissenschaftssystems verdeutlicht das Gespräch, dass ein resilientes Wissenschaftssystem mehr leisten muss, als Angriffe abzuwehren. Henke plädierte für einen vorausschauenden Ansatz, in dem Wissenschaft und Wissenschaftskommunikation eigene Themen setzen, Reformideen entwickeln und tragfähige Beziehungen aufbauen. 

Und sonst?

Der Hochschulwettbewerb im Wissenschaftsjahr 2027 – Raumfahrt* ist gestartet. Gesucht werden kreative Kommunikationsideen, die Forschung mit Bezug zur Raumfahrt lebendig und zugänglich machen. Bewerben können sich Wissenschaftler*innen am Beginn ihrer wissenschaftlichen Karriere, die allein oder gemeinsam eine Kommunikationsidee entwickeln, mit der sie ihre Forschung auf anschauliche Weise vermitteln. Eine Jury wählt aus allen Einreichungen zehn Projektideen aus, die mit jeweils 10.000 Euro Preisgeld umgesetzt werden können. Mehr Infos zur Bewerbung gibt es hier. 

Investigativjournalist Daniel Drepper startet mit Otter News eine eigene Redaktion für Umwelt- und Klimathemen. Das neue Medium soll investigative Recherche mit einer stärker öffentlichen Arbeitsweise verbinden.

Gemeinsam forschen, gestalten und Wissen teilen: Die PartWiss-Konferenzen* 2027, 2028 und 2029 werden in Mittweida, Hamburg und München zusammen mit der TU Chemnitz ausgerichtet. Insgesamt wurden 17 Bewerbungen eingereicht, eine Auswahlkommission entschied sich nach einer intensiven Beratung für die drei ausgewählten Konzepte und die damit verbundenen Ausrichtungsorte. Die Konferenzreihe wird als eine der zentralen Maßnahmen der Partizipationsstrategie Forschung vom Bundesministerium für Forschung, Technologie und Raumfahrt (BMFTR) gefördert. 

Die Preisträger*innen des Fast Forward Science Wettbewerbs* stehen fest. Aus 168 eingereichten Beiträgen wählten die Fachjurys die besten Videos und Audiobeiträge aus. Insgesamt wurden Preisgelder in Höhe von 9.000 Euro sowie professionelle Weiterbildungsangebote als Preise vergeben. Die Preisverleihung fand am 17.Oktober 2026 in der Kulturfabrik in Berlin statt. Alle Preisträger*innen und Beiträge gibt es hier zum Nachlesen. 

 
 

 
 

 

 

 
Sieh dir diesen Beitrag auf Instagram an

 

 

 

 

 

 

 

 

 

 
 

 

Ein Beitrag geteilt von Fast Forward Science (@fastforwardscience)

Und die Forschung?

Wie ein Naturkundemuseum mit komplexen Nachhaltigkeitsthemen umgeht, haben Lena Theiler vom ISOE Institut für sozial-ökologische Forschung und Simone Rödder vom Leibniz-Institut zur Analyse des Biodiversitätswandels untersucht. Am Beispiel des Senckenberg Naturmuseums in Frankfurt am Main zeigen sie, dass sich das Museumspersonal auf verschiedene Kommunikationsmodelle stützt. Auf Wissenstransfer ausgerichtete, dialogorientierte und partizipative Formate werden eingesetzt, um komplexen, kontroversen und durch Unsicherheit und Dringlichkeit geprägten Nachhaltigkeitsproblemen zu begegnen. Die Mitarbeitenden begegnen verschiedenen kommunikativen Herausforderungen – etwa, trotz schwieriger Themen den Charakter eines Freizeitangebots aufrechtzuerhalten und moralisierende Haltungen zu vermeiden. 

Welche Pressemitteilungen von Hochschulen werden durch Medien aufgegriffen? Das haben Michelle ten Dam, Nieske Vergunst und Mark Bos von der Utrecht University am Beispiel ihrer eigenen Hochschule untersucht. Ihre Inhaltsanalyse von 84 Pressemitteilungen der naturwissenschaftlichen Fakultät zeigt, dass es bei neuen, gesellschaftlich relevanten und negativen Themen besonders viele Webseiten-Interaktion gibt. Für die mediale Resonanz waren Aspekte wie damit verknüpfte Ängste sowie die wissenschaftliche Relevanz wichtiger. 

Die Instagram-Auftritte von drei prominente Astronautinnen haben Karen Shalev und Shannon Pappas von der University of Connecticut zusammen mit Jocelyn Steinke von der University of Wisconsin-Madison untersucht. Sie zeigen, wie die Wissenschafts-Influencerinnen durch die Auswahl von Themen und Fragestellungen, das Framing von Botschaften und den Einsatz spezifischer Kommunikations-Taktiken eine eigene Marke aufbauen und versuchen, ihre Reichweite zu vergrößern.
